answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is the elementary $N$ MOS cascode
gain stage with active load $I_{1}$. Often
realized with $I_{1}=P$ MOS current mirror.

$$M_{1}= {\rm common\; source\; driver} \qquad 
  M_{2}= {\rm common\; gate\; cascode} \qquad 
  I_{1}\approx AC\; {\rm open}$$

Let

$$g_{m} = \mu C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}V_{ov}\;\;\;,\;\;\; r_{o}= \frac{1}{\lambda I_{D}}\approx \frac{1}{g_{ds}}$$
$$V_{ov}=V_{GS}-V_{TH} \;\;\;,\;\;\; A_{i}=g_{m}r_{o}={\rm intrinsic\; gain} \approx 20-100$$

$W/L_{1},W/L_{2}$ carry same $DC$ current

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}=I_{D}$$

on bias $V_{b1}= {\rm const}$ so $v_{b1}=0$ for $AC$.

> In small signal $M_{1}$ is a $V \to I$ converter
> $M_{2}$ is a current buffer that presents a
> low $Z$ to the drain of $M_{1}$ and a high $Z$
> to the output and transfers the $AC$ current
> $g_{m1}v_{in}$ essentially unattenuated to $R_{out}$.

### 1. DC conditions - stay in saturation

Normal $N$ MOS, bulk = GND. Then $M_{1}$ has $V_{SB1}=0$
$M_{2}$ has $V_{SB2}=V_{X}>0$ body effect $\ne 0$
unless triple well.

$$S_{AT} : V_{DS}\ge V_{GS}-V_{TH} = V_{ov}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
M_{1}: V_{X} &\ge V_{ov1} \\
M_{2}: V_{out}-V_{X} &\ge V_{b1}-V_{X}-V_{TH2} \\
V_{out} &\ge V_{b1}-V_{TH2}
\end{aligned}$$

so

$$V_{out,min}\approx V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}$$

$$V_{X}=V_{b1}-V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_{TH2}-V_{ov2}$$

For maximum swing $V_{b1}$ is chosen

$$V_{b1}\approx V_{TH2}+2V_{ov}$$

then $V_{X}\approx V_{ov1}$ edge of saturation.

Upwards

$$V_{out,max}=V_{DD}-V_{ov,I1}$$

$V_{ov,I1}$ is saturation voltage of the $P$MOS
that implements $I_{1}$. With ideal $I_{1}$, $V_{out,max}\to V_{DD}$.

Large signal class A: $i_{d1}=I_{1}+g_{m1}v_{in}+...$
must stay $0< i_{d1} < 2I_{1}$ before one device
leaves saturation, clips.

### 2. Small signal model

```
         vout
          o
          |
         roI
          |
     D2 o-+--- ro2 ---+--X S2
          |          |      |
         gm2*vgs2  gmb2*vbs2 |
          |          |      |
         GND(vb1)    +------+
                    X o
                    |
               D1 o-+--- ro1 --- GND
                    |
                   gm1*vin
                    |
                   GND
```

$ v_{gs2}= -v_{x}\;,\;v_{bs2}= -v_{x}\;,\;v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{x}$

### 3. Impedance levels

Impedance looking into source of $CG$ with load $r_{o2}$ to
drain:

$$R_{x}= \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}$$

Capacitance at $X$ sees that low $R$. Hence

$$C_{X}\approx C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{gd1}+C_{db1}+C_{db2?}$$

Impedance looking into drain of cascode with
source degeneration $r_{o1}$:

Put $v_{in}=0$, apply $v_{t}$ at $v_{out}$, measure $i_{t}$.

$$\;R_{o,cas}= r_{o2}+ \left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]r_{o1}\;$$

$$\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}\;\; {\rm for}\;(g_{m}r_{o})\gg 1$$

If bulk tied to source for $M_{2}$, $g_{mb2}=0$ :

$$R_{o,cas}\approx g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

This is $A_{i}$ times larger than a simple $CS$
stage $r_{o1}$.

Total output resistance with load current source
$r_{oI}=r_{o1,P}$ finite:

$$R_{out}=R_{o,cas}\parallel r_{oI}$$

Ideal $I_{1}$ : $r_{oI}\to\infty$, $R_{out}=R_{o,cas}$.

Input resistance at gate $M_{1}$:

$$R_{in}\approx \infty \;{\rm capacitive}\; C_{in}=C_{gs1}+C_{gd1}(1-A_{vX})$$

but $A_{vX}=v_{x}/v_{in}$ is small:

$$A_{vX}= -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}\approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} \approx -1$$

so Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ is $\sim 2\times$
not $1+|A_{v}|\gg 1$. This is the bandwidth advantage
of cascode.

### 4. Voltage gain

KCL at $X$ and at output gives well known result

$$i_{d}\approx g_{m1}v_{in}$$

$$v_{out}= -i_{d}\,R_{out}$$

$$\;A_{v}= \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -g_{m1}R_{out}\;$$

Explicitly

$$A_{v}= -g_{m1}\left\{\left[r_{o2}+(1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2})r_{o1}\right]\parallel r_{oI}\right\}$$

Ideal:

$$A_{v,ideal}\approx -g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2} \approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

$$|A_{v}|\approx A_{i1}\cdot A_{i2}\approx 500-10\,000\;\; 54-80{\rm dB}$$

vs simple $CS$ with same load $A_{v0}=-g_{m1}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{oI})\approx -A_{i}/2$.

In other words cascode multiplies the gain by
$g_{m2}r_{o2}$.

If $r_{oI}$ dominates, e.g. $r_{oI}\ll R_{o,cas}$ :

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}r_{oI}$$

no benefit. So $I_{1}$ must be cascoded itself to keep
$r_{oI}\sim R_{o,cas}$ . Then telescopic / double cascode
$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}(g_{m}r_{o}^{2}\parallel g_{m}r_{o}^{2})$.

With body effect gain is divided by $1+\eta$ where
$\eta = g_{mb}/g_{m}\approx 0.2-0.3$.

### 5. Frequency response

Two main poles:

* Dominant pole at high $Z$ output:

$$\omega_{p,out}= \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{L}}\;,\; C_{L}=C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{oI}+C_{load}$$

* Non dominant pole at low $Z$ node $X$:

$$\omega_{pX}\approx \frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}{C_{X}}$$

Because $g_{m2}/C_{X}\gg 1/R_{out}C_{L}$ the cascode is
essentially single-pole. Condition for good settling:

$$\omega_{pX}> 3\omega_{u}\approx 3g_{m1}/C_{L}$$

Transfer function $\approx$

$$A_{v}(s)\approx \frac{A_{v0}}{(1+s/\omega_{p,out})(1+s/\omega_{pX})}$$

plus RHP zero $\approx g_{m2}/C_{gd2}$ very high.

Reverse isolation $S_{12}\approx 0$ because $CG$
shields $M_{1}$ from $v_{out}$ variations. $V_{DS1}$ almost
constant $\to$ suppress channel length modulation on $M_{1}$.

### 6. What it is good / bad for

Pro: very high DC gain without extra stage, high
output $R$, wide bandwidth for given gain, low
Miller, good PSRR, good isolation.

Con: limited output swing $\approx V_{DD}-(V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}+V_{ovI})$,
needs extra bias $V_{b1}$, headroom stacking, not
suitable for low $V_{DD}$ without folding, body
effect degrades $R_{out}$ if $n$-well not available.

Used as building block of telescopic op-amp,
folded-cascode op-amp, $LNA$ load, current mirror
with $> r_{o}$ accuracy.

> With $V_{b1}$ AC ground and $I_{1}$ ideal the circuit
> is a single-stage high-gain transconductance amplifier
> $G_{m}=g_{m1}$ loaded by $R_{out}\approx g_{m}r_{o}^{2}$.

If you have a numerical $W/L$, $I_{1}$ and process
$g_{m},r_{o}$ the formulas above give quantitative
$A_{v}, R_{out}, \omega_{p}$ directly.

answers.question: Is the circuit shown in the figure a cascode structure?

answer.text:
With the normal abuse of language {\it yes}
it is what every text book calls the {\it telescopic}
{\rm CS}+{\rm CG} {\rm stack} and with the symbols as
they are {\it normally} drawn it is what is normally called
the {\rm NMOS} - or with $V_{DD}\leftrightarrow 0$ the
{\rm PMOS} - telescopic cascode.  Pedantically as drawn
in Fig.1 it is not.

{\it Topologically} $M_{1}$ is the ordinary transconductor,
{\rm C}{\rm S}, stage

$$v_{g1}=v_{in}\;\;\;v_{s1}=0$$

and $M_{2}$ is the ordinary current buffer, {\rm C}{\rm G},
stage

$$v_{g2}=V_{b1}={\rm ac}\;0\;\;v_{s2}=v_{d1}$$

stacked on top of it on the same {\rm dc} current

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{R_{D}}$$

and loaded conventionally in $R_{D}$ to $V_{DD}$,
Fig.2.14 in Razavi.  In small signal

$$R_{o}\approx R_{D}\parallel R_{cas}$$
$$R_{cas}= r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}
\approx g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\tag{1}$$
for $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$, $r_{o1}\ne r_{o2}$ in
general, with $r_{o2}$ the $r_{o}$ of the cascode
device and $r_{o1}$ the $r_{o}$ of the ${\rm CS}$
device, so that for the ordinary $R_{D}\gg R_{cas}$
or $R_{D}\sim R_{cas}$

$$A_{v}={{v_{out}}\over {v_{in}}}\approx -g_{m1}R_{o}
\approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\parallel R_{D} \tag{2}$$

with the usual cascode advantages: $R_{o}$ $\times
g_{m}r_{o}$ over the simple ${\rm CS}$ stage,
Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ divided by
$\approx g_{m2}r_{o2}$, greatly improved reverse
isolation, {\it etc.}  Any ${\rm CS}\rightarrow {\rm
CG}$ stack on the same bias current is normally
referred to, loosely, as {\it a cascode}.

In the strict single well, single type, sense the
circuit as {\it literally} drawn is a
complementary, {\rm CMOS}, or {\it pseudo},
{\it folded} cascode.  With the conventional
${\rm NMOS}\;{\rm in}\; \to {\rm channel}$,
${\rm PMOS}\;{\rm out}\; \leftarrow {\rm channel}$
arrow convention the arrow is on the source.
$M_{2}$ is drawn conventionally with the source,
the arrow, at the low, cascode, node.
$M_{1}$ is drawn upside down, or as a ${\rm PMOS}$,
with the source, the arrow, at the {\it high},
cascode, node, its drain at ground.  The two
sources are commoned at the cascode node and the
two drains are at $0$ and at $V_{out}$.  The
conventional current can go ${\rm D}\to {\rm S}$
in $M_{2}$ and ${\rm S}\to {\rm D}$ in $M_{1}$

$$V_{DD}\to R_{D}\to {\rm D_{2}}\to {\rm S_{2}}
\to {\rm S_{1}}\to {\rm D_{1}}\to 0$$

so it does function, with $M_{1}$ a ${\rm PMOS}$
${\rm CS}$ transconductor and $M_{2}$ an ${\rm NMOS}$
${\rm CG}$ buffer, as a ${\rm PMOS}$ input
complementary cascode inverter with resistive load.
It has (1)-(2) {\it mutatis mutandis} but it is not
the conventional $n{\rm MOS}+n{\rm MOS}$ or
$p{\rm MOS}+p{\rm MOS}$ cascode with
${\rm D_{1}}={\rm S_{2}}$, ${\rm S_{1}}=0$,
${\rm B_{1}}=0$, ${\rm B_{2}}=0$ or
${\rm B_{2}}={\rm S_{2}}$, Fig.1b.  Put $M_{1}$
the right way up, arrow, source, at ground,
drain at the cascode node, $B_{1}=0$, $B_{2}=S_{2}$
in twin well, and it is the text book $n{\rm MOS}$
or $p{\rm MOS}$ telescopic cascode {\it sensu
strictu.}

> {\it Remark:} In normal ${\rm CMOS}$ the $n{\rm MOS}$
> $B=p{\rm -sub}=0$ so $M_{2}$ with $B_{2}=S_{2}\ne 0$
> needs a triple well.  $M_{1}$ as drawn with
> $B_{1}=D_{1}$ has $V_{BS1}\ne 0$ and suffers full
> body effect.  Interchanging nominal source and drain
> on a ${\rm MOS}$ transistor is of course immaterial
> to first order - the more negative, $n{\rm MOS}$,
> or more positive, $p{\rm MOS}$, terminal {\it is}
> the source - so the circuit will normally be
> re-drawn with $M_{1}$ source at ground.

In loose parlance it is universally called
{\it the cascode}.

It is normally {\it illustrated} as

> telescopic {\rm ``}cascode{\rm ''} - a $CS$ device

in the form

$${\rm V}_{DD}-R_{D}-D_{2}\equiv M_{2}\equiv
S_{2}-D_{1}\equiv M_{1}\equiv S_{1}-{\rm GND}\tag*{$R_{D}\ne \infty$}$$

with

R_{o}&\approx \left[1+g_{m2}r_{o2}\right]r_{o1}+r_{o2}\cr
A_{v}&\approx -g_{m1}\left[R_{D}\parallel R_{o}\right]

and normally quoted as the textbook {\it cascode}

  arrowed, terminal, body $\equiv S_{1}$,

answer.text:
In the loose textbook sense {\it yes}
in the strict $3/4\,T$ symbol sense {\it no}.
It is the block diagram that every body calls

$${\rm CS}\left[M_{1}\right]+ {\rm CG}\left[M_{2}\right]$$

{\it telescopic} {\it cascode} with $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$,
fig. $3.12$ in Razavi.

> {\it NB:} As it is normally drawn in a CMOS technology
> the two devices are the same polarity.

With the conventional $4\,T$ symbology the NMOS
conventional cascode is

```
            VDD
             |
             RD
             |
             D   G=Vb1
            M2  CG 
             S
             D
            M1  CS G=Vin
             S
            GND n bulk GND
```

i. e. the {\it drain} of the $g_{m}$ device $M_{1}$ goes to
the {\it source} of the $g_{m}r_{o}$ device $M_{2}$.
Put $M_{2}$ in saturation by $V_{b1}$ and you get

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}\left[R_{D}\parallel R_{o}\right]$$

$$R_{o}\approx g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}\;\;,
\;\;r_{o}^{-1}=g_{ds}$$

in the conventional small signal reduction of the
Miller effect, $C_{gd1}$ sees $1/g_{m2}$ at the
intermediate node, etc.

Taken {\it literally} as you have drawn it with the
$3\,T$ ${\rm arrow}={\rm source}$ convention you
have drawn a complementary or pseudo cascode, Fig.1b

* $M_{2}$: arrow at the lower terminal $=$ source
at the interstage node $V_{X}$ to $M_{1}$, conventional
NMOS CG, $D=V_{out}$.

* $M_{1}$: arrow at the {\it upper} terminal $=$ source
at $V_{X}$, drain $=$ {\sc gnd}.  I. e. with the normal
$\{{\rm arrow\;in}=n\}\{{\rm arrow\;out}=p\}$ convention
a $p$ device or, if you want to keep it $n$, the device
is upside down, {\it source follower} $-$ {\it common
gate} source to source connection, not drain to source.

In conventional CMOS you would call that a
CMOS inverter stack, a complementary cascode,
a source to source pseudo cascode, {\it etc.},
normally unusable as a linear amplifier with the
bulks strapped to $V_{X}$ because at least one
bulk diode is forward biased and you get full body
effect on $M_{1}$.  Turn $M_{1}$ upside down,
put the arrow on the {\sc gnd} side, body to {\sc gnd},
$M_{2}$ body to {\sc gnd}, both $n$ - or both $p$
to $V_{DD}$ - and you get the conventional integrated
cascode normally meant.  In that normal form it is
properly called the common source cascode.

> {\it Remark:} In many text books the bulk connection
> is simply omitted and the circuit of Fig.1 is loosely,
> and with that omission correctly, called {\it the}
> cascode.

With the bulk correctly shown the NMOS cascode is

* $M_{1}$ $n$, $S=$ {\sc gnd}, $D=V_{X}$, $B=${\sc gnd}
* $M_{2}$ $n$, $S=V_{X}$, $D=V_{out}$, $B=${\sc gnd}

and the PMOS cascode is the dual.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
In a simple inverting amplifier the Miller effect is large because the feedback capacitance sees the full voltage gain. The `cascode` breaks that condition.

### 1. Recall: Miller Multiplication

For any impedance $Z_f$ connected between input and output of an inverting amplifier with voltage gain $A_v = V_o/V_i < 0$:

By Miller's Theorem, seen from the input it looks like:

$$Z_{in,Miller} = \frac{Z_f}{1-A_v} \approx \frac{Z_f}{|A_v|}$$

For a capacitance $C_f$:

$$C_{M} = C_f(1-A_v) = C_f(1+|A_v|)$$

In a Common Source/Emitter amplifier $C_f = C_{gd} / C_{\mu}$ between gate/base and drain/collector.

With a normal CS stage:

$$A_v = -g_m R_D' = -g_m (r_o || R_D)$$

typically $-20$ to $-100$.

So

$$C_{in} \approx C_{gs} + C_{gd}(1+g_m R_D')$$

If $C_{gd}= 50fF$ and $|A_v|=50$, you see $2.5pF$ at the input. That with source resistance $R_{sig}$ creates a low frequency input pole:

$$f_{p,in} \approx \frac{1}{2\pi R_{sig} C_{in}}$$

This dominates and limits bandwidth. It also causes pole splitting - input pole moves down, output pole moves up.

The Miller effect requires **large voltage swing across $C_f$**.

### 2. Cascode Topology

A cascode is a Common Source - Common Gate stack, or Common Emitter - Common Base stack:

```
           Vout
            |
           (D2)
      G2 ___|___ AC ground
            |
           (S2/D1)  <- intermediate node X, low swing
            |
           (D1)
            |
           (S1)
            |
           Vin -> G1
```

$M1$ is the input CS device, $M2$ is the CG device with its gate at AC ground. The load $R_D$ is now at the drain of $M2$, not $M1$.

Total gain is still high:

$$A_{v,tot} = -g_{m1} (g_{m2} r_{o2} r_{o1} || R_D) \approx -g_{m1} R_{out}$$

But $C_{gd1}$ does **not** see $A_{v,tot}$. It only sees the *local* gain of stage 1, $A_{v1}=V_x/V_i$.

### 3. Why $A_{v1}$ is $\approx -1$

The load seen by $M1$ is not $R_D$, but the input impedance of a common-gate stage looking into its source:

$$R_{in2} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} || r_{o2} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

This is very low, $\sim 100-1000$ ohms.

Therefore:

$$A_{v1} = -g_{m1} (r_{o1} || R_{in2}) \approx -g_{m1} \cdot \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

If $M1$ and $M2$ have similar bias current and size, $g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$ so:

$$A_{v1} \approx -1$$

Now apply Miller to $C_{gd1}$:

$$C_{M1} = C_{gd1}(1 - A_{v1}) \approx C_{gd1}(1 - (-1)) = 2 C_{gd1}$$

Instead of $50 \times C_{gd1}$, you get $2 \times C_{gd1}$. The input capacitance becomes:

$$C_{in,cascode} \approx C_{gs1} + 2C_{gd1} << C_{gs1} + (1+g_m R_D)C_{gd1}$$

> Physically: The drain of $M1$, node X, is held almost constant in voltage by the low impedance source of $M2$ acting as a current buffer. Since $V_x$ hardly moves, there is almost no voltage swing across $C_{gd1}$, so almost no displacement current is pulled through it from the input. No large Miller current = no large Miller capacitance.

What about $C_{gd2}$ of the cascode device?

It is connected between $V_{out}$ and AC ground (gate of $M2$). Both terminals: one is ground, so $K = V_o/V_{g2}=0$. There is **no Miller multiplication at all**.

$$C_{gd2} \text{ appears un-multiplied at the output node as } C_{gd2}$$

It just adds to the total output capacitance $C_L'$ along with $C_{db}$.

### 4. Consequence

The cascode breaks the gain-bandwidth trade-off of a single stage:

* Single stage: High gain $\implies$ large Miller $\implies$ low $f_{p,in}$
* Cascode: High total gain $A_{v,tot}$ kept, but input Miller factor is decoupled from total gain and kept $\sim 2$.

The dominant pole is now usually at the output:

$$f_{p,out} \approx \frac{1}{2\pi R_{out} C_{out}}$$

And a second non-dominant pole appears at the intermediate node X:

$$f_{p,x} \approx \frac{g_{m2}}{2\pi (C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{gd1}+C_{db1})}$$

which is very high because $g_{m2}$ is large and capacitance is small. The input pole is pushed up by ~ $|A_v|/2$ times.

This gives much wider bandwidth, better reverse isolation $S_{12}$, and better stability. This is why almost all wideband, RF, and high-gain op-amp stages use a cascode/telescopic/folded-cascode.

In short: **The Miller effect needs inverting voltage gain across the capacitor. The cascode gives the input device a low-impedance load so it has $\sim$ unity gain, so its $C_{gd}$ is not multiplied, while the high-gain device has no feedback capacitor to the input.**

Its wording that the intermediate node hardly moves and Cgd is nearly unmultiplied overstates the reduction, but the answer gives the correct factor; the golden solution treats this overstatement as a minor flaw.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
In a Common Source/Emitter `CS/CE` the `Cgd/Cbc` is a ***Miller* capacitance** - not less pronounced, it is multiplied.

By Miller's theorem a capacitor $C$ connected between input and output

$$Z_M = \frac{Z}{1-A_v}$$

For a capacitor $C_{gd}$ between gate and drain with voltage gain $A_v = v_d/v_g <0$:

$$C_{M,input} = C_{gd}(1-A_v) = C_{gd}(1+|A_v|)$$
$$C_{M,output} = C_{gd}(1-1/A_v) \approx C_{gd}$$

In a normal CS/CE with resistive/active load $R_D$:

$$A_v = -g_m R_D \approx -g_m r_o >> 1$$

e.g. 20 to 100.

$$C_{in} = C_{gs} + C_{gd}(1+g_m R_D)$$

You may have $2-100\times C_{gd}$ at the input. That large $C_{in}$ with the source resistance $R_{sig}$ creates the dominant low frequency pole:

$$\omega_{p,in} \approx \frac{1}{R_{sig} C_{in}}$$

and kills bandwidth. This is the Miller effect. It requires two things: 1) A capacitor bridging input-output and 2) Large *inverting* voltage gain across it.

A cascode destroys 2.

### Cascode = CS driving CG

```
Vout
 |
 D2
 G2 --- AC GND
 S2 --- D1  <- internal node X
        G1 --- Vin
        S1 --- GND
```

$Q1/M1$ is CS, $Q2/M2$ is Common Gate/Base with gate/base at AC ground.

Consider the Miller capacitance that matters: $C_{gd1}$ of the *input* device $M1$, between $Vin = v_{g1}$ and $v_x = v_{d1} = v_{s2}$.

Its Miller multiplication is $1-A_{v1}$ where

$$A_{v1} = \frac{v_x}{v_{g1}}$$

is the gain of $M1$ *alone*, not the gain of the whole amplifier.

What load does $M1$ see? Not $R_D$, but the impedance looking into the source of a CG stage with gate grounded.

$$R_{in2} = \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}} \parallel r_{o2} // R_D \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

if $R_D$ is not extremely large. On the order of $50-500\ \Omega$, not $k\Omega$.

So

$$A_{v1} = -g_{m1} \cdot (r_{o1} \parallel R_{in2}) \approx -g_{m1} \frac{1}{g_{m2}} \approx -1$$

if $g_{m1} \approx g_{m2}$.

More exactly with $r_o$:

$$A_{v1} \approx \frac{-g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} \approx -0.5 \text{ to } -2$$

Therefore

$$C_{M1} = C_{gd1}(1-A_{v1}) \approx C_{gd1}(1-(-1)) = 2 C_{gd1}$$

Instead of $C_{gd1}(1+g_m R_D) \approx 50-100\,C_{gd1}$.

The input capacitance becomes:

$$C_{in,cascode} \approx C_{gs1} + 2 C_{gd1} \ll C_{gs1}+g_m R_D C_{gd1} = C_{in,CS}$$

Reduction by factor $\approx g_m R_D /2$.

Intuitively: Miller multiplication is charge. $i = C\, d(V_g-V_d)/dt$. If $V_d$ moves opposite and much more than $V_g$, you need much more charge from the input to charge $C_{gd}$. In a CS, $V_d = -g_m R_D V_g$ swings wildly. In a cascode, node $X$ barely moves - the CG transistor holds the drain of $M1$ almost constant because its source is low impedance. Little $\Delta V$ across $C_{gd1}$, little extra current, little extra capacitance.

What about the overall gain?

$$A_{v2} = \frac{v_{out}}{v_x} \approx g_{m2} R_{out}$$

where $R_{out} \approx g_{m2} r_{o2} r_{o1} \parallel R_D$ is very high.

$$A_{v,tot} = A_{v1} \times A_{v2} \approx -g_{m1} R_{out}$$

You still get the full high gain $g_m R_{out}$, but the large gain is now developed in the CG stage where $C_{gd2}$ is connected between AC ground and output. $A_v$ for that capacitor is $0$ to output, so there is no Miller multiplication:

$$C_{gd2} \text{ sees } v_{g2}=0 \to \text{ no } (1-A_v) \text{, just } C_{gd2} \text{ to ground at output.}$$

And there is no capacitor directly bridging $Vin$ at $G1$ to $Vout$ at $D2$. The feedback path is broken. The CG device acts as an electrostatic shield.

Result: The input pole $\omega_{p,in}=1/R_{sig}C_{in}$ moves up by $10-50\times$, the so called pole-splitting of the CS disappears, bandwidth is greatly extended. This is why the cascode is often called a Miller killer.

Ideal cascode with $g_{m2} \to \infty$: $R_{in2} \to 0, A_{v1} \to 0, C_{M1} \to C_{gd1}$ - Miller effect completely eliminated. In practice $\approx 2 C_{gd1}$ remains.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the low-impedance cascode node and the roughly −1 gain across M1’s Cgd, giving about 2× rather than full-stage-gain Miller multiplication. The claim of “little ΔV across Cgd1” overstates the effect, but the answer also gives the correct practical factor, and this is only a minor flaw.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
In a single device the inverting voltage gain multiplies a feedback $C$ into a large input $C$. The cascode removes the large gain from the device that has the $C$ across it.

Recall Miller's Theorem: An impedance $Z$ bridging input and output nodes with voltage gain $A_v = V_2/V_1$ can be split into

$$Z_1 = \frac{Z}{1-A_v} \;\; \text{to ground at input}$$
$$Z_2 = \frac{Z}{1-1/A_v} \;\; \text{to ground at output}$$

For a capacitor $Z=1/sC$ this is a capacitance multiplication:

$$C_M = C(1-A_v)$$

For an inverting amplifier $A_v = -|A_v|$:

$$C_{M,in} = C(1+|A_v|)$$

$$C_{M,out} = C(1+1/|A_v|) \approx C$$

### 1. Common Source/Emitter alone

High frequency model: $C_{gd}$ or $C_{\mu}$ bridges gate/base = input and drain/collector = output. $C_{gs}$ or $C_{\pi}$ is already input to ground.

$$ C_{in} = C_{gs} + C_{gd}(1-A_v) = C_{gs} + C_{gd}(1+g_m R_D)$$

where $A_v = -g_m R_D$ is the low frequency voltage gain, typically 10 to 100.

E.g. $g_m R_D = 50 \rightarrow C_{in} = C_{gs} + 51 C_{gd}$

This huge $C_{in}$ with source resistance $R_{sig}$ creates the dominant low frequency input pole:

$$\omega_{p,in} \approx \frac{1}{R_{sig} C_{in}} = \frac{1}{R_{sig}[C_{gs}+C_{gd}(1+g_m R_D)]}$$

Bandwith is severely limited. Physically a large inverted swing at the drain pulls a large displacement current $I = C_{gd} d(V_g - V_d)/dt \approx C_{gd}(1+|A_v|) dV_g/dt$ through $C_{gd}$.

### 2. Cascode - CS driving CG, CE driving CB

```
         VDD
          |
          RD
          |
Vin -G1  D2 - Vout  High gain node
     S1--D1
     |   S2
     |   G2--- AC GND
    GND
```
Q1 is Common-Source, Q2 is Common-Gate with gate at AC ground.

Consider them separately.

**a) Q1 - The device that suffers Miller effect**

Q1 does NOT see $R_D$ as its load. It sees the input impedance looking into the source of Q2.

For a common-gate stage:

$$R_{in2} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

very low, typically 50-500 ohms.

So the voltage gain of the Q1 stage alone is:

$$A_{v1}= \frac{V_{d1}}{V_{g1}} = -g_{m1} R_{in2} = -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} \approx -1$$

if devices are sized similarly. With body effect, $\approx -0.5$ to $-1$.

Therefore Miller multiplication for $C_{gd1}$ is:

$$C_{M1} = C_{gd1}(1-A_{v1}) = C_{gd1}\left(1+\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}\right) \approx 2 C_{gd1}$$

instead of $C_{gd1}(1+g_m R_D)$.

If $g_m R_D = 50$, you have reduced the Miller capacitance from $51 C_{gd}$ to $\sim 2 C_{gd}$, a factor of 25x. The input pole moves up by the same factor:

$$\omega_{p,in,cascode} \approx \frac{1}{R_{sig}[C_{gs1}+2C_{gd1}]}$$

Physically: The drain of Q1 is pinned by the low impedance source of Q2. It cannot swing much. Therefore $V_{g1} - V_{d1} \approx V_{g1}$, there is very little extra voltage to drive current through $C_{gd1}$. The feedback is effectively killed. Q2 acts as a current buffer and voltage shield.

**b) Q2 - The device that provides the gain**

Q2 provides the large voltage gain:

$$A_{v2} = g_{m2} R_D \;\; \text{and}\;\; A_{v,tot}= A_{v1}A_{v2} \approx -g_{m1} R_D$$

So the circuit still has high overall gain.

But Q2 has no Miller effect. Its $C_{gd2}$ is between drain = output and gate = AC ground. It is just a capacitor to ground at the output, $C_{M,out}\approx C_{gd2}$. Its $C_{gs2}$ is between source = low impedance node and gate = ground. It loads the intermediate node, not the input. There is no capacitance bridging input and output of an inverting amplifier to be Miller multiplied.

> The overall gain $-g_{m1}R_D$ is split into a low-gain stage where Miller $C$ exists but not multiplied, and a high-gain stage where Miller $C$ does not exist.

That is why the triode was replaced by the tetrode/pentode and why RF amplifiers are almost always cascodes.

The bandwidth limitation is now the poles at the intermediate node $ \omega_{pX} \approx g_{m2}/C_X$ where $C_X = C_{gd1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{db1}$ and at the output $\omega_{p,out} \approx 1/R_D C_{out}$. Both are at much higher frequency than the Miller input pole of the single device, and can be made similar for maximal flat bandwidth.

In short: **Cascode does not eliminate Miller capacitance, it eliminates Miller multiplication by giving the input device a low impedance load so $1-A_{v1} \approx 2$ instead of $1+g_m R_D$.**

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the low-impedance cascode node and the roughly −1 gain across the input transistor’s Cgd, giving about 2× Miller multiplication rather than multiplication by the full stage gain. It also says the effect is reduced, not eliminated. Some wording overstates how little the node swings, but the core explanation and quantitative result are correct.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a ${\rm grounded~gate}\approx{\rm common~gate}
\approx {\rm current~buffer}$ with active load. In
most technologies

> $$M_{1}={\rm P~currents~source} \qquad M_{2}={\rm N~CG~device}$$
> $$Vb_{2}=V_{SG1,DC}\qquad Vb_{1}=V_{GS2,DC}+V_{in,DC}$$

with $M_{2}$ normally laid out with $B_{2}\equiv S_{2}\equiv V_{in}$
in the figure so that $g_{mb2}\approx 0$.
If the symbol is taken literally as $2\times {\rm P}$ the
description is the same with $p\leftrightarrow n$ and a
d.c. path $V_{DD}\to M_{1}\to M_{2}\to R_{sig}\to {\rm GND}$
through the signal source. The complementary case
$P$ on top of $N$ is the normal one. With 
$g_{di}=g_{dsi}=1/r_{oi}=\lambda _{i}I_{D}$.

{\rm DC:} in saturation long channel

$$I_{D1}= {k_{p}\over 2}{W_{1}\over L_{1}}{(V_{DD}-Vb_{2}-|V_{Tp}|)^{2}}
(1+\lambda _{p}(V_{DD}-V_{out}))$$

$$I_{D2}= {k_{n}\over 2}{W_{2}\over L_{2}}{(Vb_{1}-V_{in}-V_{Tn})^{2}}
(1+\lambda _{n}(V_{out}-V_{in}))$$

and for the series connection with no other d.c. load

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}\tag{1}$$

at the $Q$ point. So $Vb_{2}$ fixes $I_{D}$ and, with
$V_{in,DC}$ given, $Vb_{1}$ must be

$$Vb_{1}=V_{in,DC}+V_{Tn}+\sqrt{2I_{D}/k_{n}(W/L)_{2}}$$

Saturation requires

$$\eqalign{
V_{out}-V_{in} &> Vb_{1}-V_{in}-V_{Tn}=V_{ov2}\cr
V_{DD}-V_{out} &> V_{DD}-Vb_{2}-|V_{Tp}|=|V_{ov1}|}$$

i. e.

$$Vb_{1}-V_{Tn}<V_{out}<V_{DD}-|V_{ov1}|$$

so headroom is $V_{DD}>V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}+V_{in,DC}$ plus
signal swing. $V_{in,DC}$ must be low enough to keep
$M_{2}$ on: $Vb_{1}-V_{in}>V_{Tn}$ and high enough to keep
$M_{1}$ saturated. The small signal current must be
sunk/sourced by the source resistance $R_{sig}$ of the
$V_{in}$ generator. I. e. $R_{sig}$ is the d.c. path to
ground. On large signal with $V_{in}\uparrow $,

$$V_{GS2}=Vb_{1}-V_{in}\downarrow \;\;,\;I_{D2}\downarrow$$

$M_{1}$ wants to keep $I_{D1}\approx I_{B}$. $V_{out}$
must rise to reduce $I_{D1}$ through $\lambda _{p}$ and
to increase $I_{D2}$ through $\lambda _{n}$ until (1) is
again satisfied. So

$${{dV_{out}}\over {dV_{in}}}>0$$

non-inverting. Large signal:

$$V_{out}\approx V_{DD}- {\rm solution~of~}I_{D1}(V_{out})=
I_{D2}(V_{in},V_{out})$$

quasi quadratic.

{\rm Small signal:} $Vb_{1},Vb_{2}$ ac ground, $R_{L}$
ac load to ground at $V_{out}$ including $C_{L}$.

Hybrid $\pi$ for $M_{2}$: $v_{gs2}= -v_{in}$ for
$R_{sig}=0$, $v_{bs2}= -v_{in}$ with body to GND,
$0$ with body to $S$, $v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{in}$.

KCL at $V_{out}$:

$$g_{ds1}v_{out}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{in})+g_{m2}v_{gs2}
+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}=0\tag{2}$$

With $v_{gs2}=v_{bs2}=-v_{in}$ if $B\to {\rm GND}$,

$$\left(g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}\right)v_{out}=
\left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}\right)v_{in}$$

so for $R_{sig}=0$, $R_{L}=\infty $

$$A_{v}\equiv {{v_{out}}\over {v_{in}}}=
{{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}\over {g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}}
\approx {{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\over {g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}}
= \left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\right)r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}>0
\tag{3}$$

With $B_{2}=S_{2}$, $g_{mb2}=0$:

$$A_{v0}\approx g_{m2}\,r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_{L}$$

typical $20-40\,{\rm dB}$ single stage.
With finite $R_{sig}$ in series with $v_{in}$:

$$A_{v}= {{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\over {g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}}
{1\over {1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})R_{sig}}}\approx
{{r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}}\over {R_{sig}+1/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})}}$$

The familiar $g_{m}R_{D}$ form. No Miller multiplication
of $C_{gd2}$ because gate is ac ground.

{\rm Input impedance:} put $v_{x}$ on source of $M_{2}$,
ground $V_{DD}$ ac, $R_{L}$ to ground at drain.
From (2) with $v_{in}\to v_{x}$, $v_{out}=v_{d}$,

$$v_{d}=v_{x}{{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}\over {g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+G_{L}}}$$

$$i_{x}= -\left[g_{m2}(-v_{x})+g_{mb2}(-v_{x})+g_{ds2}(v_{d}-v_{x})\right]$$

$$i_{x}=v_{x}\left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}\right)
- g_{ds2}v_{d}$$

$$\eqalign{
R_{in}&={{v_{x}}\over {i_{x}}}=
{{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+G_{L}}\over 
{(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})g_{ds1}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})G_{L}+g_{ds2}G_{L}}}\cr
&\approx {1\over {g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}}{{1+G_{L}/g_{ds2}}\over 
{1+{g_{ds1}\over g_{ds2}}{1\over {1+g_{m2}/g_{ds2}}}+{G_{L}\over g_{m2}}}}\cr
&\to {1\over {g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}}\;\;{\rm for}\;g_{ds}r_{o}\gg 1,
\;G_{L}\ll g_{m} } \tag{4}$$

and $1/g_{m2}$ if $B=S$.
E. g. $g_{m}=20\,{\rm mS}\to 50\,\Omega$ for matched RF
LNA. Low $Z_{in}$, current input.

More generally with $R_{sig}$ the impedance seen
{\it into} the source is (4) in parallel with $R_{sig}$.

{\rm Output impedance:} De-activate $v_{in}$, $v_{x}$ on
drain, $R_{sig}$ from source to ground.

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel R_{o,cg}$$

$$R_{o,cg}=r_{o2}+R_{sig}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}R_{sig}
\approx r_{o2}\left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})R_{sig}\right] \tag{5}$$

For $R_{sig}=0$, $R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$ high
$Z$ current output. For $R_{sig}=50\,\Omega$,
$R_{out}\approx r_{o1}\parallel g_{m}r_{o2}R_{sig}\gg r_{o}$.

So the stage is a {\it current buffer}: $i_{in}\approx
-i_{d2}\approx -i_{out}$ with current gain $\approx 1$,
transimpedance $\approx r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$, voltage
gain as above.

{\rm Frequency:} Input pole

$$\omega_{p,in}\approx {{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\over {C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{p,in}}}$$

very high because $R_{in}$ small. Output dominant pole

$$\omega_{p,out}\approx {1\over {(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_{L})C_{L}}}$$

with $C_{L}=C_{db1}+C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{L,ext}$.
Zero due to $C_{gd2}$ feedforward. No Miller effect.
Hence wide band, good for GHz LNA, $f_{T}$ limited by
$p_{in}$.

{\rm Properties:}

* non-inverting $A_{v}>0$
* low $R_{in}\approx 1/g_{m}$, high $R_{out}$
* moderate $A_{v}=g_{m}r_{o}$
* excellent reverse isolation, $y_{12}\approx 0$, unconditionally stable
* low Miller $C$, wideband
* noise figure $F\approx 1+\gamma g_{m2}R_{sig}+...$,
  $\gamma\approx 2/3$ long channel, requires
  $g_{m}R_{sig}\approx 1$ for match so $F\ge 3\,{\rm dB}$
  in simple form, can be improved with inductive
  degeneration, etc.
* suffers body effect if $B\neq S$, $R_{in}\downarrow$,
  $A_{v}\downarrow$ by $g_{mb}/g_{m}$.

{\rm Application:} Tuned or wideband LNA with $50\,\Omega$
antenna matching, current buffer in cascode/telescopic
op-amp, impedance translator, level shifter, wideband
IF stage. Often followed by common source to make
cascode for higher gain and isolation.

In short, for $B_{2}=S_{2}$:

$$A_{v}\approx +g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_{L}),\;
R_{in}\approx 1/g_{m2},\;
R_{out}\approx r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\;{\rm for}\;R_{sig}=0$$

with $g_{mb}$ correction $g_{m}\to g_{m}+g_{mb}$ if body
is grounded.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate NMOS with PMOS current-source load, places Vin at M2’s source, and gives the non-inverting gain and low input resistance. Its gain expression is equivalent to gm2(ro1 || ro2); the extra impedance and body-effect details are not needed for full credit.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is the {\rm common gate} with active
load, the building block of the cascode, telescopic and
folded cascode OPAMP and of the ${\rm CG}-{\rm LNA}$.
With the usual convention

$$M_{1}-P{\rm MOS}\;\;{\rm load}, S_{1}=V_{DD}
\;{\rm ac\;gnd},\;\;G_{1}=V_{b2}\;{\rm ac\;gnd}$$

$$M_{2}-{\rm N\-MOS}\;\;{\rm CG\;device},\;\;
D_{2}=V_{out},\;\;S_{2}=V_{in},\;\;G_{2}=V_{b1}
\;{\rm ac\;gnd}$$

In the drawing the bulk of $M_{2}$ is drawn tied to
$S_{2}$. If it is tied to the $P$ substrate $g_{mb2}\ne 0$.
With bulk tied to source $g_{mb2}=0$.
The comments are identical with $g_{m}\to g_{m}+g_{mb}$.
$M_{2}$ ${\rm P}$ is the dual. In that case $S_{2} > D_{2}$
in $DC$ and the DC current must be sunk by the driving
source.

> {\it N.B. :} As drawn with two $P$ symbols the
> DC path is $V_{DD}\to M_{1}\to M_{2}\to V_{in}$.
> The input source must sink the $DC$ bias current
> $I_{D}$. Normally this is a ${\rm N}{\rm MOS}{\rm CG}+
> {\rm P}{\rm MOS}$ load. The operation is complementary.

Let $I_{D}=I_{D1}=I_{D2}$ in $DC$.

$$I_{D}= \tfrac12\mu C_{ox}(W/L)(V_{GS}-V_{T})^{2}
\left[1+\lambda V_{DS}\right]$$

$$g_{m}=\sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}(W/L)I_{D}}=
\frac{2I_{D}}{V_{ov}}\qquad 
g_{ds}= \lambda I_{D}=r_{o}^{-1}\qquad 
g_{mb}= \eta g_{m}\;\; \eta\approx 0.1-0.3$$

In $DC$ saturation

* $M_{1}:$ $V_{SG1}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}>|V_{Tp}|$ ,
  $V_{SD1}=V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{SG1}-|V_{Tp}|=V_{ov1}$
* $M_{2}:$ $V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_{in}>V_{Tn}$ ,
  $V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_{in}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{Tn}=V_{ov2}$

$$V_{b1}=V_{in}+V_{Tn}+V_{ov2}\qquad 
|V_{b2}-V_{DD}|\approx|V_{Tp}|+|V_{ov1}|$$

so $V_{out}$ must satisfy

$$V_{in}+V_{ov2}\le V_{out}\le V_{DD}-|V_{ov1}|$$

otherwise one device goes triode. $V_{b1},V_{b2}$ normally
generated by ${\rm N}{\rm MOS}$ and ${\rm P}{\rm MOS}$
diode connected replica bias.

### Small signal low frequency

Gate and $V_{DD}$ are ac ground.  $M_{1}$ is a
resistor to ground

$$Z_{1}=r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}\;\;{\rm to\;ac\;gnd}$$

with no $g_{m1}$ contribution for $v_{sg1}=0$.

For $M_{2}$

$$i_{d}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2}$$

$$v_{gs2}= -v_{s}\;\;,\;\;v_{bs2}=
\begin{cases}
 -v_{s} & {\rm bulk\;to\;gnd}\\
 0      & {\rm bulk\;to\;source}
\end{cases}\;\;,\;\;v_{ds2}=v_{d}-v_{s}$$

$$v_{s}=v_{in}\;\;,\;\;v_{d}=v_{out}$$

KCL at $V_{out}$:

$$\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}+i_{d}=0$$

$$ \frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}+g_{m2}(-v_{in})+
g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{in})=0 \tag{1}$$

Hence, with $G_{m}=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$ if bulk grounded,
$G_{m}=g_{m2}$ if bulk tied to source,

$$v_{out}(g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}) = v_{in}(G_{m}+g_{ds2})$$

$$\,A_{v0}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\frac{G_{m}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}\approx
\frac{G_{m}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}=G_{m}\,R_{out}\,>0\,$$

$$R_{out}{\big |}_{R_{S}=0}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}
\approx \frac{1}{2}r_{o}$$

if $r_{o1}\approx r_{o2}=r_{o}$.
For long channel

$$|A_{v0}|\approx g_{m}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})
\approx \frac{g_{m}r_{o}}{2}= \frac{1}{\lambda V_{ov}}\approx
20-40\,{\rm dB}$$

{\it Non inverting.}  Physically $v_{in}\uparrow\to
v_{gs}\downarrow\to i_{d}\downarrow$ the $P$ load
pulls $v_{out}\uparrow$ until $g_{ds}\Delta v_{out}= 
G_{m}\Delta v_{in}$.

Current gain $\approx 1$. The stage is a {\it current
buffer - voltage amplifier - impedance transformer}.

KCL at the source with a test voltage $v_{x}$ and
$R_{D}=r_{o1}$ to ground:

$$v_{out}=v_{x}\frac{G_{m}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}$$

$$i_{x}= -i_{s}=G_{m}v_{x}+g_{ds2}(v_{x}-v_{out})
\approx v_{x}\frac{G_{m}}{1+g_{ds2}R_{D}}R_{D}^{-1}$$

More exactly

$$\,R_{in}=\frac{v_{x}}{i_{x}}=
\frac{1+g_{ds2}R_{D}}{G_{m}+g_{ds2}+g_{ds1}G_{m}R_{D}/(?)}\approx
\frac{1+R_{D}/r_{o2}}{G_{m}}\,$$

Normally quoted for $R_{D}\ll r_{o2}$, or to first order,

$$\,R_{in}\approx \frac{1}{G_{m}+g_{ds2}}
\approx\frac{1}{G_{m}}=\frac{1}{g_{m}+g_{mb}}\;\;
\to\; \frac{1}{g_{m}}\;{\rm with\;bulk\;tied\,}$$

$10^{1}-10^{2}\,\Omega$. With $R_{D}=r_{o1}$
$$R_{in}\approx \frac{1+r_{o1}/r_{o2}}{G_{m}}\approx
\frac{2}{G_{m}}$$
the familiar $\approx 50\,\Omega$ matching $1/g_{m}=50\,\Omega$ of the ${\rm CG}{\rm -LNA}$.

In general with a source resistance $R_{S}$ to ground the
impedance looking into the drain is

$$R_{d}=r_{o2}+ \left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]R_{S}$$

$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel R_{d}=r_{o1}\parallel
\left\{r_{o2}+\left[1+G_{m}r_{o2}\right]R_{S}\right\}$$

So for $R_{S}=0$, $R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$,
for $R_{S}\ne 0$, e.g. $50\,\Omega$, $R_{d}\gg r_{o}$ and
$R_{out}\approx r_{o1}$.

### Frequency, noise, application

* No Miller multiplication, $C_{gd}$ is between output and
ac ground.  Dominant pole at the output

$$\omega_{p,out}\approx \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{L}}$$

Input pole

$$\omega_{p,in}\approx \frac{1}{R_{in}(C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{S})}
\approx \frac{G_{m}}{C_{gs}} =\omega_{T}$$

very high. Hence wide band, good isolation $S_{12}\approx 0$.

* Input referred thermal noise $\overline{v_{n}^{2}}\approx
4kT\gamma/G_{m}$ plus load noise $4kT\gamma g_{m1}R_{out}^{2}$.
Noise figure of the $50\,\Omega$ matched ${\rm CG}{\rm -LNA}$
$\approx 1+\gamma$.

* Used where low $R_{in}$, high $R_{out}$, wide band and
no phase inversion is wanted: RF input termination, current
buffer, the input device of a cascode, folded cascode, current
mirror OTA, level shifter. Load can be resistively replaced by
$R_{D}$ with $A_{v}=G_{m}R_{D}\parallel r_{o2}$.

Cascoding $M_{1}$ or regulating the gate of $M_{2}$ raises
$R_{out}$ and gain to $G_{m}g_{m}r_{o}^{2}$.

Ideal bias $G_{m}R_{S}=1$ gives simultaneous power and noise
match only to first order; modifications - e.g. capacitive
feedthrough, $g_{m}$ boosting - are used for pure RF LNA.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate NMOS stage with a PMOS current-source load, places Vin at M2’s source and Vb1/Vb2 at the gates, and gives the non-inverting gain equivalent to gm2(ro1 || ro2) with low input resistance. The extra detailed discussion does not undermine the essential analysis.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is the grounded gate stage, Fig.1

$$M_{1}={\rm load}~~~M_{2}={\rm driver}$$

In $CMOS$ normally $M_{1}{\rm ,}p-$
$M_{2}{\rm ,}n-$ , with $p$ bulk to $V_{DD}$,
$n$ bulk to $V_{SS}=0$ . With the conventional
3 terminal symbol the arrow is on the {\it source}.
The conventional representation is

* $M_{1}$: $S\to V_{DD}$ , $G=V_{b2}=V_{GS1}+V_{DD}$ ,
$D=V_{o}$ . $V_{SG1}>|V_{Tp}|$, $V_{SD1}>V_{SG1}-|V_{Tp}|$
so that $M_{1}$ in saturation is to first order a
$DC$ current

$$I_{o}= {1\over 2}\mu _{p}C_{ox}\left({W\over L}\right)_{1}
\left(V_{SG1}-|V_{Tp}|\right)^{2}\left(1+\lambda _{p}V_{SD1}\right)$$

and for signals

$$g_{m1}= \mu _{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}(V_{SG1}-|V_{Tp}|)$$
$$r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}=1/\lambda _{p}I_{o}$$

i. e. $M_{1}$ is the $\approx r_{o1}$ to $a.c.$
ground $V_{DD}$ active load, current source load.
Its bulk is strapped to $S$ so no $g_{mb1}$ .

* $M_{2}$: $G=V_{b1}= {\rm const}$ $a.c.$ ground,
$S=V_{i}$ $D=V_{o}$ . 

$$V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_{i}>V_{Tn}$$
$$V_{DS2}=V_{o}-V_{i}>V_{GS2}-V_{Tn}=V_{ov2}$$

so that for correct $V_{b1},V_{b2}$ both devices are in
saturation and

$$I_{o}= {1\over 2}\mu _{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}
\left(V_{GS2}-V_{Tn}\right)^{2}\left(1+\lambda _{n}V_{DS2}\right)$$

fixes the $DC$ level $V_{o(DC)}$ and the $DC$ level
$V_{i(DC)}=V_{b1}-V_{GS2}$ .  Head room

$$\eqalign{
V_{o,max}&= V_{DD}-|V_{ov1}|\cr
V_{o,min}&= V_{i(DC)}+V_{ov2}\cr
V_{i,max}&= V_{b1}-V_{Tn}-V_{ov2}\cr}$$

and $V_{b1}$ is normally chosen $V_{Tn}+V_{ov2}$
above the wanted $V_{i(DC)}$ . For signals $G$ is
grounded. It is the {\it common gate - $CG$,
grounded gate} amplifier, the $n-$ complement of a
common base stage. $\delta V_{i}=-\delta V_{GS2}$ and
any $\delta V_{i}$ modulates $I_{D2}$.

Small signal with $r_{o}\ne \infty $ and
$g_{mb}\ne 0$ if the $n-$ bulk goes to $GND$ :

$$v_{gs2}= -v_{i}\;\;,\;\;v_{bs2}= -v_{i}\;\;{\rm to}\;GND\;\;,
0\;{\rm if\; bulk}\;{\rm strapped\; to}\;S$$
$$v_{ds2}=v_{o}-v_{i}$$
$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2}$$

$$i_{d2}=-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})v_{i}+g_{ds2}v_{o}\tag{1}$$

$CG$ is {\it non inverting}.

$$g_{m}={{\partial I_{D}}\over {\partial V_{GS}}}$$
$$g_{mb}=\eta g_{m}={{\gamma g_{m}}\over {2\sqrt{2\Phi _{F}+V_{SB}}}}$$
$$g_{ds}= \lambda I_{D}=1/r_{o}$$

At the output node $v_{o}$ :

tube $r_{o1}$ to $a.c.$ ground and $i_{d2}$ into the
tube. With $i_{d2}$ defined into the $D$:

$${{v_{o}}\over {r_{o1}}}+i_{d2}=0\tag{2}$$

for $R_{L}\to \infty $. If an external load $R_{L}$ to
ground is present replace $r_{o1}\to r_{o1}\parallel R_{L}$.

From (1)-(2)

$${{v_{o}}\over {r_{o1}}}+g_{ds2}v_{o}-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})v_{i}=0$$

$$A_{v}\equiv {{v_{o}}\over {v_{i}}}=
{{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}\over {g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}}>0\tag{3}$$

$$A_{v}\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})
      \approx g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})\;\;{\rm for}\;\;
      g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1\tag{4}$$

$\approx +\,$ intrinsic gain of the process.
E. g. $g_{m}=1\,{\rm mS}$, $r_{o}=10-50\,{\rm k\Omega }$
$A_{v}=10-50$, $20-34\,{\rm dB}$ for a single stage.
If bulk strapped to source $g_{mb2}=0$.

With a signal source resistance $R_{sig}$ in series
with $v_{i}$

$$A_{v}= {{(g_{m}+g_{mb})(r_{o1}\parallel R_{L})}
\over {1+(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})R_{sig}+R_{sig}/r_{o2}+R_{L}/r_{o2}}}$$

so for $R_{sig}=0$ (3) is recovered. The $CG$ has no
Miller multiplication of $C_{gd}$.

Input resistance at the source, $R_{in}=v_{x}/i_{x}$
with $v_{x}$ applied to the $S$ of $M_{2}$ and $D$
terminated in $R_{D}=r_{o1}\parallel R_{L}$ :

Put $v_{x}=v_{i}$, $v_{d}=v_{o}$ in (1) and
$v_{d}/R_{D}+i_{d2}=0$ , and $i_{x}=i_{d2}$ in magnitude,

$$i_{x}=-(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})v_{x}+g_{ds}v_{d}$$
$$v_{d}=-R_{D}i_{d2}$$

eliminating $v_{d}$

$$R_{in}= {{v_{x}}\over {i_{x}}}=
{{1+g_{ds}R_{D}}\over {g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}+g_{ds}g_{ds1}R_{D}}}
      \approx {{R_{D}+r_{o2}}\over {1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o2}}}\tag{5}$$

For the circuit as drawn $R_{D}=r_{o1}$ :

$$R_{in}= {{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}\over {1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}}
       ={{1+r_{o1}/r_{o2}}\over {g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+1/r_{o2}}}\tag{6}$$

So that

* $R_{D}\ll r_{o2}$ : $R_{in}\approx 1/(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})
      \approx 1/(g_{m}+g_{mb})$
* $R_{D}\sim r_{o}$ : $R_{in}\approx 2/(g_{m}r_{o})\,r_{o}
      \approx 2/g_{m}$
* $R_{D}\gg g_{m}r_{o}^{2}$ : $R_{in}\to R_{D}/(g_{m}r_{o})$
      i. e. large.

Normally $g_{m}r_{o}\approx 20-100$ so up to
$R_{D}\sim r_{o}$ the $CG$ remains a low impedance
input, of order $50\,\Omega$ to $1\,{\rm k\Omega }$,
which is its main use as a $50\,\Omega $ wide band
termination for $RF$ $LNA$'s, $R_{in}=1/g_{m}=50\,\Omega $.

Neglecting $r_{o}$ and $g_{mb}$ simply

$$R_{in0}\approx 1/g_{m2}\tag{7}$$

Output resistance at $v_{o}$ with a source resistance
$R_{sig}$ driving the source:

By duality

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel \left\{ r_{o2}+ \left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]R_{sig}\right\}\tag{8}$$

* $R_{sig}=0$, ideal voltage drive, $R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$

* $R_{sig}\ne 0$ the impedance looking into the
  drain of $M_{2}$ is boosted to
  $\approx g_{m}r_{o}R_{sig}$, the cascode effect.
  The circuit then becomes the cascode device.

Frequency response: two open circuit poles

$$p_{in}\approx -{{1}\over {(R_{sig}\parallel R_{in})C_{in}}}\;\;,
  C_{in}\approx C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{sig}$$

$$p_{out}\approx -{{1}\over {R_{out}C_{out}}}\;\;,
  C_{out}\approx C_{db1}+C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{gd1}+C_{L}$$

Because $R_{in}$ is low, $p_{in}$ is at very high
frequency. There is no Miller $C_{gd}$ multiplier
because $G$ is grounded. The $CG$ is inherently wide
band, the dominant pole is normally $p_{out}$.

$$\omega_{-3{\rm dB}}\approx 1/R_{out}C_{out}$$

$$GBW\approx A_{v}\omega_{-3{\rm dB}}\approx g_{m}/C_{out}$$

Large signal, $v_{o}$ follows $v_{i}$ in phase, the
stage is a {\it current buffer}: low $R_{in}$, high
$R_{out}$, voltage gain $>1$, current gain $\approx 1$,
and a {\it voltage non-inverting amplifier}.

In $PMOS$-only version interchange $V_{DD}\leftrightarrow GND$,
$|V_{Tp}|\leftrightarrow V_{Tn}$.

> {\it Remark:} Interchanging $S$ and $D$ as drawn
> does not change the small signal result to first order.
> Strapping the bulk of $M_{2}$ to its $S$ eliminates
> $g_{mb2}$. In a $p-$ substrate twin well process the
> $nMOST$ bulk is $GND$ by construction and $g_{mb}$ is
> unavoidable unless a triple well is used.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate NMOS stage with a PMOS current-source load, places Vin at M2’s source, and identifies both bias voltages. It gives the non-inverting gain as approximately gm2(ro1 || ro2) and describes the low input resistance; its additional detail does not alter the essential result.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit shown in the figure have?

answer.text:
With the usual lumped h.f. model the
circuit is a second order circuit.  The $5$
energy storing elements

$${\rm C}_{GS}\;\;{\rm C}_{GD}\;\;{\rm C}_{DB}\;\;
{\rm C}_{GD_{2}}\;\;{\rm C}_{DB_{2}} \tag{*}$$

have the graph

$$\eqalign{
Q_{G}&=C_{GS}V_{G}+C_{GD}(V_{G}-V_{D})\cr
Q_{D}&=C_{DB}V_{D}+C_{DB_{2}}V_{D}+C_{GD_{2}}V_{D}
      +C_{GD}(V_{D}-V_{G})}$$

$$ {\bf C}=\left\Vert \matrix{
C_{GS}+C_{GD}&-C_{GD}\cr
-C_{GD}&C_{DB}+C_{DB_{2}}+C_{GD_{2}}+C_{GD}\cr}\right\Vert \tag{1}$$

${\rm det}\,{\bf C}\ne 0$.
$C_{DB}\parallel C_{DB_{2}}\parallel C_{GD_{2}}:=C_{o}$ are
all to the {\it a.c. earth} at the drain node {\it e.g.}
$C_{GD_{2}}$ is to the ${\rm a.c.}$ earth at the gate of
${\rm M}_{2}$, and the ${{C}_{GS}-C_{GD}-C_{DB}}$
loop ${\rm det}{\bf C}=0$ removes one state, so there are
in the normal language only two different natural
frequencies.  Putting

$$C_{T}=C_{o}+C_{GD}\qquad g_{o}=g_{ds_{1}}+g_{ds_{2}}\qquad 
R_{o}=g_{o}^{-1}$$

the nodal equations in the low frequency small signal
model, Fig. 1, are, with $V_{g}\equiv V_{G_{1}}$

$$\eqalign{
{{V_{g}-V_{i}}\over {R_{S}}}+sC_{GS}V_{g}+sC_{GD}(V_{g}-V_{o})&=0\cr
g_{m}V_{g}+g_{o}V_{o}+sC_{o}V_{o}+sC_{GD}(V_{o}-V_{g})&=0\cr} \tag{2}$$

i. e.

$$\left\Vert \matrix{
{1\over {R_{S}}}+s(C_{GS}+C_{GD}) &-sC_{GD}\cr
g_{m}-sC_{GD} &g_{o}+sC_{T}\cr}\right\Vert 
\left\Vert \matrix{V_{g}\cr V_{o}\cr}\right\Vert =
\left\Vert \matrix{{V_{i}\over {R_{S}}}\cr 0\cr}\right\Vert \tag{3}$$

$${{V_{o}}\over {V_{i}}}(s)={1\over {R_{S}}}{{sC_{GD}-g_{m}}\over 
{\Delta (s)}} \tag{4}$$

and, from (3),

$$\eqalign{
\Delta (s)&=\left[{1\over {R_{S}}}+s(C_{GS}+C_{GD})\right]
\left[g_{o}+sC_{T}\right]+sC_{GD}\left(g_{m}-sC_{GD}\right)\cr
&={g_{o}\over {R_{S}}}+s\left[{C_{T}\over {R_{S}}}+g_{o}(C_{GS}+C_{GD})
+g_{m}C_{GD}\right]+s^{2}\left[(C_{GS}+C_{GD})C_{T}-C_{GD}^{2}\right]\cr
&={g_{o}\over {R_{S}}}+s\left[{C_{T}\over {R_{S}}}+g_{o}(C_{GS}+C_{GD})
+g_{m}C_{GD}\right]+s^{2}\left[C_{GS}C_{T}+C_{GD}C_{o}\right] } \tag{5}$$

is ${\cal O}(s^{2})$.  I. e. in the ordinary sense the
voltage transfer function is a low pass second order
function with, from (4), the conventional Miller RHP
zero at

$$s_{z}=+{{g_{m}}\over {C_{GD}}}\tag{6}$$

In the Miller approximation (5) is normally written as

$$\Delta (s)\approx {g_{o}\over {R_{S}}}\left[1+sR_{S}
\left(C_{GS}+C_{GD}(1+g_{m}R_{o})\right)\right]\left[1+sR_{o}C_{o}^{\ast}\right] \tag{7}$$

with

$$\eqalign{
\omega _{p_{i}}^{-1}&\approx R_{S}\left[C_{GS}+C_{GD}(1+g_{m}R_{o})\right]
\tag{8a}\cr
\omega _{p_{o}}^{-1}&\approx R_{o}\left[C_{DB}+C_{DB_{2}}+C_{GD_{2}}
+C_{GD}\left(1-{1\over {g_{m}R_{o}}}\right)\right]\approx R_{o}C_{o} \tag{8b}}$$

the conventional Miller multiplied input pole and the
output pole.  For $R_{S}\to 0$ (8a) goes to infinity and
the circuit becomes the familiar dominant pole
$R_{o}C_{o}$ single pole circuit, Fig. 2.

If you want to count $C_{DB}\parallel C_{DB_{2}}\parallel
C_{GD_{2}}$ as different poles (7)--(8) is normally
quoted as a three capacitance, three pole, one zero,
circuit, the output pole being triple,
$C_{o}=C_{DB}+C_{DB_{2}}+C_{GD_{2}}$, and with the usual
abuse of language the $C_{GD}$ Miller pole counted as a
third pole.  Counting every physical capacitance in
$(\ast )$ separately (5) is formally ${\cal O}(s^{5})$,
${\cal O}(s^{4})$ with the $C_{GS}-C_{GD}-C_{DB}$ all
capacitance loop removed, with three coincident poles at
$\omega _{p_{o}}$.

> {\it Remark:}  In most text books the three coincident
> output capacitances are lumped as $C_{o}$ and the circuit
> is quoted as a {\it three pole, one zero} circuit,
> {\it i. e.} as a {\it two pole} low pass function in the
> strict network theoretic sense.

For $R_{S}=0$ the conventional single pole dominant pole
approximation

$${{V_{o}}\over {V_{i}}}(s)\approx -{{g_{m}R_{o}}\over {1+sR_{o}C_{o}}}
{{1-sC_{GD}/g_{m}}\over {1+sR_{S}(C_{GS}+C_{GD}g_{m}R_{o})}} \tag{9}$$

is recovered.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the gate and output as the two independent capacitive nodes, assigns the capacitors to the right nodes, and derives a quadratic denominator. Its loose discussion of informal pole counting does not change the strict answer of two poles.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit shown in the figure have?

answer.text:
With the ideal ${\rm  ac.\,ground}$ on the gate of
${\cal M}_{2}$ the only high ${\rm d.\,c.}$ impedance
${\rm nodes}$ are

$${\rm N}_{1}= {\cal G}_{1}\qquad {\rm N}_{2}=
{\cal D}_{1}\equiv {\cal D}_{2}\equiv V_{o}\tag*{1}$$

so that with

$$R_{D}^{\prime}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\qquad 
C_{L}=C_{DB}+C_{DB2}+C_{GD2}\tag{2}$$

the ${\rm a.\,c.}$ small signal circuit is Fig. 1
and, putting e. {\rm g.} $g_{mb}=0$,

$$\eqalign{
{\rm N}_{1}:&\;(V_{1}-V_{i})/R_{S}+sC_{GS}V_{1}
+sC_{GD}(V_{1}-V_{o})=0\cr
{\rm N}_{2}:&\;V_{o}/R_{D}^{\prime}+sC_{L}V_{o}
+sC_{GD}(V_{o}-V_{1})+g_{m1}V_{1}=0\cr} \tag{3}$$

i. e. with

$$\eqalign{
A(s)&=R_{S}^{-1}+s\left(C_{GS}+C_{GD}\right)\cr
B(s)&=R_{D}^{\prime -1}+s\left(C_{L}+C_{GD}\right)\cr}\tag{4}$$

$$\left[\,{\rm M}(s)\,\right]
\left[\,{\rm V}\,\right]=\left[\,{\rm I}\,\right]\qquad 
\left[\,{\rm M}\,\right]=\left\Vert
\matrix{A &-sC_{GD}\cr
g_{m1}-sC_{GD} &B\cr}\right\Vert \tag{5}$$

$${\rm det\,}{\rm M}(s)=D(s)=A(s)B(s)
+sC_{GD}\left(g_{m1}-sC_{GD}\right) \tag{6}$$

$$D(s)=R_{S}^{-1}R_{D}^{\prime -1}
+s\left[{{C_{GS}+C_{GD}}\over {R_{D}^{\prime}}}
+{{C_{L}+C_{GD}}\over {R_{S}}}+g_{m1}C_{GD}\right]
+s^{2}\left[C_{GS}C_{L}+C_{GS}C_{GD}+C_{GD}C_{L}\right] \tag{7}$$

and, e. {\rm g.},

$${{V_{o}}\over {V_{i}}}(s)={{R_{S}^{-1}\left(sC_{GD}
-g_{m1}\right)}\over {D(s)}}\tag{8}$$

so that, in the conventional lumped terminology, the
finite transfer function is second order with a
right half plane feed through zero at

$$s_{z}=+{{g_{m1}}\over {C_{GD}}}\tag{9}$$

The quadratic $D(s)=0$, $D(s)\propto (s-p_{1})(s-p_{2})$,
is conventionally spoken of as the {\it input,}
Miller multiplied, pole and the {\it output} pole,

$$p_{1}\approx -{{1}\over {R_{S}
\left[C_{GS}+C_{GD}\left(1+g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}\right)
\right]}}\tag{10a}$$

$$p_{2}\approx -{{1}\over {R_{D}^{\prime}
\left[C_{L}+C_{GD}{{1+g_{m1}R_{S}C_{GS}/
\left(C_{GS}+C_{GD}\right)}\over {1+g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}}}
\right]}}\approx -{{1}\over {R_{D}^{\prime}
\left(C_{L}+C_{GD}\right)}}\quad {\rm for}\;\;
g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}\gg 1 \tag{10b}$$

with the obvious $g_{m}R_{D}^{\prime}\rightarrow \infty $
Miller limits

$$p_{1}\rightarrow -{{1}\over {R_{S}
\left(C_{GS}+C_{GD}\right)}}\qquad 
p_{2}\rightarrow -{{1}\over {R_{D}^{\prime}C_{L}}}
\tag{11}$$

if the Miller multiplication is exhibited explicitly.

In terms of physical capacitors there are

* $C_{GS}$ ${\cal G}_{1}-{\rm gnd}$
* $C_{GD}$ ${\cal G}_{1}-{\cal D}_{1}$ - the Miller
feedback capacitor
* $C_{DB}$ ${\cal D}_{1}-{\rm gnd}$
* $C_{GD2}$ ${\cal D}_{2}-{\rm gnd}$ [${\cal G}_{2}=
{\rm ac\,gnd}$]
* $C_{DB2}$ ${\cal D}_{2}-{\rm ac\,gnd}$

i. e. five physical capacitors.  For ${\rm a.\,c.}$
${\rm gnd}\equiv V_{DD}$ the last three are in
parallel between the same electrical node ${\rm N}_{2}$
and ${\rm ac\,gnd}$,

$$C_{L}=C_{DB}\parallel C_{GD2}\parallel C_{DB2}\tag{12}$$

so that three pole frequencies are conventionally
distinguished, one at the gate, one Miller and one
triple at the drain.  With the parallel combination
(12) carried out there are two independent state
variables, i. e. two independent poles in the
strict determinant sense, Eq.\,(7).  Loosely the
circuit is often quoted as a three pole  - two pole
plus RHP zero - Miller amplifier, five poles with
three coincident at the output if every physical
capacitor is counted separately.

> {\it Remark:}  Counting distinct $R\,C$ products
> before the $C_{L}$ parallel combination is carried
> out the circuit is normally abbreviated to the
> familiar dominant pole - non dominant pole
> two pole low pass with the Miller zero (9).  With
> distinct capacitors exhibited it is a three
> frequency, $C_{GS}$, $C_{GD}$, $C_{L}$, amplifier,
> five capacitors with $C_{DB}\parallel
> C_{DB2}\parallel C_{GD2}$.  Any other
> degeneracies, e. {\rm g.} $R_{S}=0$, $R_{D}^{\prime}
> =0$, remove one of the poles in the usual way.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies two independent nodes and derives a second-order determinant, but then explicitly claims three or five poles by counting capacitor-related frequencies. That contradicts the required two-pole answer and the golden solution’s limit for answers giving another pole count.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit shown in the figure have?

answer.text:
With the (ac) short on the $2$ gates and on the
top plate of the two drift bulk capacities there is,
ac, only one high impedance node in the circuit, the
common drain node, ${\rm D}_{1}\equiv {\rm D}_{2}\equiv
{\rm O}$, Fig.1, and one low impedance node, the gate
of ${\rm M}_{1}$.  Putting ${\rm V}_{i}=0$,

$${\rm G}_{1}\left(R_{s}{\rm\;to\;earth}\right)
 \left\{\eqalign{
C_{GS}&{\rm G}_{1}-{\rm earth}\cr
C_{GD}&{\rm G}_{1}-{\rm O}\cr}\right.
\qquad 
{\rm O}\left\{\eqalign{
C_{DB}&{\rm O}-{\rm earth}\cr
C_{DB_{2}}&{\rm O}-{\rm earth}\cr
C_{GD_{2}}&{\rm O}-{\rm earth}\cr}\right.\tag{*}$$

so that for distinct elements you have four, ac
physical, capacities but $C_{DB}\parallel C_{DB2}\parallel
C_{GD2}\equiv C_{o}$ is a single ac capacity to earth.
For independent capacities you have the three capacities

$$C_{GS}\;\;,\;\;C_{GD}\;\;,\;\;C_{o}=C_{DB}+C_{DB2}+
C_{GD2}\tag{**}$$

with the capacitive loop $C_{GS}-C_{GD}-C_{o}$.
Hence two independent state variables.  In the
nodal equations, with $R_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$,

$$\eqalign{
{{V_{1}-V_{i}}\over {R_{s}}}+V_{1}sC_{GS}+(V_{1}-V_{o})
sC_{GD}&=0\cr
g_{m}V_{1}+{{V_{o}}\over {R_{o}}}+(V_{o}-V_{1})sC_{GD}+
V_{o}sC_{o}&=0\cr}\tag{***}$$

$$\left| \matrix{
{{1}\over {R_{s}}}+s\left(C_{GS}+C_{GD}\right) &-sC_{GD}\cr
g_{m}-sC_{GD}&{{1}\over {R_{o}}}+s\left(C_{o}+C_{GD}\right)\cr}\right|
\cdot \left| \matrix{V_{1}\cr V_{o}\cr}\right| =
\left| \matrix{{{V_{i}}\over {R_{s}}}\cr 0\cr}\right| $$

$$\eqalign{
{{V_{o}}\over {V_{i}}}(s)&=-{{g_{m}-sC_{GD}}\over {R_{s}}}\cr
&\times \left\{ s^{2}\left[C_{GS}C_{o}+C_{GD}\left(C_{GS}+
C_{o}\right)\right]+s\left[{{C_{GS}+C_{GD}}\over {R_{o}}}+
{{C_{o}+C_{GD}}\over {R_{s}}}+g_{m}C_{GD}\right]+{{1}\over
{R_{s}R_{o}}}\right\}^{-1}\cr}\tag{****}$$

i. e. in strict mathematics a two pole, one zero,
second order, system, third order if you keep
$C_{DB}$ and $C_{DB2}$ distinct, fourth order if you
keep $C_{GD2}$ distinct, the three, four, capacities
hanging on the ${\rm O}$ node being coincident.
With $C_{o}\to C_{DB}+C_{DB2}$ the system is normally
quoted as a three pole - one zero system, the
well known RHP feed forward zero

$$s_{z}=+{{g_{m}}\over {C_{GD}}}\tag{1}$$

With $g_{m}R_{o}\gg 1$ the two, three, poles can be
split in the Miller approximation as an {\it input
pole\/} and a {\it , dominant, output pole\/},

$$s_{p1}\approx -{{1}\over {R_{s}\left[C_{GS}+
\left(1+g_{m}R_{o}\right)C_{GD}\right]}}\tag{2a}$$

$$s_{p2}\approx -{{1}\over {R_{o}\left[C_{o}+
{{C_{GS}C_{GD}}\over {C_{GS}+C_{GD}}}\right]}}
\approx -{{1}\over {R_{o}C_{o}}}\tag{2b}$$

with

$$C_{o}=C_{DB}+C_{DB2}+C_{GD2}+C_{GD}\left(1+{{1}\over
{g_{m}R_{o}}}\right)\approx C_{DB}+C_{DB2}+C_{GD2}\tag{3}$$

so that, $R_{s}\ll R_{o}$, the normal hand calculation
is a dominant pole amplifier

$$\left| s_{p2}\right| ={1\over {R_{o}C_{o}}}\ll \left|
s_{p1}\right| \tag{4}$$

and, with (1), the familiar one pole Miller
approximated transfer function

$${{V_{o}}\over {V_{i}}}(s)\approx
-{{g_{m}R_{o}}\over {1+sR_{o}C_{o}}}{{1-sC_{GD}/g_{m}}
\over {1+sR_{s}\left[C_{GS}+g_{m}R_{o}C_{GD}\right]}}
\tag{5}$$

Normally quoted simply as {\it a two pole amplifier
with a RHP zero, effectively a single dominant pole
amplifier with $\omega _{-3{\rm dB}}\approx 1/R_{o}C_{o}$
\/}.  Keeping $C_{DB}$ and $C_{DB2}$ and $C_{GD2}$
distinct this is three coincident output poles plus the
input Miller pole, i. e. four poles plus one zero
coincident to two finite pole frequencies, normally
abbreviated to {\it three poles and one zero\/},
$C_{GS}\to p_{1}$, $C_{GD}\to p_{2}$,
$C_{o}=C_{DB}\parallel C_{DB2}\parallel C_{GD2}\to
p_{o}$, the last, dominant, often the only one quoted.

> {\it Remark:\/}  With the conventional
> $R_{s}\rightarrow 0$ signal source the input pole
> $\left|s_{p1}\right|\rightarrow \infty $ and the
> circuit is normally quoted as a one pole, dominant
> output pole, circuit,
> $$|s_{p}|\approx {1\over {(r_{o1}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})
> \left(C_{DB}+C_{DB2}+C_{GD2}\right)}}\tag{6}$$
> to which, in the exact analysis, the Miller pole
> (2a) and the RHP zero (1) have to be added.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It initially identifies the two independent nodes and correctly derives two poles, but then incorrectly claims that separate capacitors on the same output node create three or four poles and calls the circuit three-pole. That contradicts the central answer; the golden solution caps such pole-count errors at 1.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a ${\rm ``self~cascode''}$
or {\it composite} $NMOS$ common source
with $R_{D}$ load. The $2T$ pull down can
be considered as $1T$ with

$$L_{eq}=L_{1}+L_{2}\;\;\;{\rm and}\;\;\;
{(W/L)}_{eq}^{-1}={(W_{1}/L_{1})}^{-1}+
{(W_{2}/L_{2})}^{-1}$$

in first approximation. i. e. a long channel
device made by stacking.

$$\eqalign{
M_{1}&: V_{GS1}=V_{in}\cr
& V_{DS1}=V_{x}\cr
M_{2}&: V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_{x}\cr
& V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_{x}} \qquad V_{x}=V_{D1}=V_{S2}$$

Put $I_{D}=V_{DD}-V_{out}/R_{D}=I_{D1}=I_{D2}$,
$k_{n}= \mu _{n}C_{ox}$, $\lambda =1/V_{A}$
in the conventional

$$I_{D,sat}={1\over 2}k_{n}{W\over L}
\left(V_{GS}-V_{T}\right)^{2}\left[1+\lambda V_{DS}\right]$$
$$I_{D,lin}=k_{n}{W\over L}\left[\left(V_{GS}-V_{T}\right)V_{DS}
-{1\over 2}V_{DS}^{2}\right]$$

* {\it Cut off} $V_{in}<V_{T}$ :

$$I_{D}=0\;\;,\;\;V_{out}=V_{DD}\;\;,\;\;V_{x}\approx 0$$

* {\it On} $V_{in}>V_{T}$ , for $\lambda\to 0$,

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}$$

With $a=V_{in}-V_{T}$ .

E. {\rm g}. for $k_{1}=k_{2}=k$ and $M_{2}$ sat,
$M_{1}$ lin:

$$k\left(aV_{x}-{1\over 2}V_{x}^{2}\right)=
{1\over 2}k\left(a-V_{x}\right)^{2}$$

$$2V_{x}^{2}-4aV_{x}+a^{2}=0$$

$$V_{x}=a\left(1-{\sqrt{2}\over 2}\right)\approx 0.29a>0$$

$$V_{GS2}=a-V_{x}\approx 0.71a$$

$$I_{D}={1\over 2}k\left(0.71a\right)^{2}
\approx {1\over 2}\left({1\over 2}k\,a^{2}\right)$$

i. e. the {\it composite} carries $\approx 1/2$
the current of a single $W/L$ device for the same
$a$, the same as a $W/L_{eq}=W/2L$ device.
In general

$$V_{x}=a\left[1-\sqrt{{(W_{1}/L_{1})\over (W_{2}/L_{2})}}\;\right]
\qquad \lambda =0$$

so $V_{x}<a$. Hence

$$\eqalign{
V_{DS1}&=V_{x}<V_{GS1}-V_{T}\cr
& M_{1}\;{\rm is\;in\;triode}}$$

$$V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_{x}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{T}=a-V_{x}$$

$$\;V_{out}\ge a=V_{in}-V_{T}\;:\;M_{2}\;{\rm sat.}$$

is the saturation condition of the {\it composite}
device. I. e. the composite is {\it saturated}
when $M_{2}$ is saturated, although $M_{1}$ is
in triode. Its $I_{D}$ is essentially flat with
$V_{out}$. For

$$V_{out}<V_{in}-V_{T}$$

$M_{2}$ also goes triode and

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-R_{D}I_{D,lin1,lin2}\to \approx 0$$

for $V_{in}\gg V_{T}$. The large signal
transfer $V_{out}\left(V_{in}\right)$ is the
conventional $R_{D}$ inverter transfer with

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-R_{D}I_{D}\left(V_{in},V_{out}\right)$$

high $=V_{DD}$ for $V_{in}<V_{T}$, sharp
transition around $V_{in}\approx V_{T}+
\sqrt{2I_{D}/k_{eq}}$ and low $\approx R_{on,eq}/
\left(R_{D}+R_{on,eq}\right)V_{DD}$ for
$V_{in}\to V_{DD}$.

> Remark: With the same $V_{T}$ the two devices
> can never be saturated together. With
> $V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_{x}$, $V_{x}\ge a$ to saturate
> $M_{1}$ implies $V_{GS2}-V_{T}\le 0$ and $M_{2}$
> is off. The normal operating {\it amplifying}
> bias has $M_{1}$ linear , $M_{2}$ saturated.
> By ratioing $(W_{2}/L_{2})\gg (W_{1}/L_{1})$
> $V_{x}$ can be made large and $M_{1}$ can be
> brought close to saturation, but never fully.

### Small signal

For the signal put $V_{DD}\;ac\;0$, $v_{in}$ on
both gates.

{\small
$$\eqalign{
i_{d1}&=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x}\cr
i_{d2}&=g_{m2}\left(v_{in}-v_{x}\right)+
       g_{mb2}\left(-v_{x}\right)+g_{ds2}\left(v_{out}-v_{x}\right)\cr
& {\rm with\;body\;to\;ground.\;If\;as\;drawn\;
body\;of\;M_{2}\;{\rm to}\;V_{x},\;g_{mb2}=0}
}$$

}
KCL at $V_{x}$ and $V_{out}$:

$$\eqalign{
i_{d2}&=i_{d1}\tag{1}\cr
{v_{out}\over R_{D}}+i_{d2}&=0\tag{2}}$$

From (1)-(2) $i_{d1}= -v_{out}/R_{D}$

$$v_{x}=-r_{ds1}\left[g_{m1}v_{in}+{v_{out}\over R_{D}}\right]
\tag{3}$$

with $r_{ds1}=1/g_{ds1}$. In saturation $r_{ds1}=r_{o1}$,
in triode $r_{ds1}=1/\left[k_{1}\left(a-V_{x}\right)\right]
\ll r_{o1}$.

Putting (3) in (2):

$$ {v_{out}\over R_{D}}+g_{m2}v_{in}
-g_{m2}v_{x}+g_{ds2}\left(v_{out}-v_{x}\right)
+g_{mb2}(-v_{x})=0$$

$$g_{m2}v_{in}+v_{out}\left(g_{ds2}+{1\over R_{D}}\right)
-v_{x}\left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}\right)=0$$

With $v_{x}$ from (3), for $g_{mb2}=0$:

$${v_{out}\over v_{in}}=
- R_{D}{\,r_{o1}g_{m1}\left(g_{m2}+g_{ds2}\right)
+g_{m2}\,\over R_{D}+r_{o2}+r_{o1}\left(1+g_{m2}r_{o2}\right)}
\tag{4}$$

including $g_{mb2}$ replace $g_{m2}\to g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$.

For the usual $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$:

$$A_{v}\approx
-R_{D}{\,g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}g_{m1}\,\over
r_{o1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}=-g_{m1}R_{D}\,
{1\over 1+{R_{D}+r_{o2}\over r_{o1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}}
\tag{5}$$

If $R_{D}\ll r_{o1}g_{m2}r_{o2}$

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}\left(R_{D}\parallel R_{o}\right)$$

where

$$R_{o}=r_{o2}+r_{o1}+g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}
\approx g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\tag{6}$$

is the impedance looking into the drain of $M_{2}$
with $v_{in}=0$, i. e. the normal cascode
formula. If $M_{1}$ is triode $r_{o1}\to r_{ds1}$:

$$R_{o}\approx g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{ds1}+r_{o2}+r_{ds1}
\approx g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{ds1}$$

still $\gg r_{o2}$ but $\ll g_{m}r_{o}^{2}$.

More compactly

$$A_{v}=-G_{m}\left(R_{D}\parallel R_{o}\right)$$

with short circuit transconductance

$$G_{m}={i_{sc}\over v_{in}}\Biggr|_{v_{out}=0}
\approx g_{m1}$$

Indeed from (1) with $v_{out}=0$:

$$g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_{x})-g_{ds2}v_{x}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x}$$

$$v_{x}=v_{in}{g_{m2}-g_{m1}\over g_{m2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}\approx 0
\;{\rm for}\;g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$$

$$i_{sc}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x}\approx g_{m1}v_{in}$$

So the composite has essentially the $g_{m}$ of the
bottom device, but the $r_{o}$ of a cascode.

With $g_{mb}\ne 0$ :

$$R_{o}\approx \left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\right)r_{o1}r_{o2}\;\;,
\;\;A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}\left(R_{D}\parallel R_{o}\right)$$

Intrinsic gain of the composite itself, $R_{D}\to\infty$:

$$A_{o}=-G_{m}R_{o}\approx -g_{m1}r_{o1}g_{m2}r_{o2}$$

$\approx (g_{m}r_{o})^{2}$, a factor $g_{m}r_{o}$
larger than a single device, but with $r_{ds1}$
in place of $r_{o1}$ if $M_{1}$ is linear the
improvement is $g_{m2}r_{o2}\,(r_{ds1}/r_{o1})$.

In practice this gives $2$ to $5\times$ larger
$R_{o}$ than a simple $L=L_{1}+L_{2}$ device
for the same current, without paying the
$1/(L_{1}+L_{2})$ reduction in $g_{m}$ that a
true long device would give, and it can be used
at low $V_{DD}$ because $V_{DS,sat,eq}\approx
V_{GS}-V_{T}+V_{x}$, only a few $100\,{\rm mV}$
larger than a single device, versus $2(V_{GS}-V_{T})$
for a conventional cascode with separate bias.

Drawbacks: $M_{1}$ in triode adds its thermal
noise as $4kTg_{ds1}$ and the swing is reduced
by $V_{x}$, headroom $V_{out,min}\approx
I_{D}r_{ds1}+V_{DS,sat2}$.

For hand calculation with $\lambda =0$,
$A_{v}=-g_{m1}R_{D}$, the same as a simple
common source with $R_{D}$, but the real
$\lambda\ne 0$ gain is higher because
$R_{D}\parallel R_{o}\approx R_{D}$ is larger
than $R_{D}\parallel r_{o}$ of the simple stage.
If $R_{D}$ is replaced by a $PMOS$ current source
$R_{D}=r_{op}$, the gain improvement is fully
realized: $A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}(r_{op}\parallel
g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{ds1})$.

This is widely used as a low voltage high gain
load, ``double length'' or ``composite''
transistor in $CMOS$ $op$-amps.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies the common-gated series NMOS structure, the lower device in triode, and the effective length L1+L2. But it then claims cascode-like output-resistance and gain multiplication, contrary to the modest output-resistance increase expected here; that is a significant design-consequence error.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a ${\ldouble }N$ type ${\it self\;cascode}$ or
${\it composite\; }W/L$ common source stage.

$$\eqalign{
M_{1}&: CS \;\;S_{1}=0\;\;D_{1}=S_{2}\;\;G_{1}=V_{in}\cr
M_{2}&: CG \;\;D_{2}=V_{out}\;\;G_{2}=V_{in}\cr
R_{D}&: passive\;load\;to\;V_{DD}}$$

Drawn as laid out the bulks are

* $B_{1}=0$ on $S_{1}$
* $B_{2}=S_{2}$ on arrow

so $g_{mb2}=0$. In a bulk $n$ substrate
$B_{2}=0$ and you have to keep $g_{mb2}\ne
0$ and $V_{T2}=V_{T0}+\gamma \left(\sqrt{2\phi _{F}+V_{x}}-
\sqrt{2\phi _{F}}\right)$ . Formally replace $g_{m2}$ by
$g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$ below.

It is normally used as a 2 $T$ composite
device $M_{eq}=M_{1}+M_{2}$ in series with
common gate.

### 1. Large signal - composite $W/L$

Put $k_{i}=\mu C_{ox}W_{i}/L_{i}$, $V_{Gx}=V_{x}=$
voltage at $D_{1}=S_{2}$.

$$V_{GS1}=V_{in}\;\;\;V_{DS1}=V_{x}$$
$$V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_{x}\;\;\;V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_{x}$$

Cut off:

$$V_{in}<V_{T}\;:\;I_{D}=0\;,\;V_{out}=V_{DD}$$

Above $V_{T}$ the two currents must be
equal

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}= {V_{DD}-V_{out}\over R_{D}}$$

If the composite is saturated as a whole the
upper device is saturated and the lower device
is in triode. E. g. $k_{1}=k_{2}=k$,
$\lambda =0$ :

$$\eqalign{
I_{D}&=k\left[(V_{in}-V_{T})V_{x}-V_{x}^{2}/2\right]
      = {k\over 2}(V_{in}-V_{x}-V_{T})^{2}\cr
V_{x}&\approx 0.29\;(V_{in}-V_{T})\cr
I_{D}&\approx {k\over 4}(V_{in}-V_{T})^{2}
      ={k_{eq}\over 2}(V_{in}-V_{T})^{2}}$$

In general for $V_{out}>V_{in}-V_{T}$, composite
saturation :

$$I_{D}\approx {1\over 2}\mu C_{ox}\left({W\over L}\right)_{eq}
(V_{in}-V_{T})^{2}(1+\lambda_{eq}V_{out})$$

with

$${1\over (W/L)_{eq}}={1\over (W_{1}/L_{1})}+{1\over (W_{2}/L_{2})}
\qquad {\rm e.g.}\;(W/L)_{eq}=(W/L)/2\;{\rm for}\;W_{1}=W_{2},L_{1}=L_{2}$$

$$L_{eq}\approx L_{1}+L_{2}\qquad V_{A,eq}\approx V_{A1}+V_{A2}$$
$$r_{o,eq}\approx {1\over \lambda_{eq}I_{D}}\gg r_{o1},r_{o2}$$

i. e. the stack acts like a single long channel
device to first order. The condition for the
stack to stay saturated is

$$V_{out}\ge V_{GS,eq}-V_{T}=V_{DSAT1}+V_{DSAT2}$$

so it costs one $V_{DSAT}$ more head room than
a single $T$.

For $V_{out}< V_{in}-V_{T}$ $M_{2}$ goes triode,
for large $V_{in}$ both $M_{1},M_{2}$ triode

$$R_{on,i}\approx \left[ k_{i}(V_{in}-V_{T})\right]^{-1}$$
$$V_{OL}=V_{DD}{R_{on1}+R_{on2}\over R_{D}+R_{on1}+R_{on2}} > V_{OL,1T}$$

The DC transfer $V_{out}(V_{in})$ is the normal
$NMOS$ inverter with $R_{D}$ load, threshold

$$V_{M}:V_{in}=V_{out}\;:\;{V_{DD}-V_{M}\over R_{D}}=
{k_{eq}\over 2}(V_{M}-V_{T})^{2}$$

with $V_{OH}=V_{DD}$,
$V_{OL}$ above, high small signal gain at $V_{M}$.

### 2. Small signal - low frequency

Gate impedance $=\infty$.

$$R_{in}\approx \infty $$

Small signal with channel length modulation,
$g_{ds}=1/r_{o}$ :

$$\eqalign{
i_{d1}&=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x}\cr
i_{d2}&=g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_{x})+g_{mb2}(-v_{x})+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})\cr
i_{d1}&=i_{d2}\cr
i_{d2}&=-v_{out}/R_{D}}$$

gives in exact form for $g_{mb2}=0$:

$$A_{v}={v_{out}\over v_{in}}=
 -R_{D}{g_{m1}r_{o1}+g_{m2}r_{o2}+g_{m1}r_{o1}g_{m2}r_{o2}
 \over R_{D}+r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}} \tag{1}$$

with $g_{mb2}\ne 0$ replace $g_{m2}\to g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$
in the denominator and $g_{m2}r_{o2}\to (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}$ in
the cross term.

For $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$ :

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}\;R_{D}\;{1+{\cal O}(1/g_{m}r_{o})\over
1+{R_{D}\over r_{o,eq}}}$$

where the impedance looking into $D_{2}$ with
$v_{in}=0$, i. e. $G_{2}$ ac ground, is the normal
cascode resistance

$$R_{o,eq}= r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}
\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}\gg r_{o1},r_{o2}$$

so that

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}\left(R_{D}\parallel R_{o,eq}\right)$$

and for the usual $R_{D}\ll R_{o,eq}$

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}R_{D}$$

$$|A_{v0}|\approx g_{m,eq}r_{o,eq}\approx g_{m1}r_{o,eq}
\gg g_{m1}r_{o1}$$

Formally $g_{m,eq}\approx g_{m1}$ - the upper
gate being driven does ${\it not}$ double $g_{m}$
because $v_{x}$ follows $v_{in}$ and
$V_{GS2}=v_{in}-v_{x}$ is small. The short circuit
current is $\approx g_{m1}v_{in}$.

With an active $PMOS$ load $R_{D}\to r_{op}$
the improvement is large: $A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}
\left(r_{o,eq}\parallel r_{op}\right)$ which can be
$10-20\,{\rm dB}$ higher than a single $T$
$CS$ stage of the same $W/L$.

The output resistance at the $V_{out}$ node is

$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel R_{o,eq}\approx R_{D}\quad{\rm if\;
R_{D}\;is\;passive}$$

### 3. Remarks

* To first order the circuit can be analysed as a
normal $CS$ stage with device $M_{eq}$ : $W_{eq}$ above,
$L_{eq}=L_{1}+L_{2}$, $g_{m}=g_{m1}$, $r_{o}=R_{o,eq}$.
* Advantage over a single device: $r_{o}$ increased by
$\times g_{m}r_{o}$, short channel effects, DIBL,
$\lambda $ reduced by channel length doubling without
requiring a separate cascode bias. Compact layout - shared
diffusion.
* The same composite is widely used as high swing
self-biased cascode current mirror / load,
band-gap, op-amp input stage, etc. where no extra bias
voltage is available and low voltage operation is required.
* Cost: $V_{DSAT,eq}=V_{DSAT1}+V_{DSAT2}$, lower $I_{D}$ for
given $W$, larger $C_{gg}=C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+C_{gd2}(1-A_{v})$
Miller, extra pole at $v_{x}$ :

$$p_{out}\approx -{1\over R_{out}C_{L}}\;,\;
p_{x}\approx -{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}\over C_{x}}$$
$$C_{x}\approx C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{db1}+C_{gd1}$$

which is non dominant if $g_{m2}/C_{x} \gg 1/R_{out}C_{L}$.
* Noise: ${\overline {v_{n}^{2}}}\approx 4kT\gamma
(g_{m1}+g_{m2})/g_{m1}^{2}+K_{F}/WLC_{ox}f$.

In short: DC inverter $V_{OH}=V_{DD}$, $V_{OL}$ slightly
higher than $1T$ case, AC it is a common source
amplifier with effective transconductance $g_{m1}$, effective
output impedance $g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$ and voltage gain
$\approx -g_{m1}R_{D}$ for $R_{D}$ load, $\approx
-g_{m1}R_{o,eq}$ for active load, input impedance
capacitive $\infty$ at DC.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies the common-gate-driven stack, the lower device’s triode operation, and the effective channel length of approximately L1 + L2. However, it then analyzes the stack as a true cascode and claims a gm·ro-multiplied output resistance, a major error that contradicts the actual modest output-resistance increase.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is the $M_{1} \times M_{2}$ {\it composite}
or {\it self cascoded} common source stage.
With small $R_{D}$ it is the normal $C.S$.
With large $R_{D}$ it is formally a cascode with
$R_{D}\parallel R_{o}\approx R_{o}$.

$$S_{1}= {\rm bulk}-S_{1}\;\;,\;\;S_{2}={\rm bulk}-S_{2}$$

so that ideally $g_{mb}=0$ for small signal.
If the bulk is to $GND$ $g_{m2}\rightarrow g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$.

> {\it Remark} on large signal: With long channel
> square law and $V_{T1}=V_{T2}$ the two devices
> can {\it not} both be saturated with $V_{G1}=V_{G2}$.
> For

$$I_{D1}= {\beta_{1}\over 2}(V_{in}-V_{T})^{2}\;\;,\;\;
  I_{D2}= {\beta_{2}\over 2}(V_{in}-V_{x}-V_{T})^{2}$$

$I_{D1}=I_{D2}\Rightarrow $

$$V_{x}=V_{DS1}=(1-\sqrt{\beta_{1}/\beta_{2}})(V_{in}-V_{T})<V_{in}-V_{T}$$

so $M_{1}$ is linear, $M_{2}$ is saturated for the
normal high $V_{out}$ bias, Fig.1.  The composite as a
whole is saturated.  Let $Y=V_{in}-V_{T}$

$$ \beta_{1}(YV_{x}-V_{x}^{2}/2)= {\beta_{2}\over 2}(Y-V_{x})^{2}$$

$$\;V_{x}=Y\left[1-\sqrt{{\beta_{1}\over \beta_{1}+\beta_{2}}}\right]\;  $$

$$\;I_{D}= {\beta_{c}\over 2}Y^{2}\;\;,\;\;{\beta_{c}={\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\over \beta_{1}+\beta_{2}}}\;$$

For $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\beta$

$$V_{x}\approx 0.30\,Y\qquad I_{D}\approx {\beta\over 4}Y^{2}$$

i.e. the series combination is equivalent to one
device with

$$\left({W\over L}\right)_{c}^{-1}=\left({W\over L}\right)_{1}^{-1}
      +\left({W\over L}\right)_{2}^{-1}\qquad L_{c}=L_{1}+L_{2}$$

in first order.  If you keep both devices
in saturation by e.g. different $V_{T}$ or short
channel effects the small signal description below
with both $r_{o}'s$ is conventionally used in
text books. In that idealised case $M_{1}$ is taken
as saturated. The formulas remain formally the same
with $g_{m1},g_{o1}$ taken as triode values,
$g_{o1}\gg g_{o2}$.

### 1. Small signal model

Put $v_{in}=v_{g1}=v_{g2}$, $v_{x}=v_{d1}=v_{s2}$,
$v_{o}=v_{d2}$.

$$\eqalign{
i_{d1}&=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{o1}v_{x}\cr
i_{d2}&=g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_{x})+g_{o2}(v_{o}-v_{x})\cr
i_{d1}&=i_{d2}=i_{o}\cr
v_{o}&=-i_{o}R_{D}\;\;{\rm if}\;R_{D}{\rm\;is\;the\;load}}$$

$$ (g_{o1}+g_{m2}+g_{o2})v_{x}=(g_{m2}-g_{m1})v_{in}+g_{o2}v_{o}$$
$$ (1+g_{o2}R_{D})v_{o}+g_{m2}R_{D}v_{in}=(g_{m2}+g_{o2})R_{D}v_{x}$$

Eliminating $v_{x}$

$$v_{o}\left[g_{o1}+g_{m2}+g_{o2}+g_{o1}g_{o2}R_{D}\right]
      =-R_{D}\left[g_{m1}g_{m2}+g_{m1}g_{o2}+g_{m2}g_{o1}\right]v_{in}$$

$$\;A_{v}={v_{o}\over v_{in}}=
   -R_{D}{{g_{m1}g_{m2}+g_{m1}g_{o2}+g_{m2}g_{o1}}
               \over {g_{m2}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}+g_{o1}g_{o2}R_{D}}}\; \tag{1}$$

For $g_{m}\gg g_{o}$  numerator $\approx g_{m1}g_{m2}$,
denominator $\approx g_{m2}+g_{o1}g_{o2}R_{D}$.

### 2. Output resistance

Put $v_{in}=0$, apply $v_{x}=V_{test}$ at drain of
$M_{2}$.

$$g_{o1}v_{x1}= -g_{m2}v_{x1}+g_{o2}(V_{test}-v_{x1})$$

$$v_{x1}= {g_{o2}\over g_{o1}+g_{m2}+g_{o2}}V_{test}$$

$$I_{test}=g_{o1}v_{x1}= {g_{o1}g_{o2}\over g_{o1}+g_{m2}+g_{o2}}V_{test}$$

$$\;R_{o}\equiv {V_{test}\over I_{test}}
        ={g_{o1}+g_{m2}+g_{o2}\over g_{o1}g_{o2}}
        =r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\; \tag{2}$$

with body effect $g_{m2}\rightarrow g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$,

$$R_{o}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}\approx
 (g_{m2}r_{o2})r_{o1}$$

This is formally the cascode resistance.  With
$g_{in}=0$, $v_{in}=0$ it is the same as a cascode
because the two gates are AC ground for $R_{o}$.

For the real bias $M_{1}$ linear,
$g_{o1}=\beta_{1}(Y-V_{x})\approx g_{m2}\sim \beta Y$,
$g_{o2}= \lambda I_{D}\ll g_{o1}$ ,

$$R_{o}\approx {g_{o1}+g_{m2}\over g_{o1}g_{o2}}\approx {2\over g_{o2}}=2r_{o2}$$

i.e. only $\times 2$ over a single device.  If both
devices are forced saturated e.g. by $V_{T}$ engineering
$R_{o}\approx g_{m}r_{o}^{2}\gg r_{o}$.

Eq.(1) can be written with (2) as

$$A_{v}= -(R_{D}\parallel R_{o})\,
        {{g_{m1}g_{m2}+g_{m1}g_{o2}+g_{m2}g_{o1}\over g_{o1}+g_{m2}+g_{o2}}}$$

$$\;A_{v}\approx -(R_{D}\parallel R_{o})\,G_{m}\;$$

$$G_{m}={g_{m1}g_{m2}+g_{m1}g_{o2}+g_{m2}g_{o1}\over g_{m2}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}}
 \xrightarrow[g_{o}\ll g_{m}]{}g_{m1}$$

and for matched devices $G_{m}=g_{m}$ exactly.
I.e.

$$\;A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}\,(R_{D}\parallel R_{o})\;
      \approx -g_{m1}R_{D}\;\;{\rm for}\;R_{D}\ll R_{o}\; \tag{3}$$

Normal cascode gain $-g_{m1}(R_{D}\parallel g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2})$
is recovered. With ideal current source load
$R_{D}\rightarrow \infty$

$$|A_{v0}|\approx g_{m1}R_{o}\approx g_{m}r_{o}\;{\rm for\;triode\;}M_{1}
  \approx g_{m}^{2}r_{o}^{2}\;{\rm for\;ideal\;saturated\;}M_{1}M_{2}$$

### 3. Large signal inverter characteristic

* $V_{in}<V_{T}$ : $M_{1},M_{2}$ off, $I_{D}=0$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$
* $V_{T}<V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{T}|+V_{x}$ : $M_{1}$ linear,
  $M_{2}$ saturated. $V_{out}=V_{DD}-R_{D}I_{D}(V_{in})$,
  $I_{D}=(\beta_{c}/2)(V_{in}-V_{T})^{2}$, inverting
  high gain region with slope (3).
* $V_{out}<V_{in}-V_{T}$ : $M_{2}$ enters triode,
  both linear, $V_{out}=V_{OL}=I_{D}R_{on}\approx 0$.

$V_{M}$ where $V_{in}=V_{out}$ is shifted to higher
$V_{in}$ with respect to a single $W/L$ device because
$\beta_{c}<\beta_{1}$.

Input impedance $Z_{in}\approx 1/s(C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+C_{gd2}(1-A_{v}))$
capacitive, very high at DC.  Miller multiplication is
essentially by $C_{gd2}$ only; $C_{gd1}$ is between
$v_{in}$ and $v_{x}\approx 0.3v_{in}$ so Miller $\approx 0.7$.

In short: at DC it is a logic inverter / common source
amplifier whose pull down is a composite NMOS of effective
length $L_{1}+L_{2}$. To first order it gives the same
$g_{m}$ as $M_{1}$ but with $r_{o}$ multiplied by
$g_{m}r_{o}$ in the ideal saturated limit, and by $\sim 2$
in the ordinary $V_{T}$ matched long channel bias. It is
widely used as self cascode current mirror, high swing
cascode load and as a way to get a long $L$ device without
a long $L$ layout. Drawbacks: $\sim C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}$ input
cap, limited headroom $V_{DS,sat,c}=V_{DS,sat1}+V_{DS,sat2}$,
somewhat lower $f_{T}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies the common-gate series NMOS composite, places M1 in triode and M2 in saturation, and derives the effective channel length as approximately L1 + L2. Its actual-bias output resistance is also correctly distinguished from the hypothetical both-saturated cascode case.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is the $NMOS$, $n-$ channel
{\it long tail} or {\it source coupled pair} with
single sided resistive load. In bipolar form the
vacuum tube form.

$$M_{1}-M_{2}:{\rm pair}\;\;{\rm sources\;common}\;\;{\rm on}\;I_{1}$$
$$M_{1}:G=V_{in}\;\;D=V_{DD}{\rm\;ac\;0}\equiv {\rm CD}$$
$$M_{2}:G=V_{b}{\rm\;ac\;0}\;\;D=R_{D}{\rm\;to\;}V_{DD}\equiv {\rm CG}$$

so the circuit is a ${\rm CD}$ driving a ${\rm CG}$.
With $V_{b}= {\rm ac\;0}$ it is a non inverting
voltage amplifier and with $V_{b}\ne 0$ it is
a $V_{in}-V_{b}$ differential to single ended
transducer. For $|V_{in}-V_{b}|$
small enough both devices are saturated.

> In the normal form both drains have a $R_{D}$ and
> the balanced differential output is $g_{m}R_{D}(V_{in}-V_{b})$.
> With one $R_{D}$ omitted the single ended output is
> $1/2$ of that.

### 1. Qualitative

$I_{1}=I_{D1}+I_{D2}= {\rm const}$ for ideal tail.

Increase $V_{in}\to$ $V_{GS1}\uparrow \to I_{D1}\uparrow \to$
since $I_{1}$ const $I_{D2}\downarrow \to $ drop on
$R_{D}$ $\downarrow \to V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D}\uparrow$.
