```
        |  Cx RB=roB             gm1vgs
 Iin>---|---X --- GB -----------o    
              |
             GND
```

$G_{1}=g_{ds1}=r_{o1}^{-1}$ , $G_{2}=g_{ds2}$ ,
$G_{I}=g_{oI1}=r_{oI1}^{-1}$ , $G_{B}=g_{oB}=r_{oB}^{-1}$
$C_{X},C_{Y}$ the total capacitance at $X$ and $Y$,
$g_{m1}^{\prime}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}\approx g_{m1}$ if
$M_{1}$ $B$ to $S$.

Small signal $V_{b}=0$.

$$v_{gs1}=-v_{x}\;\;v_{bs1}=-v_{x}\;\;v_{ds1}=v_{y}-v_{x}$$
$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}^{\prime}v_{gs1}+G_{1}v_{ds1}
=-g_{m1}^{\prime}v_{x}+G_{1}(v_{y}-v_{x})\;\;D\to S\tag{1}$$
$M_{2}$ $S=V_{DD}=0$

$$v_{sg2}=-v_{y}\;\;v_{sd2}=-v_{x}$$
$$i_{s2d2}=g_{m2}v_{sg2}+G_{2}v_{sd2}
=-g_{m2}v_{y}-G_{2}v_{x}\;\;S\to D\tag{2}$$
enters node $X$, leaves $V_{DD}$.
Currents $i_{d1}$ and $i_{s2d2}$ both enter $X$ and
$i_{d1}$ leaves $Y$.

KCL ac:

$$i_{in}+i_{d1}+i_{s2d2}-(G_{B}+sC_{X})v_{x}=0\tag{3}$$
$$-(G_{I}+sC_{Y})v_{y}-i_{d1}+i_{t}=0\tag{4}$$
$i_{t}$ test current at $Y$. For closed loop signal
$i_{t}=0$.

Put (1)(2) in (3)(4):

$$\left.\begin{aligned}
i_{in}+(G_{1}-g_{m2})v_{y}-
\left[g_{m1}^{\prime}+G_{1}+G_{2}+G_{B}+sC_{X}\right]v_{x}=0\\
\left[g_{m1}^{\prime}+G_{1}\right]v_{x}
-\left[G_{1}+G_{I}+sC_{Y}\right]v_{y}+i_{t}=0
\end{aligned}\right\}\tag{5}$$

#### D.C. bias

$$V_{GS1}=V_{b}-V_{X}\qquad V_{X}\approx V_{b}-V_{Tn}-V_{ov1}$$
$$I_{D1}=I_{1}\tag{6}$$
$$I_{D2}=I_{B}-I_{1}-I_{in,DC}\tag{7}$$
in saturation

$$V_{DS1}=V_{Y}-V_{X}>V_{ov1}\;\;V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{X}>V_{ov2}$$
$$r\approx V_{DD}-|V_{ov,I1}|>V_{Y}>V_{X}+V_{ov1}$$
Normal design $I_{B}>I_{1}>0$, $M_{1},M_{2}$ saturated.
$V_{in}=V_{X}$ sets the input common mode by $V_{b}$.

The loop is negative:
$\uparrow v_{x}\to \downarrow v_{gs1}\to \downarrow i_{d1}
\to \uparrow v_{y}\to \downarrow v_{sg2}\to
\downarrow i_{s2d2}\to \downarrow v_{x}$.

#### Feedforward amp and loop gain

To first order, with the loop broken, the ${\rm CG}$
stage loaded by $R_{D}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{oI1}=
1/(G_{1}+G_{I})$ has

$$A_{v}=v_{y}/v_{x}\approx g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{D}\quad
R_{m0}=v_{y}/i_{in}\approx R_{D}\tag{8}$$

in shunt-shunt ${\rm Y}$ model.

Feedback

$$\beta =i_{f}/v_{y}\approx -g_{m2}\tag{9}$$

Loop gain with $X$ and $Y$ loaded

$$T_{0}=A_{m0}\beta \approx -g_{m2}R_{D}
=-\frac{g_{m2}}{G_{1}+G_{I}}\gg 1\tag{10}$$
if $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$.
Usually $|T_{0}|\approx 20$-$50\,{\rm dB}$.

#### Closed loop - small signal stationary, $s=0$

From (5) with $i_{t}=0$

$$v_{x}=v_{y}\frac{G_{I}+G_{1}}{g_{m1}^{\prime}+G_{1}}\tag{11}$$

$$i_{in}=v_{y}\left[g_{m2}+G_{I}+
\frac{(G_{I}+G_{1})(G_{2}+G_{B})}{g_{m1}^{\prime}+G_{1}}\right]\tag{12}$$

$$\;R_{m}\equiv \frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=
\frac{1}{g_{m2}+G_{I}+{\displaystyle
\frac{(G_{I}+G_{1})(G_{2}+G_{B})}{g_{m1}^{\prime}+G_{1}}}}\;
\tag{13}$$

In the ideal limit $r_{o}\to\infty$,
$G\to 0$,

$$R_{m0}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}\tag{14}$$
$$v_{x}\approx 0\;{\rm virtual\;ground}\tag{15}$$
i.e. the current is forced through the feedback
$g_{m2}$.  With Blackman
$R_{m}=R_{m0}/(1+T_{0})\approx -1/\beta$.

$$R_{in}= \frac{v_{x}}{i_{in}}=
R_{m}\frac{G_{I}+G_{1}}{g_{m1}^{\prime}+G_{1}}
\approx \frac{G_{I}+G_{1}}{g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}}
=\frac{1}{g_{m1}^{\prime}}\frac{1}{1+T_{0}}\tag{16}$$

Ideal:

$$R_{in}\to 0 \tag{17}$$

In practice

$$R_{in}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D}}
\approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}^{\prime}|T_{0}|}\ll \frac{1}{g_{m1}^{\prime}}$$

e.g. $g_{m1}=g_{m2}=1\,{\rm mS}$, $R_{D}=50\,{\rm k\Omega}$,
$|T_{0}|=50$, $1/g_{m1}=1\,{\rm k\Omega}\to R_{in}\approx
20\,{\rm \Omega}$.

That is the regulated ${\rm CG}$ principle: low $R_{in}$
without burning current in $g_{m1}$ for wide band
photodiode ${\rm TIA}$ operation.

Output impedance, set $i_{in}=0$, inject $v_{t}=v_{y}$
from (5):

$$v_{x}=v_{t}\frac{G_{1}-g_{m2}}
{g_{m1}^{\prime}+G_{1}+G_{2}+G_{B}+sC_{X}}\tag{18}$$

$$i_{t}=v_{t}(G_{I}+sC_{Y})+g_{m1}^{\prime}v_{x}
+G_{1}(v_{t}-v_{x})\tag{19}$$

$$Z_{out}(s)=\frac{v_{t}}{i_{t}} \tag{20}$$
$$R_{out}=Z_{out}(0)=
\frac{g_{m1}^{\prime}+G_{1}+G_{2}+G_{B}}
{(g_{m2}+G_{I})(g_{m1}^{\prime}+G_{1})
+(G_{I}+G_{1})(G_{2}+G_{B})}\tag{21}$$

Ideal $G\to 0$

$$R_{out}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+G_{I}}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}
\parallel r_{oI1}\tag{22}$$

again shunted by $1+T_{0}$ :

$$R_{out}=R_{D}/(1+T_{0})$$

In the ideal shunt at input, shunt at output both
impedances are divided by the loop gain.

Finite $r_{o}$ correction is $O(1/g_{m}r_{o})$.

#### Poles - stability

Put $G_{B},G_{2}\to 0$ for clarity.
From (5) the characteristic polynomial is

$$D(s)=(G_{I}+G_{1}+sC_{Y})
(g_{m1}^{\prime}+G_{1}+sC_{X})+(g_{m1}^{\prime}+G_{1})
(g_{m2}-G_{1})\approx 0\tag{23}$$
$$D\approx s^{2}C_{X}C_{Y}+s\left[C_{Y}g_{m1}^{\prime}
+C_{X}(G_{I}+G_{1})\right]+g_{m1}^{\prime}(g_{m2}+G_{I})\tag{24}$$

Two real poles for $|T_{0}|\gg 1$

$$p_{o}\approx -\frac{g_{m2}+G_{I}}{C_{Y}}\approx -\frac{1}{R_{out}C_{Y}}$$

$$p_{i}\approx -\frac{g_{m1}^{\prime}}{C_{X}}
\tag{25}$$
with the node $X$ pole pushed to very high
frequency because $R_{in}$ is small. The loop
has $\approx 90^{o}$ phase shift at each pole,
$\approx 180^{o}$ total, the circuit is conditonally
stable. If

$$p_{i}\approx p_{o}$$

large peaking and ringing occurs. Usually
$C_{X}\gg C_{Y}$ is the photodiode case so
$p_{i}<p_{o}$ and the dominant pole is at the input.
Because $R_{in}$ is tiny the dominant pole is
pushed out $\times |T_{0}|$, extending bandwidth
by the regulation factor compared to a simple ${\rm CG}$
$1/g_{m1}C_{X}$ TIA.  $Z_{in}(s)$ looks inductive,
$Z_{in}\approx sC_{Y}/g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}$, usable as
active inductor peaking.

A small compensation $C_{c}$ at $Y$ or series resistor
can be added for phase margin $>60^{o}$.

> *Regulated cascode / flipped voltage follower TIA*
> : sh-sh voltage-sampling current-mixing feedback,
> ideal transresistance $1/g_{m2}$, ideal $R_{in}=0$,
> ideal $R_{out}=1/g_{m2}$, large bandwidth because
> both poles are at $g_{m}/C$.

Non-ideally add $r_{o}$ corrections (13)(16)(21).
Including $g_{mb1}$ just replace $g_{m1}\to g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$.
Noise is dominated by $M_{1},M_{2}$ and $R_{B},R_{I}$,
input referred $\overline{i_{n}^{2}}\approx
4kT\gamma(g_{m1}+g_{m2})/|T_{0}|^{2}+4kT/R_{D}|T_{0}|^{2}$.

Large signal swing: $I_{in,peak}<I_{D2}$ positive,
$|I_{in,peak}|<I_{1}$ negative before $M_{1}$ or $M_{2}$
triodes / cuts off.

Application: low power low impedance current buffer,
current conveyor ${\rm CCII}$, optical receiver
front end, active inductor load.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate input device and M2 as the output-driven feedback device, describes the loop back to the input node, and derives very low input resistance with transimpedance and output resistance approximately 1/gm2. The additional analysis does not undermine the essential result.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Circuit is the {\it regulated cascode} or
shunt-shunt active feedback transimpedance amplifier.
In its present form it is also called the flipped
voltage follower TIA.

$$M_{1} :N\;CG\qquad M_{2}:P\;CS$$
$$V_{GS1}=V_{b}-V_{X}\qquad V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{Y}$$
$$V_{DS1}=V_{Y}-V_{X}\qquad V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{X}$$

Ideal small signal $C_{gs},C_{gd}=0$, $r_{ob}=1/g_{b}=\infty
,$$V_{b}~ac=0$ , $V_{DD}~ac=0$ . Bodies on the sources so that
$g_{mb}=0$. With bodies to supply

$$g_{m}\rightarrow g_{m}+g_{mb}\tag*$$

> $$ {\rm ideal: }g_{b1}=g_{b2}=0\;\; ,r_{oI1}=1/G_{I1},
r_{oIb}=1/G_{Ib}\rightarrow \infty {\rm  for\;hand\;calc.}$$

$$\eqalign{
I_{M1}&=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}\cr
&=-g_{m1}v_{x}+g_{ds1}(v_{y}-v_{x})\cr
&=-(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})v_{x}+g_{ds1}v_{y}\;\;{\rm D\rightarrow S}\cr
I_{M2}&=g_{m2}v_{sg2}+g_{ds2}v_{sd2}\cr
&=-g_{m2}v_{y}+g_{ds2}(-v_{x})\cr
&=-g_{ds2}v_{x}-g_{m2}v_{y}\;\;{\rm S\rightarrow D} }$$

where $I_{M1}$ is the conventional NMOS $D\rightarrow S$ current
leaving $Y$ and entering $X$ and $I_{M2}$ the PMOS $S\rightarrow D$
current entering $X$.

```
Y=Vout o----+----g M2
            |     |
           ro1   gm2,ro2
            |     |
M1 D--------+-+   +---X----o Iin
 |  gm1,ro1 | |   |   |
 M1 S-------+-----+---o--Ib , Cib
            |         |
           Cx        Cy
```

Nodal $ac$ KCL, $G_{I1}=g_{oI1}$ , $G_{Ib}=g_{oIb}$,

$$Y:\;\;I_{M1}+G_{I1}v_{y}=I_{testY}\tag{1}$$
$$X:\;\;I_{M1}+I_{M2}-G_{Ib}v_{x}+I_{in}=0\tag{2}$$

For $I_{test}=0$

$$-(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})v_{x}+(g_{ds1}+G_{I1})v_{y}=0\tag{3}$$

$${{v_{y}}\over{v_{x}}}={{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}\over{g_{ds1}+G_{I1}}}
\equiv A_{v0} \approx g_{m1}r_{o1}\parallel R_{I1}>0 \tag{4}$$

The $CG$ stage is non inverting. With
$R_{Y}=1/(g_{ds1}+G_{I1})=r_{o1}\parallel R_{I1}$

$$A_{v0}\approx g_{m1}R_{Y}\gg 1$$

From (2)-(3)

$$I_{in}= \left[g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+G_{Ib}
+{{(g_{m2}-g_{ds1})(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})}\over{g_{ds1}+G_{I1}}}\right]v_{x}
\tag{5}$$

$$\eqalign{
Z_{in}&={{v_{x}}\over{I_{in}}}=
{{g_{ds1}+G_{I1}}\over{(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})(g_{m2}+G_{I1})
+(g_{ds1}+G_{I1})(g_{ds2}+G_{Ib})}}\cr
&\approx {{G_{I1}+g_{ds1}}\over{g_{m1}g_{m2}}}
={{1}\over{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{Y}}}\approx {{1}\over{g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}}}
\;\;{\rm for}\;G_{I1},G_{Ib}\ll g_{ds} } \tag{6}$$

So called $1/g_{m}$ boosted by the loop gain.
Without $M_{2}$

$$Z_{in0}\approx {1\over{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+G_{Ib}}}
\approx 1/g_{m1}$$

With regulation

$$Z_{in}={{Z_{in0}}\over{1+T_{0}}}\qquad 
T_{0}\approx g_{m2}R_{Y} \tag{7}$$

$$R_{m}={{v_{y}}\over{I_{in}}}={{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}\over
{(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})(g_{m2}+G_{I1})+(g_{ds1}+G_{I1})(g_{ds2}+G_{Ib})}}
\tag{8}$$

$$R_{m}\approx {1\over{g_{m2}+G_{I1}}}\approx {1\over g_{m2}}\tag{9}
 {\rm ideal\;shunt-shunt\;value\;}R_{M,ideal}=-1/\beta ,\,
\beta \approx g_{m2}$$

Sign is $>0$ for the $P/N$ choice. In the usual $n-n$
implementation $R_{M}\approx -1/g_{m2}$ inverting.
More generally with a finite load $R_{D}$ to ground at $Y$,

$$R_{M}\approx -R_{D}\;{{T_{0}}\over{1+T_{0}}}\rightarrow -R_{D}
\;{\rm for}\;T_{0}\gg 1\;\;{\rm and}\;\;
R_{M}\rightarrow -1/g_{m2}\;{\rm for}\;R_{D}\rightarrow \infty $$

From (1) with $I_{in}=0$ and a test source at $Y$

$$Z_{out}={{v_{y}}\over{I_{test}}}=
{{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+G_{Ib}}\over
{(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})(g_{m2}+G_{I1})+(g_{ds1}+G_{I1})(g_{ds2}+G_{Ib})}}
\tag{10}$$

$$Z_{out}\approx {1\over g_{m2}}\;{{g_{m1}R_{Y}}\over{1+g_{m2}R_{Y}}}
+{\cal O}(r_{o}^{-1})\approx {1\over g_{m2}}\tag{11}$$

again ${{R_{Y}}\over{1+T_{0}}}$. The open loop output
resistance without feedback is $R_{Y}=r_{o1}\parallel R_{I1}$.

That is the classical shunt-shunt result:

sampling voltage at $Y$, mixing shunt at $X$.
Loop gain with the loop broken at the gate of $M_{2}$:

$$T(s)\approx {{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{Y}Z_{X}(s)}\over{1+g_{m1}Z_{X}(s)}}
{1\over{1+sR_{Y}C_{Y}}}{1\over{1+sZ_{X}C_{X}}}$$

low frequency

$$T_{0}\approx g_{m2}R_{Y}\;{{g_{m1}Z_{X0}}\over{1+g_{m1}Z_{X0}}}
\approx g_{m2}R_{Y}\gg 1\tag{12}$$

$$Z_{X0}=1/(g_{ds2}+G_{Ib})$$

Exact second order:

$$T(s)\approx {{g_{m1}g_{m2}}\over{(g_{ds1}+G_{I1}+sC_{Y})
(g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+G_{Ib}+sC_{X})}} \tag{13}$$

### DC bias

$$V_{X}=V_{b}-V_{GS1}\tag{14}$$
$$V_{Y}=V_{DD}-V_{SG2}\tag{15}$$
$$I_{D1}\approx I_{1}\tag{16}$$
$$I_{D1}={1\over 2}\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}(V_{GS1}-V_{Tn})^{2}(1+\lambda_{n}V_{DS1})$$
$$I_{D2}={1\over 2}\mu_{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}(V_{SG2}-|V_{Tp}|)^{2}(1+\lambda_{p}V_{SD2})$$
$$I_{Ib}=I_{D1}+I_{D2}+I_{in,DC}\tag{17}$$

Needed for saturation

$$V_{DS1}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{Tn}\;,\;\;V_{SD2}\ge V_{SG2}-|V_{Tp}|$$
$$V_{b}>V_{X}+V_{Tn}+V_{ov1}\;,\;\;
V_{Y}<V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|-V_{ov2}$$

Headroom $V_{DD,min}\approx V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}+|V_{Tp}|+V_{Tn}$.

### High frequency

Let $C_{X}=C_{gs1}+C_{sb1}+C_{db2}+C_{Ib}+C_{PD}$ ,
$C_{Y}=C_{gd1}+C_{gd2}+C_{db1}+C_{I1}+C_{L}$ .

Closed loop poles are the roots of $1+T(s)=0$,

$$\omega_{pY}\approx {1\over R_{Y}C_{Y}}(1+T_{0})^{-1}\approx
{g_{m2}\over C_{Y}}$$

$$\omega_{pX}\approx {g_{m1}\over C_{X}}(1+T_{0})\approx
{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{Y}\over C_{X}}$$

so the former dominant $R_{Y}C_{Y}$ pole is pushed to
$\sim g_{m2}/C_{Y}$ and the input pole
$1/g_{m1}C_{X}$ is pushed out by $T_{0}$.
Bandwidth is hence $\sim \min (\omega_{pX},\omega_{pY})$
and can be made much larger than a simple $CG$ stage
with $R_{in}=1/g_{m1}$ which is limited by $C_{PD}R_{in}$.

Both poles in the left half plane for $T_{0}>0$ - negative
feedback. Two-pole system may have peaking if
$\omega_{pX}\approx \omega_{pY}$. Usually $C_{X}\gg C_{Y}$
in photoreceiver use so $\omega_{pY}>\omega_{pX}$ and the
response is stable; otherwise a capacitance to ground at $Y$
or series peaking resistor is added for phase margin.

### Remarks

* Low $Z_{in}\propto 1/g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{Y}$ isolates the large
photodiode capacitance from bandwidth.
* Moderate transimpedance $\approx 1/g_{m2}$ without an
explicit resistor. To obtain larger $R_{M}$ add $R_{D}$ from
$Y$ to $ac$ ground: $R_{M}\rightarrow -R_{D}$ for $T_{0}\gg 1$.
This is the conventional RGC TIA.
* Input referred current noise $\approx 4kT\gamma(g_{m1}+g_{m2})
+4kT/R_{Y}$ dominated by $M_{2}$ reflected as
$\overline{i_{n,in}^{2}}\approx 4kT\gamma g_{m2}$.
* Can be seen as a flipped voltage follower FVF: $M_{1}$
is the follower device, $M_{2}$ the level shifter that
keeps $V_{X}$ constant.
* With ideal $R_{I1},R_{Ib}\rightarrow \infty$:

$$Z_{in}\approx 1/g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1},\;
Z_{out}\approx 1/g_{m2},\;
R_{m}\approx 1/g_{m2},\;
A_{v}=v_{y}/v_{x}\approx g_{m1}r_{o1}$$

E.g. $g_{m}=1\,{\rm mS},r_{o}=10\,{\rm k\Omega}\rightarrow
Z_{in}\sim 100\,\Omega ,\,R_{m}\sim 1\,{\rm k\Omega},\,
A_{v}\sim 10$.

That is the small-signal, low-frequency analysis. Inclusion of
body effect: $g_{m1}\rightarrow g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$, i.e.
$$Z_{in}\approx (g_{ds1}+G_{I1})/(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})g_{m2}.$$
Any finite $C$ restores the exact second-order expressions
above.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate NMOS and M2 as the PMOS feedback device, describes feedback from the output node to the input node, and gives the expected very low input resistance and transimpedance/output resistance of approximately 1/gm2.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
With ideal current sources $g_{I1}=1/r_{I1}\to 0$
$g_{I2}=1/r_{I2}\to 0$ put

$${\rm M_{1}}: n{\rm MOST}\;\;D\equiv {\rm out}\;,\;S\equiv x\;,\;G\equiv
V_{b}\approx {\rm ac\;gnd}$$
$${\rm M_{2}}: p{\rm MOST}\;\;S\equiv V_{DD}\approx {\rm ac\;gnd}\;,\;
D\equiv x\;,\;G\equiv {\rm out}$$

$$g_{m1,2}\;\;g_{ds1,2}=1/r_{o1,2}\;\;g_{mb1}$$

$$I_{D1}=I_{1}\qquad I_{D2}=I_{B}-I_{D1}-I_{in}\approx I_{B}-I_{1}$$

on dc $I_{in}=0$ for bias. Saturation requires

$$\eqalign{
V_{GS1}&=V_{b}-V_{x} >V_{Tn}\cr
V_{DS1}&=V_{out}-V_{x} >V_{GS1}-V_{Tn}=V_{ov1}\cr
\left|V_{SG2}\right|&=V_{DD}-V_{out}> \left|V_{Tp}\right|\cr
V_{SD2}&=V_{DD}-V_{x}> \left|V_{SG2}\right|-\left|V_{Tp}\right|=V_{ov2}}$$

$$V_{x}\approx V_{b}-V_{GS1}\qquad 
V_{out}\approx V_{DD}-\left|V_{SG2}\right|$$

$$g_{m1}=\sqrt{2\mu _{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}I_{1}}\;\;,\;
g_{m2}=\sqrt{2\mu _{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}I_{D2}}$$

is the normal regulated - cascode, super common
gate, flipped voltage follower, shunt - shunt
feedback TIA. In ac

```
                VDD ac gnd ----o----o
                               |    |
                              roI1  S M2 G---o Vout
                               |    D      |
                               o----o------o
                               |    |
                              D M1  Cgs2+ro2
                              S |
              Vb---G M1       o----o Vx ---- Iin + IB roI2 to gnd
                     gmb1 ro1 Cgs1 Cgd1 Cgd2 Cx
```

*Forward amplifier:* $M_{1}$ common gate
$x\to out$

$$v_{gs1}=-v_{x}\;\;v_{ds1}=v_{out}-v_{x}$$

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{mb1}v_{bs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}$$

with $v_{bs1}=-v_{x}$ put $g_{m1}^{\prime}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$

$$i_{d1}=-g_{m1}^{\prime}v_{x}+g_{ds1}(v_{out}-v_{x})\tag{1}$$

*Feed back amplifier:* $M_{2}$ common source
$out\to x$

$$v_{sg2}=-v_{out}\;\;v_{sd2}=-v_{x}$$

small signal {\it source to drain } current entering
$x$ :

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{sg2}+g_{ds2}v_{sd2}
      =-g_{m2}v_{out}-g_{ds2}v_{x}\tag{2}$$
enters $x$.

KCL at $out$ , current $I_{1}$ to ac gnd $g_{I1}$:

$$i_{d1}+g_{I1}v_{out}=0\tag{3}$$

$1\to 3$:

$$-(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})v_{x}+(g_{ds1}+g_{I1})v_{out}=0\tag{4}$$

$$v_{x}= {g_{ds1}+g_{I1}\over g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}}v_{out}
      \approx {1\over g_{m1}^{\prime}r_{o1}}v_{out}\propto v_{out}$$

for $g_{I1}\ll g_{ds1}$. So voltage gain $x\to out$

$$A_{vx}= {v_{out}\over v_{x}}={g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\over
g_{ds1}+g_{I1}}\approx g_{m1}^{\prime}r_{o1}\parallel r_{I1}\gg 1\tag{5}$$

{\it non inverting}.

Gain of $M_{2}$, loaded by $x$ :

$$A_{2}= {v_{x}\over v_{out}}\vert_{I_{in}=0}
      \approx -{g_{m2}\over g_{m1}^{\prime}}\;\;{\rm inverting}$$

Loop gain broken at $G_{2}$:

$$T_{0}\approx A_{vx}A_{2}\approx -g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{I1})
\qquad |T_{0}|\gg 1\tag{6}$$

KCL at $x$ , $I_{in}$ entering:

$$I_{in}+i_{d1}+i_{d2}-g_{I2}v_{x}=0\tag{7}$$

$$I_{in}-(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+g_{I2})v_{x}
      +(g_{ds1}-g_{m2})v_{out}=0\tag{8}$$

With $4$ eliminates $v_{x}$

$$I_{in}= \left[ g_{I1}+g_{m2}+{(g_{ds2}+g_{I2})(g_{ds1}+g_{I1})
\over g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}}\right] v_{out}\tag{9}$$

Hence shunt - shunt closed loop transimpedance

$$R_{m}={v_{out}\over I_{in}}=
{1\over g_{m2}+g_{I1}+{(g_{ds1}+g_{I1})(g_{ds2}+g_{I2})\over
g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}}} \tag{10}$$

For $r_{I1},r_{I2}\to \infty $

$$R_{m0}\approx {1\over g_{m2}+{g_{ds1}g_{ds2}\over g_{m1}^{\prime}}}
\approx {1\over g_{m2}} >0\tag{11}$$

$I_{in}>0\to v_{x}\uparrow\to v_{gs1}\downarrow\to
i_{d1}\downarrow\to i_{I1}{\rm \;excess\;charges\;}
v_{out}\uparrow$.
Feedback $v_{out}\uparrow\to v_{sg2}\downarrow\to i_{d2}\downarrow
\to v_{x}\downarrow$ {\it negative} feedback.

If $g_{I1}\ne 0$ the load at $out$ is $r_{I1}$ so (11) is
$1/(g_{m2}+g_{I1})$. To get large $R_{m}$ the load must be a
resistor $R_{D}=1/g_{I1}$ and (11) is really $R_{D}/(1+g_{m2}R_{D})$
in parallel with the feedback. With the ideal current source
load the asymptotic $R_{m}$ is limited to $1/g_{m2}$, typically
$0.2-2\,{\rm k\Omega}$. Normally $R_{D}$ is kept as $R_{D}=
r_{o1}\parallel r_{I1}$ and the RGC is used as {\it input
stage} to get very low $R_{in}$ without losing the $R_{D}$
gain. In the simple circuit shown the large $A_{vx}$ is degenerated
to $1/g_{m2}$ because most of $I_{in}$ is shunted by the feedback
device. More generally with a $R_{D}$ to $V_{DD}$ at $out$,
$R_{m}\approx R_{D}$ for $|T_{0}|\gg 1$.

By (4)(9)

$$R_{in}={v_{x}\over I_{in}}=
{g_{ds1}+g_{I1}\over g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}}R_{m}
={g_{ds1}+g_{I1}\over (g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})(g_{m2}+g_{I1})
+(g_{ds1}+g_{I1})(g_{ds2}+g_{I2})}\tag{12}$$

$$R_{in0}\approx {g_{ds1}\over g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}}
={1\over g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}r_{o1}}\tag{13}$$

A simple common gate has $R_{in,CG}\approx 1/g_{m1}^{\prime}$.
Regulation improves it by the loop gain

$$R_{in,RGC}\approx {R_{in,CG}\over 1+|T_{0}|}
\approx {1\over g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}r_{o1}}\;\;10-50\times{\rm lower}$$

Typically $50-200\,\Omega$, capable of absorbing the large
photodiode capacitance $C_{PD}$ at the input.

Output resistance seen at $v_{out}$ for $I_{in}=0$, test source
$v_{t}=v_{out}$ injecting $i_{t}$:

$$i_{t}= (g_{ds1}+g_{I1})v_{t}-(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})v_{x}$$
$$0=-(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+g_{I2})v_{x}+(g_{ds1}-g_{m2})v_{t}$$

$$R_{out}={v_{t}\over i_{t}}=
{g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+g_{I2}\over
(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})(g_{m2}+g_{I1})+(g_{ds1}+g_{I1})(g_{ds2}+g_{I2})}
\tag{14}$$

$$R_{out0}\approx {1\over g_{m2}+g_{I1}}\approx {1\over g_{m2}}\tag{15}$$

if $g_{I1}=0$. Low impedance, the RGC is a good voltage driver.
If the output is taken at $x$ - the flipped voltage follower
usage - $R_{out,x}=R_{in}$, ultra low $\approx 1/g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o}$,
voltage follower gain $\approx 1$.

Poles: with $C_{x}=C_{gs1}+C_{sb1}+C_{gd2}+C_{db2}+C_{PD}$ at $x$
and $C_{out}=C_{gd1}+C_{db1}+C_{gs2}+C_{db2}+C_{L}$ at out

$$p_{x}\approx -{1\over R_{in}C_{x}}\qquad 
  p_{out}\approx -{1\over R_{out}C_{out}} \tag{16}$$

Because $R_{in}$ is $\propto 1/|T_{0}|$ the input pole is pushed
out by $|T_{0}|$, extending bandwidth by $g_{m2}r_{o1}$ over the CG.
Normally

$$|p_{x}|\approx {g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}r_{o1}\over C_{x}}\;\;,
  |p_{out}|\approx {g_{m2}\over C_{out}}$$

both at high frequency, giving GHz bandwidth for $C_{PD}\sim 100{\rm fF}$.
The two poles are close, loop is second order. Need

$$|p_{out}|>2|p_{x}|\;\;{\rm or\;capacitive\;compensation\;at\;}out$$

for $PM>60^{\circ}$. Peaking and possible oscillation for large
$C_{PD}$.

Large signal swing: $\Delta V_{out}^{+}$ limited by $M_{1}$ entering
triode, $\Delta V_{out}^{-}$ by $M_{2}$ entering triode, typically
$V_{DD}-2V_{ov}-V_{Tn}-|V_{Tp}|\approx 0.5-1\,{\rm V}$ in low $V_{DD}$.

Noise: input referred current noise

$$\overline{i_{n,in}^{2}}\approx 4kT\gamma(g_{m1}+g_{m2})+
4kT/R_{B}+ \overline{i_{n,I1}^{2}}+\overline{i_{n,I2}^{2}}$$

dominated by $M_{1},M_{2}$.

In summary the circuit is the {\it regulated cascode / super
common gate / active feedback common gate transimpedance stage}.
It samples the output voltage with $M_{2}$ and mixes a current at the
input, shunt-shunt feedback, giving

* $R_{m}\approx 1/g_{m2}$ - low but wideband, can be increased to
$R_{D}$ with a resistive load,
* $R_{in}$ reduced by $1+|T_{0}|\approx g_{m2}r_{o1}$ to $1/g_{m}g_{m}r_{o}$
$\sim 10^{1}-10^{2}\Omega$,
* $R_{out}\sim 1/g_{m2}$,
* bandwidth $\times |T_{0}|$ over simple CG, used almost universally
as the low $Z_{in}$ front end of CMOS optical receivers, current
conveyors CCII, and low voltage flipped voltage followers. With
output taken at $x$ it is the $g_{m}$-boosted source follower with
gain $\approx 1$ and $R_{out}\approx 1/g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate NMOS and M2 as the PMOS feedback device driven by Vout, describes feedback to the input node, and gives the very low input resistance and vout/iin and Rout ≈ 1/gm2 results. This satisfies the golden solution’s full-credit rule.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
With the usual first order small signal model
the statement is, in the strict sense, false.
Put, for the $i$ th inverter,

$$A_{v}=-g_{m}R_{o}\qquad R_{o}=r_{on}\parallel r_{op}
\qquad \tau =R_{o}C_{L}$$

so that with the ``load'' $C_{L}$

$$A(s)= {{-A_{v}}\over {1+s\tau}} \tag{*}$$

and, open the loop e. {\it g.} at the input of
$I_{1}$,

$$L(s)=A(s)^{3}= -{{A_{v}^{3}}\over {(1+s\tau )^{3}}}\tag{1}$$

at $s=0$, $L(0)=-A_{v}^{3}$, $180^{{\rm o}}$
mod. $360^{{\rm o}}$.

$$\eqalign{
|{L(j\omega )} |&={{A_{v}^{3}}\over {\left[1+(\omega \tau )^{2}
\right]^{3/2}}}\cr
{\rm arg}L(j\omega )&= 3\pi -3{\rm arctan}\,\omega \tau
\equiv \pi -3{\rm arctan}\,\omega \tau \;{\rm mod}\;2\pi \cr} \tag{2}$$

The conventional Barkhausen
$L(j\omega _{0})=+1$ is

$$\eqalign{
\pi -3{\rm arctan}\,\omega _{0}\tau &\equiv 0\;{\rm mod}\;2\pi\cr
{{A_{v}^{3}}\over {\left[1+(\omega _{0}\tau )^{2}\right]^{3/2}}}&=1
\cr} \tag{3}$$

i. {\it e.} put ${\rm arg}L=\,0$,

$${\rm arctan}\,\omega _{0}\tau ={\pi \over 3}\tag{4}$$

$$\omega _{0}\tau =\sqrt{3}\tag{5}$$

and, at that $\omega _{0}$,

$$|L(j\omega _{0})|={{A_{v}^{3}}\over {8}}=1\tag{6}$$

So that the circuit is normally put as

$$A_{v}>2\tag{7}$$

for oscillation.
In terms of closed loop poles $1-L(s)=0$,

$$(1+s\tau )^{3}+A_{v}^{3}=0\tag{8}$$

$$1+s\tau =A_{v}\root 3 \of {-1}=A_{v}\times
\cases{-1\cr 
{1\over 2}\pm j{{\sqrt{3}}\over 2}\cr}\tag{9}$$

$$\eqalign{
s_{1}\tau &= -1-A_{v}\cr
s_{2,3}\tau &= -1+{{A_{v}}\over 2}\pm j{{\sqrt{3}}\over 2}A_{v}\cr}\tag{10}$$

${\rm Re}s_{2,3}>0$ for $A_{v}>2$.  The conventional
logic inverter has $A_{v}\sim 10-30$ at the trip point
$V_{in}=V_{out}=V_{DD}/2$, so the bias point $V_{1}=
V_{2}=V_{3}=V_{trip}$ is a repellor with a complex pair
in the RHP, Fig.1.

The value of $\tau =R_{o}C_{L}$ cancels out of (7).  It
only scales the frequency,

$$\omega _{0}={{\sqrt{3}}\over {R_{o}C_{L}}}\tag{11}$$

in the small signal picture, and the large signal
``propagation delay''

$$t_{p}\approx 0.69R_{o}C_{L}\approx {{I_{av}}\over {C_{L}V_{DD}}}\tag{12}$$

$$f_{osc}\approx {1\over {6t_{p}}}\propto {1\over {C_{L}}}\tag{13}$$

more exactly, in large signal, $T\approx 3C_{L}V_{DD}/I_{av}$,
so for any {\it finite} $C_{L}$ the RHP poles stay in the
RHP with

$${\rm Re}s_{2,3}={{A_{v}/2-1}\over {R_{o}C_{L}}}>0\qquad
{\rm Im}s_{2,3}={{\sqrt{3}A_{v}}\over {2R_{o}C_{L}}}\tag{14}$$

and the small signal amplitude grows as
$\exp \left[({\rm Re}s_{2,3})t\right]$.
Increasing $C_{L}$ simply pushes $\omega _{0}\to 0$ and
${\rm Re}s_{2,3}\to 0^{+}$.  There is no finite critical
$C_{L,{\rm crit}}$ beyond which $|L|<1$ when
${\rm arg}L=0$.

In the mathematical limit

$$C_{L}\to \infty \qquad \tau \to \infty \tag{15}$$

$$\omega _{0}\to 0\qquad s_{2,3}\to 0\qquad T_{osc}\to \infty \tag{16}$$

the circuit becomes ``frozen'' at the trip point.
The start up time constant

$$\tau _{st}\approx 1/{\rm Re}s_{2,3}\propto C_{L}\to \infty \tag{17}$$

so that any normally negligible shunt loss $G_{p}$,
leakage, finite $g_{o}$, supply noise, etc.,

$$(1+s\tau )^{3}+A_{v}^{3}{{1}\over {1+G_{p}R_{o}}}\approx 0\tag{18}$$

will pull the poles back into the LHP for
$C_{L}$ large enough in a physical circuit and the
circuit will sit, to all intents and purposes, on its
metastable dc point $V_{trip}$ with $f_{osc}\approx 0$.
In that practical sense it can be said to have
``stopped oscillating''.

> {\it Remark:}  If the inverter is idealised as
> $R_{o}\to 0$, $A(s)=-A_{v}$, ($*$) is $C_{L}$
> independent.  The conventional odd number Boolean
> loop has no stable dc state and with $R_{o}=0$
> formally oscillates with $f\to \infty $.  A
> finite $R_{o}$ is what makes ($*$) a low pass and
> what makes $f_{osc}\propto 1/C_{L}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The core small-signal analysis is correct: the oscillation condition is independent of capacitance, and the frequency falls as capacitance increases. However, the claim that any small parasitic loss will eventually move the poles into the LHP as capacitance grows is not supported by the model and muddies the central conclusion.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
In the idealised theory the ${\rm sh.}-C$ is
not a ${\rm sh.}-C$.  Put the customary small signal
model on the inverter,

$${\rm out}= -g_{m}{\rm in}\;Z_{o}\qquad
Z_{o}=R_{o}\parallel {1\over {sC_{L}}}$$

so that for the $N=3$ loop, Fig.1,

$${\cal L}(s)=\left[-g_{m}Z_{o}(s)\right]^{N}
=-{(g_{m}R_{o})^{N}\over {\left(1+sR_{o}C_{L}\right)^{N}}}\tag{*}$$

in the conventional one pole per stage approximation.
$R_{o}$ is the small signal, large signal, mean,
$V_{DD}/I_{DD}$ output resistance of the inverter.
For a hard CMOS inverter $R_{o}\sim 1/g_{m}$,
$A_{v}=g_{m}R_{o}\gg 1$ at the trip point.  For $N$ odd
the unique d. c. solution

$$V_{1}=f(V_{3})\;,\;V_{2}=f(V_{1})\;,\;V_{3}=f(V_{2})\tag{**}$$

$$V\equiv f\circ f\circ f(V)\qquad f^{\prime}<0$$

is $V_{1}=V_{2}=V_{3}=V_{{\rm trip}}\approx V_{DD}/2$
and its small signal loop gain is $(-A_{v})^{N}$,
${\cal L}(0)={\cal O}(-10^{3})$, i. e. the d. c.
equilibrium is metastable - unstable - for any
$C_{L}$.

Put $s=j\omega $ in $({*})$,

$$|{\cal L}(j\omega )|={(g_{m}R_{o})^{N}\over 
\left[1+(\omega R_{o}C_{L})^{2}\right]^{N/2}} \tag{1}$$

$${\rm arg}{\cal L}(j\omega )=N\pi -N{\rm arctg}
\omega R_{o}C_{L}\tag{2}$$

mod $2\pi $.  Barkhausen, ${\cal L}(j\omega _{0})=1
+{\rm j}0$, is

$$N{\rm arctg}\omega_{0}R_{o}C_{L}= \pi \;\;{\rm mod}\;2\pi \tag{3}$$

$${{|{\cal L}(j\omega_{0})|>1}\over{{\rm for\;start\;up}}}$$

For the conventional $0<{\rm arctg}<\pi /2$ solution

$$\omega _{0}R_{o}C_{L}= {\rm tg}{\pi \over N}\tag{4}$$

$$|{\cal L}(j\omega _{0})|=
\left[{g_{m}R_{o}\over {\sqrt{1+{\rm tg}^{2}{\pi /N}}}}\right]^{N}
=\left[g_{m}R_{o}\cos {\pi \over N}\right]^{N}>1\tag{5}$$

for oscillation to be able to build up.
For $N=3$,

$$\eqalign{
\omega_{0} &={1\over {R_{o}C_{L}}}{\rm tg}{\pi \over 3}
 ={\sqrt{3}\over {R_{o}C_{L}}}\cr
|{\cal L}(j\omega_{0})|&={(g_{m}R_{o})^{3}\over 8}>1\cr
g_{m}R_{o}&>2\tag{6}}$$

$c.{\rm f.}$ the conventional aperiodic condition
$g_{m}R_{o}>1/\cos \pi /N$.  With the customary
$A_{v}\approx 10-30$ it is very well satisfied.
In particular {\it (5) is $C_{L}$ independent}.  By
choosing $\omega_{0}\propto C_{L}^{-1}$ the loop
 contrives to keep

$$\omega_{0}C_{L}={\rm tg}{\pi /N}\over R_{o}={\rm const.}\tag{7}$$

so that

$$|Z_{o}(j\omega_{0})|={R_{o}\over 
\sqrt{1+{\rm tg}^{2}{\pi /N}}}=R_{o}\cos {\pi\over N}\tag{8}$$

is finite even for $C_{L}\to \infty $.

In large signal, digital, language the inverter
takes a time

$$t_{d}\approx 0.69R_{o}C_{L}\approx  {C_{L}V_{DD}\over
2I_{D}} \tag{9}$$

to charge the next $C_{L}$ to the trip point
$V_{DD}/2$ and the familiar

$$f_{{\rm osc}}\approx {1\over {2Nt_{d}}}\approx
{1\over {1.38NR_{o}C_{L}}}\tag{10}$$

${\rm more\;accurately}\;f_{0}=\omega_{0}/2\pi $ in
(4), is obtained.  E. {\rm g.} for $N=3$

$$f_{0}={\sqrt{3}\over {2\pi R_{o}C_{L}}}\approx
{0.28\over {R_{o}C_{L}}}\tag{11}$$

to be compared with $1/6t_{d}\approx 0.24/R_{o}C_{L}$.

In particular for every finite $C_{L}$ the pole

$$\omega_{p}={1\over {R_{o}C_{L}}}\tag{12}$$

is finite and (3) has a finite solution $\omega_{0}$.
Increasing $C_{L}$ just pushes $\omega_{p}$ and
$\omega_{0}$ down proportional to $C_{L}^{-1}$.
Mathematically the circuit never ceases to satisfy
Barkhausen if it satisfied it for small $C_{L}$.
In the strict $C_{L}\to \infty $ limit

$$f_{0}\to 0\qquad T_{0}={1\over {f_{0}}}\to \infty \tag{13}$$

and, what is more important for the bench, the
complex poles of the closed loop

$$1-{\cal L}(s)=0\tag{14}$$

go to

$$s_{p}= {1\over {R_{o}C_{L}}}\left[-1+
g_{m}R_{o}e^{j2k\pi /N}\right]\qquad k=0\ldots N-1
\tag{15}$$

so that for the unstable pair $k=1,N-1$,

$${\cal R}{\rm e}\,s_{p}= {g_{m}R_{o}\cos 2\pi /N-1
\over {R_{o}C_{L}}}>0\tag{16}$$

goes to $0^{+}$ as $C_{L}^{-1}$.  The build up
time constant

$$\tau_{{\rm bu}}\approx 1/{\cal R}{\rm e}\,s_{p}
\propto C_{L}\to \infty \tag{17}$$

goes to infinity.  Loosely speaking the circuit
freezes on its metastable d. c. point (**) and for
all practical purposes, on any finite observation
time, looks as if it were latched and not
oscillating.  For $C_{L}\equiv \infty $, i. e. an a.
c. short to ground, the loop is of course broken
and

$$|{\cal L}(j\omega )|\equiv 0\qquad \omega\ne 0\tag{18}$$

so that there is no a. c. feedback at all.

{\it Remark on the modelling:} (1)-(2) presume a
finite $R_{o}$ - i. e. a finite charging current -
to make a $R_{o}C_{L}$ low pass interstage.
An ideal digital gate normally idealised as a
zero output impedance voltage source with a
lumped propagation delay $t_{pd}$,

$$V_{o}(t)=f\!\left(V_{i}(t-t_{pd})\right)\tag{19}$$

has $Z_{o}\equiv 0$ and a ${\rm sh.}\,C_{L}$ to
ground draws current but does not develop voltage
and does not introduce a linear pole in ${\cal L}(s)$.
The linearised ${\cal L}(s)=-A_{v}e^{-sNt_{pd}}$ has
no finite $\omega_{0}$ satisfying (3) with $C_{L}$.
The circuit then oscillates - in the digital
simulation sense - as the conventional odd inverter
chain at

$$f_{0}\approx {1\over {2Nt_{pd}}}\tag{20}$$

essentially $C_{L}$ independent, apart from the
trivial $t_{pd}(C_{L})$ dependence normally put in
by hand.  In that idealisation the ${\rm sh.}\,C_{L}$
of Fig.1 is not a phase shift network at all.  The
conventional $RC$ phase shift oscillator is the high
pass $C_{{\rm series}}-R_{{\rm shunt}}$ network.  With
finite $R_{o}$ the ${\rm sh.}\,C_{L}$ plus $R_{o}$ is
its low pass dual and (4)-(6) apply.

> {\it In short: with the usual $R_{o}-C_{L}$ low
> pass model the Barkhausen magnitude at the
> $360^{\rm o}$ frequency is $C_{L}$ independent,
> (5)-(6), so that if the loop oscillates for small
> $C_{L}$ it oscillates for arbitrarily large finite
> $C_{L}$, but at a frequency $f_{0}\propto
> 1/C_{L}\to 0$ and with a start up time $\propto
> C_{L}\to \infty $, so that in the $C_{L}=\infty $
> limit and for all practical bench purposes the
> circuit is frozen on the metastable
> $V_{DD}/2$ point and can be said to have
> ``stopped oscillating''.  With ideal
> $R_{o}=0$ voltage source inverters the shunt
> $C_{L}$ introduces no pole at all.}

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly concludes that equal capacitors at all three nodes do not stop oscillation for any finite capacitance. The RC/Barkhausen analysis gives a capacitance-independent oscillation condition and frequency proportional to 1/CL, consistent with the delay argument; the literal infinite-capacitance caveat does not change that conclusion.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
With the usual lumped text book model the
condition for the birth of the limit cycle has
nothing to do with $C_{L}$.

Put

$${\cal A}_{v}(s)=-{{g_{m}R_{0}}\over {1+sR_{0}C_{L}}}
=-{{A_{0}}\over {1+s/\omega _{p}}}\qquad \omega _{p}^{-1}=
R_{0}C_{L}\tag{*}$$

for one loaded inverter in the neighbourhood of
the $V_{I}=V_{O}=V_{M}$ bias point.
For the normal CMOS inverter $A_{0}=g_{m}R_{0}\gg 1$.
The normal $3$ phase shift oscillator has

$${\cal L}(s)={\cal A}_{v}^{3}(s)=
-{{A_{0}^{3}}\over {(1+s/\omega _{p})^{3}}}\tag{**}$$

so that, on $s=j\omega $,

$$\eqalign{
|{\cal L}|&={{A_{0}^{3}}\over {\left[1+(\omega /\omega _{p})^{2}\right]^{3/2}}}\cr
\angle {\cal L}&=-3\pi -3{\rm tg}^{-1}(\omega /\omega _{p})\equiv
-3{\rm tg}^{-1}(\omega /\omega _{p})\;({\rm mod}\;2\pi )\cr}$$

$$|{\cal L}|=1\;\;{\rm at}\;\;3{\rm tg}^{-1}\omega /\omega _{p}=\pi
\;{\rm mod}\;2\pi \tag{***}$$

i.e.

$${\rm tg}^{-1}\omega_{0}/\omega _{p}={\pi\over 3}\tag{1}$$

$$\omega _{0}= \sqrt{3}\,\omega _{p}={\sqrt{3}\over {R_{0}C_{L}}}\tag{2}$$

is the {\it small signal\/} frequency at which the loop
can give $2\pi $ of phase shift, the $-\pi $ being
supplied by the d.c. inversion.  At that frequency

$$|{\cal L}(j\omega_{0})|={{A_{0}^{3}}\over 8}\tag{3}$$

so that the Barkhausen {\it modulus\/} condition is

$$A_{0}=g_{m}R_{0}\ge 2\tag{4}$$

and, within $(*)$, has nothing to do with $C_{L}$.

In terms of the conventional pole pattern that is the
conventional Hopf bifurcation.  Put $x_{i}=V_{i}-V_{M}$,
$\tau =R_{0}C_{L}$, $a=g_{m}R_{0}$ and, linearised,

$$\tau \dot x_{i+1}+x_{i+1}=-ax_{i}\qquad i=1,2,3\;{\rm mod}\;3 \tag{5}$$

so that with $x\propto e^{st}$

$$(1+s\tau )^{3}+a^{3}=0\tag{6}$$

$$s_{k}={-1-ae^{j2k\pi /3}\over {\tau }}\qquad k=0,1,2 \tag{7}$$

$$s_{1,2}={-1+a/2\mp ja{\sqrt{3}}/2\over {\tau }}\tag{8}$$

$${\cal R}s_{1,2}>0\iff a>2\tag{9}$$

which is ($4$) and $\tau $ only scales the
{\it magnitude\/} of ${\cal R}s$ and ${\cal I}s$.
For $a<2$ the d.c. solution $x_{i}\equiv 0$, i. e.
$V_{i}\equiv V_{M}$, is a normal stable node and the
circuit latches on $V_{M}$ on the $1/\tau $ time scale.
For

$$a=g_{m}R_{0}>2\tag{10}$$

the d.c. solution is a saddle with a two dimensional
unstable manifold spanned by the complex pair ($8$).
The normal supercritical Hopf bifurcation gives birth
for $a>2$ to a stable essentially sinusoidal limit cycle
of {\it small signal\/} angular frequency

$$\omega_{0s}=a{\sqrt{3}}\over {2\tau }={\sqrt{3}\over {R_{0}C_{L}}}
\tag{11}$$

collapsing to ($2$) at the bifurcation.

In large signal the limit cycle rapidly becomes the
normal astable square wave relaxation oscillation.
With the conventional $0-V_{DD}$ idealisation the
inverter can be idealised as a threshold $V_{M}\approx
V_{DD}/2$ comparator with a Thevenin $R_{0}$ charging
the $C_{L}$.  E.{\it g}. with $R_{0}^{p}=R_{0}^{n}=R_{0}$

$$T_{0}\approx 2\times 3R_{0}C_{L}\log 2\approx 4.2R_{0}C_{L}
\tag{12}$$

normalised to

$$f_{0}={1\over {T_{0}}}\propto {1\over {R_{0}C_{L}}}\tag{13}$$

and ($11$) is normally quoted, allowing for a shape
factor, as

$$f_{0}\approx {1\over {5\sim 7R_{0}C_{L}}}\tag{14}$$

So that, {\it in the model $(*)$}, increasing $C_{L}$
just displaces the pole $\omega_{p}$ to lower and lower
frequency and the {\it small signal\/}
$\omega_{0}= {\sqrt{3}}\omega_{p}$ and the large signal
astable frequency ($13$)--($14$) go to zero as
$1/C_{L}$.  The start up time constant

$$\tau_{s}^{-1}={\cal R}s_{1,2}={a/2-1\over {\tau }}\propto {1\over {C_{L}}}
\tag{15}$$

goes to infinity as $C_{L}$.

In ordinary language the circuit goes on oscillating
but slower and slower and it takes longer and longer to
start.

For $R_{0}\rightarrow 0$, the usual ``digital'' idealisation,
$\tau \rightarrow 0$ for any finite $C_{L}$ and the $C_{L}$
has no effect at all to this order.  You have to put in
the intrinsic unloaded pole $\omega_{0}^{\ast }$ of the
inverter,

$${\cal A}_{v}=-{{A_{0}}\over {(1+s/\omega_{0}^{\ast })
(1+s/\omega_{p})}}\tag{16}$$

to get an effect, and then for $\omega_{p}\ll \omega_{0}^{\ast }$
($16$) goes back to $(*)$.

That is the mathematics.  In the laboratory, of course,
a $f_{0}\rightarrow 0$ square wave with a $\tau_{s}\rightarrow
\infty $ start up time and a $I_{pk}=C_{L}dV/dt$ current drive
requirement $\propto C_{L}$ looks very much like
``no oscillation''.  The $V_{M}$ metastable state lives
for a time $\propto C_{L}$, the available small signal
gain at $\omega_{0}\propto C_{L}^{-1}$ falls below the
wide band noise floor, the second pole $\omega_{0}^{\ast }$,
supply leakage, the finite slew rate $I_{0}/C_{L}$ etc.
dominate, and the circuit will normally be quoted as
latched.  If you want to be pedantic the circuit
``fails to oscillate in any finite observation time'' for

$$C_{L}>C_{L{\rm max}}\approx {I_{0}\over {V_{DD}}}\,
{1\over {f_{{\rm min}}}}\tag{17}$$

where $f_{{\rm min}}$ is the lowest frequency you are
prepared to wait for.  With the conventional $a<2$ low
gain inverter the circuit fails to oscillate at all,
for any $C_{L}$.

> {\it Remark:\/}  With the usual $A_{0}\gg 1$ CMOS inverter
> the textbook statement is often abbreviated to:  the
> loaded $3$ inverter loop is unconditionally unstable
> and always oscillates, with $f_{0}\propto 1/C_{L}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly concludes that the three-node-loaded ring continues oscillating at a frequency that falls roughly as 1/CL. Its small-signal phase and gain analysis supports that result; the practical caveats do not change the essential answer.

answers.question: What happens to the phase noise if the three capacitors in the figure are doubled?

answer.text:
With ideal square law devices the circuit is

$${{f_{0}}\approx {1\over 2NT_{d}}\approx {1\over {2N{{C_{L}}\over
{g_{m}}}}}\propto {1\over {C_{L}}}} \tag{*}$$

so that, to first order, $R_{o}={\rm const}$,

$$f_{0}{\cal \to}{1\over 2}f_{0}\qquad 
{\cal P}_{D}=NC_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}={\rm const}\tag{1}$$

apart from the trivial ${\rm Leesson}\;\;20\,{\rm log}\,
f_{0}/\Delta f$ factor.  Put in the ${\rm Hajimiri}$ form
the normal {\it white} ${\cal SSB}$ phase noise at a Fourier
frequency $\Delta \omega $ from the carrier is

$${\cal L}\{\Delta \omega \}={1\over 2}{\,{{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}
\over {\Delta f}}\,{\Gamma_{{\rm rms}}^{2}\over
{q_{{\rm max}}^{2}\Delta \omega ^{2}}} \tag{2}$$

modulo the $1/f$ up conversion, $q_{{\rm max}}=C_{L}V_{DD}$ is
the maximum charge on the load and $i_{n}^{2}/\Delta f\approx
4kT\gamma g_{m}$ is the white current noise of the inverter.
$\Gamma _{{\rm rms}}$ is the rms value of the impulse
sensitivity function.  For the $N=3$ ring $\Gamma (t)$ is a
periodic train of pulses of width $\approx t_{r}$,
$t_{r}\propto R_{o}C_{L}$ and period $T_{0}=1/f_{0}\propto
R_{o}C_{L}$, so that $\Gamma _{{\rm rms}}^{2}\propto
t_{r}/T_{0}={\rm const}$ to first order.  I. e. to first order
the only $C_{L}$ dependence in (2) is in $q_{{\rm max}}$

$${\cal S}_{\phi }\propto {\cal L}\propto {1\over {q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}}
\propto {1\over {C_{L}^{2}}}\qquad {\rm at\;given\;
}\Delta \omega \tag{3}$$

so that at the same {\it absolute} Fourier frequency

$${\cal L}{\cal \to}{1\over 4}{\cal L}\approx {\cal L}-6{\rm dB}
\tag{4}$$

in power, $3\,{\rm dB}$ in voltage.  In terms of the normal
time jitter put $\Delta V_{n}^{2}=kT/C_{L}$ on the capacitor and
${\rm SR}=I_{0}/C_{L}$ for the slewing so that the one
transition r. m. s. jitter is

$$\sigma _{t}^{2}={{\overline{\Delta V_{n}^{2}}}\over {{\rm SR}^{2}}}
={{kTC_{L}}\over {I_{0}^{2}}}\propto C_{L}\tag{5}$$

so that the absolute period jitter, $\sigma _{T}^{2}=N\sigma
_{t}^{2}\propto C_{L}$, {\it increases} by $3\,{\rm dB}$, a factor
$\sqrt{2}$ in r. m. s. value, on doubling $C_{L}$.

The phase jitter in one period is

$$\sigma _{\phi }^{2}= \left(2\pi f_{0}\right)^{2}\sigma _{T}^{2}
\propto {1\over {C_{L}^{2}}}C_{L}\propto {1\over {C_{L}}}\tag{6}$$

i. e. $3\,{\rm dB}$ {\it better} in phase, $6\,{\rm dB}$ better
in ${\cal S}_{\phi }$.  Indeed, for the diffusion constant of
the Wiener phase random walk $D_{\phi }=\sigma _{\phi
}^{2}f_{0}\propto 1/C_{L}^{2}$,

$${\cal S}_{\phi }(\Delta \omega )={{D_{\phi }}\over {\Delta
\omega ^{2}}}\propto {1\over {C_{L}^{2}\Delta \omega ^{2}}}\tag{7}$$

which is (2).  Referred to the new carrier, i. e. at
$\Delta \omega \propto \omega _{0}$,

$${\cal L}\left\{{\Delta \omega \over {\omega _{0}}}={\rm const}
\right\}\approx {\rm const}\tag{8}$$

so that the usual figure of merit

$${\rm FoM}= {\cal L}-20\,{\rm log}\,{{f_{0}}\over {\Delta f}}
+10\,{\rm log}\,{{{\cal P}_{D}}\over {1{\rm mW}}}\tag{9}$$

is, to first order, $C_{L}$ independent.  With (1) this is
normally quoted as a $3\,{\rm dB}$ improvement of the
normalized phase noise, $6\,{\rm dB}$ at the same absolute
$\Delta f$, for a capacitance doubling.  If the extra $20\,{\rm
log}\,f_{0}/\Delta f$ is factored out the improvement is
normally quoted as

> {\it At constant $\Delta f/f_{0}$, at constant power,
> doubling the total tank energy, $E\propto C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}$,
> halves the normalized white phase noise power, $\propto
> 1/E$, i. e. $10\,{\rm log}\,2\approx 3\,{\rm dB}$ better.
> At constant $\Delta f$ the $20\,{\rm log}\,f_{0}$ Leeson
> factor adds a further $6\,{\rm dB}$, for a total of
> $\approx 6\,{\rm dB}$ at the same absolute offset.}

In particular with $R_{o}={\rm const}$ the unbiased ring goes
from $f_{0}$ to $f_{0}/2$ and from ${\cal L}(\Delta f)$ to
${\cal L}(\Delta f)-20\,{\rm log}\,2\approx {\cal L}-6\,{\rm
dB}$ in the $1/f^{2}$ region.  Modulo the $20\,{\rm log}\,
f_{0}/\Delta f$ normalisation this is a $3\,{\rm dB}$
improvement of ${\cal S}_{\phi }$, ${\cal L}$ and of
$\sigma _{\phi }$, no improvement of the ${\rm FoM}$,
and, from (5), a $3\,{\rm dB}$ {\it degradation} of the
absolute period jitter $\sigma _{T}$.  If you keep $f_{0}$
constant by doubling the device widths, $g_{m}\propto 1/R_{0}
\propto C_{L}$, $i_{n}^{2}\propto g_{m}\propto C_{L}$, the
familiar $3\,{\rm dB}$ per energy doubling is obtained at
constant $f_{0}$, ${\cal L}\propto 1/C_{L}$.

> {\it Remark:}  The $1/f^{3}$ close in noise scales in
> the same way, ${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto 1/q_{{\rm max}}^{2}
> \propto 1/C_{L}^{2}$ at given $\Delta \omega $, but the
> $1/f^{3}$ corner, $\Delta \omega _{1/f^{3}}\propto 1/C_{L}$,
> moves in by a factor $2$, so that very close to the carrier
> the $1/f^{3}$ noise can appear to degrade.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly concludes that doubling the capacitors halves the oscillation frequency and reduces phase noise by a factor of four (about 6 dB) at a fixed absolute offset, with supporting charge/edge-rate reasoning.

answers.question: What happens to the phase noise if the three capacitors in the figure are doubled?

answer.text:
With the usual somewhat white noise
model the circuit is {\it not} improved.
In first order

$${T_{D}\propto R_{o}C_{L}\propto {C_{L}V_{DD}\over I_{D}}
\qquad f_{0}={1\over {2NT_{D}}}\propto {1\over C_{L}} \tag{1}$$

$$P_{av}=Nf_{0}C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}\propto N{C_{L}\over C_{L}}=
{\rm const.}\tag{2}$$

for $N=3$ on the $CV^{2}f$ power.
For the normal Hajimiri - Lee - Abidi white
${\rm FM}$ noise, e. {\rm g.} in the form

$${\cal L}\left\{\Delta \omega \right\}
={{{\bar {i_{n}^{2}}}/\Delta f}\over {8q_{{\rm max}}^{2}\Delta
\omega ^{2}}}{\bar {\Gamma _{rms}^{2}}}\qquad 
q_{{\rm max}}=C_{L}V_{DD} \tag{3}$$

$\Gamma _{rms}\approx 0.3-1$ for the large signal
rail to rail ring and $i_{n}^{2}/\Delta f =4kT\gamma g_{m}
\approx 4kT/R_{o}$ is to first order independent of the
external $C_{L}$,

$${\cal L}\propto {1\over q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}\propto 
{1\over C_{L}^{2}}\propto f_{0}^{2}\tag{4}$$

in the more familiar Leeson form

$${\cal L}\left\{\Delta f\right\}\propto {FkT\over P_{av}}
\left({f_{0}\over 2Q\Delta f}\right)^{2}\propto
{f_{0}^{2}\over P_{av}}\tag{5}$$

so that, with $P_{av}=$ const. from (2),

$${\cal L}\propto f_{0}^{2}\propto {1\over C_{L}^{2}}\tag{6}$$

in power.  I. {\rm e.} at {\it the same absolute}
${\cal L}\left\{\Delta f\right\}$ e. {\rm g.} at
$1\,{\rm MHz}$ from the {\it new} carrier

$$f_{0}\rightarrow f_{0}/2\qquad 
{\cal L}\rightarrow {\cal L}/4\tag{7}$$

about $-6\,{\rm dB}$ in conventional ${\rm dBc/Hz^{-1}}$.
Normalised to the carrier, i.e. at the same
$\Delta f/f_{0}$ or, what is the same thing, in terms
of the conventional figure of merit

$${\rm FoM}={\cal L}-20\log {f_{0}\over \Delta f}
+10\log {P_{av}\over 1{\rm mW}} \tag{8}$$

(2) cancels (6) to

$${\rm FoM}= {\rm const.}\tag{9}$$

so that at the same {\it fractional} offset,
$\Delta f\propto f_{0}$, e. {\rm g.} $\Delta f/f_{0}
=10^{-2}$,

$${\cal L}_{n}\propto {1\over C_{L}}\;,\qquad 
{\cal L}(2C_{L})={1\over 2}{\cal L}(C_{L})\tag{10}$$

$-3\,{\rm dB}$ in power, $1/\sqrt{2}$ in voltage,
normally quoted in text books in the shorthand
form

$${\cal L}\approx {{kT}\over {C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}}}
\left({f_{0}\over \Delta f}\right)^{2}\tag{11}$$

as {\it $3\,{\rm dB}$ per doubling of $C$ if the
comparison is made at the same $f_{0}$}.
If you want to keep $f_{0}$ constant you have to
double the $W$'s, $I_{D}\propto C_{L}$, $P_{av}
\propto C_{L}$ and (6) becomes (10)-(11), the
customary $1/C_{L}$ law.

In the time domain the {\it absolute} jitter,
the $kT/C$ voltage noise divided by the slew rate
$S=I_{D}/C_{L}$ at threshold,

$$\sigma _{V}^{2}={{kT}\over {C_{L}}}\qquad 
S={{I_{D}}\over {C_{L}}}\tag{12}$$

$$\sigma _{t}={{\sigma _{V}}\over S}={{\sqrt{kTC_{L}}}
\over {I_{D}}}\tag{13}$$

per transition, variance

$$\sigma _{t}^{2}\propto C_{L}\tag{14}$$

so that for the $2N$ transitions per period

$$\sigma _{T}^{2}=2N\sigma _{t}^{2}\propto C_{L}\tag{15}$$

$$\sigma _{T}(2C_{L})=\sqrt{2}\,\sigma _{T}(C_{L})\tag{16}$$

$+3\,{\rm dB}$ in variance, $+1.5\,{\rm dB}$, a factor
$\sqrt{2}\approx 1.4$, in rms seconds.  The often
quoted {\it improvement} in ${\cal L}$ is the
improvement in {\it fractional} jitter

$${{\sigma _{T}}\over {T_{0}}}\propto {{\sqrt{C_{L}}}
\over {C_{L}}}={1\over {\sqrt{C_{L}}}}\tag{17}$$

$$T_{0}\sigma _{T}^{-1}\propto \sqrt{C_{L}}\tag{18}$$

$-1.5\,{\rm dB}$ rms, $-3\,{\rm dB}$ in power,
$-6\,{\rm dB}$ at fixed absolute $\Delta f$,
cf. (7).  Any $1/f$ induced $1/f^{3}$ component,
${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto K\,f_{0}^{2}/C_{L}^{2}
\Delta f^{3}$, scales in the same way, to first
order $-6\,{\rm dB}$ at fixed $\Delta f$, $-3\,{\rm dB}$
at fixed $\Delta f/f_{0}$, ${\rm FoM}=$ const.

> {\it Remark:} In the text book shorthand (11)
> this is normally phrased as {\it the {\rm (white)}
> phase noise power is halved, $-3\,{\rm dB}$, for a
> doubling of the {\rm (total)} tank capacitance at
> constant $f_{0}$ and ${\rm FoM}$}.  With the
> inverters left alone the carrier itself is halved
> and the conventional ${\cal L}\{\Delta f\}$ at the
> same {\it absolute} $\Delta f$ is quartered,
> $-6\,{\rm dB}$.  The price is $\sqrt{2}$ more
> absolute period jitter.  Second order effects,
> short channel excess noise $\gamma >2/3$, supply
> and substrate noise, the $R_{o}(V_{DD})$ non
> linearity, etc., will normally make the improvement
> less than the ideal $1/C$ - $1/C^{2}$ law.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly explains that doubling the capacitors halves f0 and reduces phase noise by about a factor of four (−6 dB) at a fixed offset, meeting the full-credit rule. The extra fractional-offset discussion is not needed for the central result.

answers.question: What happens to the phase noise if the three capacitors in the figure are doubled?

answer.text:
For a first order 3 invertor model put
$R_{o}\approx 1/g_{m}$ , $t_{D}\approx 0.69R_{o}C_{L}
\approx C_{L}V_{DD}/2I_{D}$ and

$${\rm f}_{0}\approx {1\over 6t_{D}}\propto {1\over C_{L}}\tag *$$

so that apart from second order changes of the
wave form

$$f_{0}^{\prime }\approx {1\over 2}f_{0}\qquad 
P\approx Nf_{0}C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}={\rm const.}\tag {**}$$

in first order.  Put e. {\rm g.} the conventional
Leeson - Hajimiri estimate

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )
      \approx 10\log \left[{{{\bar \Gamma}_{rms}^{2}\over 2}
                 {{{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}/\Delta f}\over {q_{max}^{2}
                 \Delta \omega ^{2}}}}\right] \tag{*}$$

$\Gamma $ is the impulse sensitivity function,
$q_{{\rm max}}=C_{L}V_{{\rm max}}$ the maximum charge
swing on the load and ${\overline{i_{n}^{2}}/\Delta f}
=4kT\gamma g_{m}$ the white drain current noise of
the invertor which to first order does not know about
$C_{L}$.

$$S_{\phi }(\Delta \omega )\propto 
     {{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}/\Delta f\over q_{{\rm max}}^{2}
            \Delta \omega ^{2}}\propto {1\over {C_{L}^{2}}}
            {1\over {\Delta \omega ^{2}}}\tag{1}$$

so that at {\it the same absolute\/} $\Delta \omega $
$${\cal L}^{\prime }={\cal L}-20\log 2\approx {\cal L}-6{\rm dB}
\qquad {\rm white\;FM}\;\propto 1/\Delta \omega ^{2} \tag{2}$$
and in power $\propto 1/4$.
With the normal ${\cal F}{\cal O}{\cal M}$ normalisation

$${\cal F}{\cal O}{\cal M}={\cal L}(\Delta \omega )
      -20\log {{f_{0}}\over {\Delta f}}+10\log P\tag{3}$$

(2) is the ${\cal F}{\cal O}{\cal M}={\rm const}$ law.
At the same {\it fractional\/} off set $\Delta \omega
\propto \omega_{0}$, $\Delta \omega ^{\prime }=
\Delta \omega /2$, (1) is normally quoted with the
$\omega_{0}$ taken out,

$$S_{\phi }\propto {{kT}\over {C_{L}V^{2}}}
        \left({{\omega_{0}}\over {\Delta \omega }}\right)^{2}
        {1\over {\Delta \omega^{2}}}\propto {1\over {C_{L}}}
        \tag{4}$$

i. e. the familiar $kT/C$ law

$${\cal L}(k\omega_{0})\approx {\cal L}(k\omega_{0}^{\prime })
      -10\log 2\approx {\cal L}-3{\rm dB}\tag{5}$$

in power, a factor $2$ , in the loose normal
language ``the phase noise does not change, the
${\cal F}{\cal O}{\cal M}$ is invariant''.
In text book shorthand (5) is quoted as ``$3\,{\rm dB}$
better phase noise'' for $C\to 2C$.

In the time domain the {\it absolute\/} jitter gets
worse.  With e. {\rm g.} the $RC$ noise

$${\overline{v_{n}^{2}}}=kT/C_{L}\tag{6}$$

and, at the threshold, the slew rate

$$SR=\left.{{dV}\over {dt}}\right|_{V_{th}}\approx
{I_{D}\over C_{L}}\approx {V_{DD}\over {R_{o}C_{L}}}\tag{7}$$

$${\overline{\delta t^{2}}}\approx 
   {{{\overline{v_{n}^{2}}}}\over {SR^{2}}}\approx
   {{kT/C_{L}}\over {I_{D}^{2}/C_{L}^{2}}}={{kTC_{L}}\over {I_{D}^{2}}}
   \propto C_{L}\tag{8}$$

$${\sigma _{T}^{\prime }}^{2}=2\sigma _{T}^{2}\qquad 
  \sigma _{T}^{\prime }=\sqrt{2}\,\sigma _{T}\tag{9}$$

$\approx +3\,{\rm dB}$ in power, $+1.5\,{\rm dB}$ in rms
value.  The period jitter, sometimes loosely called
``phase noise'', is $\sqrt{2}$ larger.  The phase
jitter,

$$S_{\phi }(\Delta \omega )\propto f_{0}^{3}\sigma _{T}^{2}
/\Delta \omega ^{2}\propto 1/C_{L}^{2}\tag{10}$$

goes as (1) and is $\approx 6\,{\rm dB}$, $3\,{\rm dB}$
fractional, better, ${\cal F}{\cal O}{\cal M}={\rm const}$.

> {\it Remark:}  With (**) $P={\rm const}$ this is
> normally expressed as ${\cal L}\propto (kT/P)
> (\omega_{0}/\Delta\omega )^{2}$.  Any $1/f^{3}$
> flicker induced component scales $\propto 1/C_{L}$ at
> fixed absolute $\Delta \omega $ and is ${\cal F}{\cal O}
> {\cal M}$ invariant at fixed $\Delta \omega /\omega_{0}$.

In round numbers: $f_{0}\to f_{0}/2$, ${\rm CV^{2}f}$
power $\approx {\rm const}$, spot $1/f^{2}$ noise
$\approx -3\,{\rm dB}$ at $k\,f_{0}$, $-6\,{\rm dB}$ at
fixed $\Delta f$, ${\cal F}{\cal O}{\cal M}$ invariant to
first order, rms period jitter $+\sqrt{2}$.  With the
usual $10\log $ shorthand the oscillator is said to be
``$3\,{\rm dB}$ quieter'', and with the $\Delta f\propto
f_{0}$ normalisation ``unchanged''; the $6\,{\rm dB}$
number is for comparison at the same absolute frequency
off set.  Neglecting the $\omega_{0}$ shift this is
quoted as ${\cal L}\propto kT/C_{L}$, i. e. half the
noise power for $2C_{L}$.  The absolute cycle to cycle
jitter is $\sqrt{2}$ larger.  Any statement that the
phase noise is ``unchanged'' or ``$3\,{\rm dB}$ better
($6\,{\rm dB}$ at fixed $\Delta f$)'' is the same
${\cal F}{\cal O}{\cal M}={\rm const}$ statement to
within the normal textbook approximations.  Including
wave form and $\Gamma_{rms}$ changes the improvement is
normally $2$--$4\,{\rm dB}$, $4$--$6\,{\rm dB}$ absolute.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly predicts frequency halving and a fourfold (6 dB) phase-noise reduction at a fixed absolute offset, supported by charge/noise scaling. Its extra fixed-fractional-offset discussion is muddled, but does not change the required conclusion.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if CL becomes arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
If you want to be very pedantic about it the
answer is: {\it in the linear, small signal, near
sinusoidal, Barkhausen sense} yes and {\it in the
large signal, rail to rail, {\it digital} sense}
no.  What is normally quoted as ``the ring does
not have a stable Boolean state'' remains true.

Put $R_{0},C_{0}$ for the output resistance and the
{\it intrinsic} output capacitance of one inverter,
$A_{0}=g_{m}R_{0}>>1$ for its small signal
voltage gain and

$$p_{0}={1\over {R_{0}C_{0}}}\qquad 
  p_{1}={1\over {R_{0}(C_{0}+C_{L})}}=k\,p_{0}\tag{*}$$

$$k={{C_{0}}\over {C_{0}+C_{L}}}<1$$

for the pole at the loaded node.  With the usual
one pole model for the inverter the loop gain is

$${\cal L}(s)={{(-A_{0})^{3}}
     {\left(1+s/p_{1}\right)\left(1+s/p_{0}\right)^{2}}}
     =-{A_{0}^{3}\over {\left(1+s/kp_{0}\right)
        \left(1+s/p_{0}\right)^{2}}}\tag{1}$$

$${\cal L}(j\omega )=
   {{A_{0}^{3}e^{{j\pi}}}\over {
      \sqrt{1+(\omega /kp_{0})^{2}}
      \left[1+(\omega /p_{0})^{2}\right]}}
      e^{-j\left[\tan ^{-1}\!\omega /kp_{0}+
                  2\tan ^{-1}\!\omega /p_{0}\right]} \tag{2}$$

so that

$$\angle {\cal L}= \pi -\tan ^{-1}{\omega\over {kp_{0}}}
                    -2\tan ^{-1}{\omega\over {p_{0}}}\tag{3}$$

$|{\cal L}|=A_{0}^{3}/\sqrt{1+(\omega /kp_{0})^{2}}
\left[1+(\omega /p_{0})^{2}\right]$.
For $k=1$ the $0\pmod{2\pi }$ cross over is at

$$3\tan ^{-1}x=\pi \;\;,\;\;x=\omega /p_{0}=\sqrt{3}
\tag{4}$$

and, with $x=\omega /p_{0}$,

$$\tan ^{-1}{x\over k}+2\tan ^{-1}x =\pi \tag{5}$$

always has a solution. For $k\ll 1$, $\tan ^{-1}x/k
\approx \pi /2$ and (5) is at $x\approx 1$, $\omega
\approx p_{0}$.  At that $\omega $

$$|{\cal L}(j\omega _{0})|\approx
  {{A_{0}^{3}k}\over {x\left(1+x^{2}\right)}}\approx
  {{A_{0}^{3}}\over 2}k=
  {{A_{0}^{3}}\over 2}{{C_{0}}\over {C_{0}+C_{L}}}\tag{6}$$

i. e. the gain at the Barkhausen phase cross over
rolls off as $1/C_{L}$.

The closed loop characteristic $1-{\cal L}=0$,

$$\left(1+{s\over {kp_{0}}}\right)\left(1+{s\over {p_{0}}}
  \right)^{2}+A_{0}^{3}=0\tag{7}$$

is with $y=s/p_{0}$

$$y^{3}+(2+k)y^{2}+(1+2k)y+k\left(1+A_{0}^{3}\right)=0
\tag{8}$$

which is Hurwitz iff

$$(2+k)(1+2k)>k\left(1+A_{0}^{3}\right)\tag{9}$$

The Hopf bifurcation $y=j\omega_{0}$ is at

$$ \omega _{0}^{2}=1+2k \tag{10}$$
$$kA_{0}^{3}=2(1+k)^{2}\tag{11}$$

i. e. up to $k\approx 1$

$$A_{0}^{3}\approx {2\over k}\tag{12}$$

for $k\ll 1$.  In ordinary language

$$\eqalign{
C_{L,{\rm crit}}&\approx C_{0}\left({A_{0}^{3}\over 2}-1\right)
\cr
&\approx {{g_{m}R_{0}}^{3}\over 2}C_{0}\tag{13}}$$

and for $C_{L}>C_{L,{\rm crit}}$ all three
closed loop poles are in the ${\rm Re}\,s<0$ half
plane, the $V_{M}$ equilibrium where all three
inverters are in the high gain region is small
signal stable and a small perturbation, noise,
decays to $V_{M}$.  In the ${\cal L}\to \infty $,
$C_{L}\to \infty $ limit $p_{1}\to 0$ the loaded
node is an a. c. ground, $|{\cal L}|\to 0$, and,
linearly, the loop is broken.  In that linear
Barkhausen sense the ``nice'' quasi sinusoidal
oscillation does disappear for

$$k<k_{c}=2/A_{0}^{3}\tag{14}$$

For a normal CMOS inverter $A_{0}\sim 10-30$,
$A_{0}^{3}\sim 10^{3}-3\times 10^{4}$, so that

$$C_{L,{\rm crit}}\sim 5\times 10^{2}-10^{4}\;C_{0}\tag{15}$$

is astronomically large on the scale of the normal
parasitic.  For any normal design value the circuit
is small signal unstable and starts up.

If the inverters are idealized as high gain
comparators, $A_{0}\to \infty $, $k_{c}\to 0$,
$C_{L,{\rm crit}}\to \infty $, the phase condition
(5) can always be satisfied with $|{\cal L}|>1$ and
the circuit is astable for any finite $C_{L}$.
Large signal the three inverters saturate rail to
rail.  Putting $\tau_{L}=R_{0}C_{L}\gg \tau_{0}=
R_{0}C_{0}$ and eliminating the two fast poles
adiabatically, $V_{B}\approx f(V_{A})$, $V_{C}\approx
f(V_{B})$,

$$\tau_{L}\dot V_{A}=f\!\left(f\!\left(f(V_{A})\right)\right)
      -V_{A}\equiv h(V_{A})-V_{A}\tag{16}$$

$h$ is monotone decreasing, $h(0)=V_{DD}$,
$h(V_{DD})=0$, so $h(V_{M})=V_{M}$ is the unique
(Boolean inconsistent) d. c. solution, but (16) is
normally operated saturated.  Idealising $f$ as
$V_{DD}$ for $V_{in}<V_{M}-\epsilon $ and $0$ for
$V_{in}>V_{M}+\epsilon $ the loaded node ramps
exponentially towards the rail dictated by the two
inverter buffer with time constant $\tau_{L}$,
crosses $V_{M}$, the buffer snaps, the drive
reverses and the ramp reverses.  I. e. the circuit
goes over into the familiar $R_{0}C_{L}$ relaxation
oscillator with, to first order,

$$T\approx 2\tau_{L}\ln {2V_{DD}\over {V_{DD}-V_{M}}}
      \approx 2R_{0}C_{L}\ln 2\tag{17}$$

for $V_{M}\approx V_{DD}/2$, $f_{osc}\propto 1/C_{L}
\to 0$ as $C_{L}\to \infty $, but $\ne 0$ for any
finite $C_{L}$.  In a conventional SPICE large
signal transient simulation the circuit will keep
switching rail to rail for any finite $C_{L}$ if you
kick it out of the $V_{M}$ metastable point.  With
finite $A_{0}$ that metastable point is small
signal stable for $C_{L}>C_{L,{\rm crit}}$ so that
it will not start up from noise, but it is still
large signal astable - the normal digital `` the
odd ring has no stable Boolean state'' - and a
large kick will put it on the relaxation limit
cycle.

In particular for all practical values $C_{L}\sim
{\cal O}(C_{0})$ the ring oscillates, just more
slowly, $f_{osc}\approx 1/2N\tau_{0}\to 1/2\tau_{L}$
when the loaded stage dominates.  The textbook
``it stops oscillating'' is the $C_{L}\to \infty $
a.c. short, $k\to 0$, $|{\cal L}|\to 0$ linear
result (13)-(14).  With $A_{0}\to\infty $ that
limit is pushed to infinity.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies the dominant pole from loading only one node and shows that, for finite inverter gain, the loop gain at phase crossover falls below unity beyond a finite CL, stabilizing the small-signal equilibrium. The large-signal relaxation-oscillation caveat is additional and does not negate that core result.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if CL becomes arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
In the ideal rail to rail picture {\it no};
in the small signal pole picture {\it yes} and the
two pictures coincide in $C_{L}=\infty $.
Put, for the normal analysis $g_{ds}=g$,

$$Z_{o1}={1\over g+sC_{1}}\qquad Z_{o2,3}={1\over g+sC_{0}}\qquad 
C_{1}=C_{0}+C_{L}$$

and, at the metastable, $V_{DD}/2$, bias

$$A_{v}=g_{m}r_{o}=g_{m}/g\tag{1}$$

$$L(s)=-A_{v}^{3}{(1+s\tau_{0})^{-2}(1+s\tau_{1})^{-1}}\tag{2}$$

$$\tau_{0}=C_{0}/g\;\;,\;\;\tau_{1}=C_{1}/g=K\tau_{0}\tag{3}$$

$L(j\omega )$ can have $\angle L=0\;{\rm mod}\;2\pi $
iff

$$\pi -\sum_{1}^{3}{\rm atan}\;\omega \tau_{i}=0\tag{4}$$

$$ \sum {\rm atan}\;\omega \tau_{i}=\pi \tag{4a}$$

For $K=1$

$$\omega_{0}={\sqrt{3}\over {\tau_{0}}}\qquad 
|L(j\omega_{0})|={A_{v}^{3}\over 8}\tag{5}$$

and $A_{v}>2$ will start.  For $K\gg 1$
${\rm atan}\;\omega \tau_{1}\rightarrow \pi /2$ and (4a)
is

$${\pi \over 2}+2{\rm atan}\;\omega \tau_{0}=\pi \tag{6}$$

$$\omega_{1}\approx {1\over {\tau_{0}}}\tag{7}$$

and

$$|L(j\omega_{1})|={{A_{v}^{3}}\over
{\sqrt{1+\omega_{1}^{2}\tau_{1}^{2}}\left(1+\omega_{1}^{2}\tau_{0}^{2}
\right)} }={{A_{v}^{3}}\over {2\sqrt{1+K^{2}}}}
\approx {{A_{v}^{3}}\over {2K}}\tag{8}$$

for $K\gg 1$.  I. e. the 180 deg. frequency is
still there, ${\cal O}(1/\tau_{0})$, but the gain
there goes as $1/K\propto 1/C_{L}$.

In closed loop form the poles are the roots of

$$1-L(s)=0\tag{9}$$

$$(1+s\tau_{1})(1+s\tau_{0})^{2}+A_{v}^{3}=0\tag{10}$$

$$K\tau_{0}^{3}s^{3}+(2K+1)\tau_{0}^{2}s^{2}+(K+2)\tau_{0}s+
1+A_{v}^{3}=0\tag{11}$$

Routh:

$$a_{3}=K\;\;a_{2}=2K+1\;\;a_{1}=K+2\;\;a_{0}=1+A_{v}^{3}\tag{12}$$

stable $=$ all ${\rm Re}\,s<0$ iff $a_{2}a_{1}>a_{3}a_{0}$.

$$\left(2K+1\right)\left(K+2\right)>K\left(1+A_{v}^{3}\right)\tag{13}$$

I. e. for sufficiently large $K$

$$K>K_{{\rm crit}}\approx {1\over 2}A_{v}^{3}\;\;,\;\;{\rm for}\;\;
A_{v}\gg 1\tag{14}$$

$$C_{L{\rm crit}}\approx \left({A_{v}^{3}\over 2}-1\right)C_{0}\tag{15}$$

the linearised circuit is stable.
With $A_{v}=10-20$, $A_{v}^{3}=10^{3}-8\times 10^{3}$,
$C_{L{\rm crit}}\sim 5\times 10^{2}-4\times 10^{3}C_{0}$.
For $C_{L}>C_{L{\rm crit}}$ a small noise ${\rm e}^{st}$
is damped to the metastable

$$V_{1}=V_{2}=V_{3}\approx V_{DD}/2\tag{16}$$

bias where all three devices are in saturation.
In that conventional small signal, Barkhausen,
describing function sense the oscillator is
{\it dead} to noise.  For $C_{L}\rightarrow \infty $
$Z_{o1}\rightarrow 0$ ac, the loop is ac open, $L\equiv 0$.

That is the conventional textbook ``it stops
oscillating''.

If the inverters are idealised as infinite gain
hard comparators, $V_{o}=V_{DD}{\rm sgn}\left(V_{TH}-V_{i}\right)$,
with an $R\,C_{L}$ charge at the loaded node, the
equation is non linear and (15) is irrelevant.
Put $T_{d}=t_{d2}+t_{d3}$ the delay of the two
unloaded inverters and $R=1/g$, $V_{TH}=V_{DD}/2$.
With the notation of the figure $B\equiv V_{o1}$,
$C\equiv V_{o2}$, $A\equiv V_{o3}$: $C=\bar B$ after
$t_{d2}$, $A=\bar C$ after $t_{d3}$.  For $A=0$, $B$
charges to $V_{DD}$ as

$$B(t)=V_{DD}-(V_{DD}-V_{L}){\rm e}^{-t/RC_{L}}\tag{17}$$

and for $A=1$ discharges as $B(t)=V_{H}{\rm e}^{-t/RC_{L}}$.
Continuity at the switching gives

$$\eqalign{
V_{L}&=V_{TH}{\rm e}^{-T_{d}/RC_{L}}\cr
V_{H}&=V_{DD}-\left(V_{DD}-V_{TH}\right){\rm e}^{-T_{d}/RC_{L}}\cr
t_{r}&=t_{f}=RC_{L}\log {{V_{H}\over {V_{TH}}}}
      =RC_{L}\log {{V_{DD}-V_{L}\over {V_{DD}-V_{TH}}}
      =RC_{L}\log \left(2-{\rm e}^{-T_{d}/RC_{L}}\right)\cr}\tag{18}$$

so that a full period is, $R\,C_{L}\ne 0$,

$$T=2\left(t_{r}+T_{d}\right)=
2RC_{L}\log \left(2-{\rm e}^{-T_{d}/RC_{L}}\right)+2T_{d}\tag{19}$$

For $RC_{L}\ll T_{d}$, $T\approx 2RC_{L}\log 2+2T_{d}
\approx 2\sum t_{di}$ the normal $2N\,t_{d}$ ring.
For $RC_{L}\gg T_{d}$

$$\eqalign{
\Delta V &=V_{H}-V_{TH}=V_{TH}-V_{L}={V_{DD}\over 2}
\left(1-{\rm e}^{-T_{d}/RC_{L}}\right)\approx {V_{DD}\over 2}
{T_{d}\over {RC_{L}}}\rightarrow 0\cr
t_{r}&\approx T_{d}\cr
T&\approx 4T_{d}=4\left(t_{d2}+t_{d3}\right)\approx 8t_{d0}\cr}\tag{20}$$

I. e. with ideal comparators a limit cycle exists for
every finite $C_{L}$.  Its saw tooth at $B$ collapses as
$1/C_{L}$ and its frequency asymptotes to a constant
determined by the two fast inverters, ${\cal O}(1/T_{d})$,
normally a little larger than the $6t_{d0}$ unloaded
$3$ stage frequency.  In describing function language the
large signal gain $N(A)\approx 4V_{DD}/\pi A$ can be
made arbitrarily large for small $A$, so (8) can always
be made $>1$ if you allow $A\rightarrow 0$.

In a real CMOS inverter the comparator gain is finite,
$\approx A_{v}$, and (20) ceases to be valid once
$\Delta V$ becomes comparable with the linear transition
width $\approx V_{DD}/A_{v}$.  Then $C$ and $A$ no longer
switch rail to rail and (8) takes over.  In SPICE you
will continue to see the $4T_{d}$ relaxation oscillation
with $\Delta V\propto 1/C_{L}$ for a long while, but its
start up from noise becomes exponentially slow for
$C_{L}>C_{L{\rm crit}}$ and for all practical purposes
the circuit looks latched at (16).  With an ideal
$C_{L}=\infty $ ac short it is latched in any picture.

> {\it Remark:}  Many textbooks quote the first, ideal,
> result as ``the odd ring never stops, it just gets
> slower and its loaded node swing vanishes''.
> Strictly Barkhausen wise the second result is the
> correct small signal one.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies the extra pole from the one-node load, shows that loop gain falls below unity at the phase crossover for sufficiently large CL, and concludes that the finite-gain circuit settles near its DC operating point. The ideal-comparator caveat is explicitly distinguished from the real finite-gain behavior and does not overturn the essential conclusion.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if CL becomes arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
With ideal switches it does not. With
linearised $g_{m}$'s it does.  In the text
books the first is called oscillation.

Put $Z_{o}=R_{o}\parallel 1/sC_{0}$ for an
unloaded inverter and

$$Z_{o1}=R_{o}\parallel 1/s\left(C_{0}+C_{L}\right)$$

for the loaded one and linearise the $3-T$
about $V_{DD}/2$

$$\eqalign{
A_{v}&=g_{m}R_{o}\cr
\omega _{0}&=1/R_{o}C_{0}\cr
\omega _{1}&=1/R_{o}\left(C_{0}+C_{L}\right)=1/b\cr}$$

Break the loop at $C$.

$$L(s)=-A_{v}^{3}{(1+s/a)^{-2}(1+s/b)^{-1}}\tag{1}$$

$$a=R_{o}C_{0}\qquad b=R_{o}(C_{0}+C_{L})$$

The closed loop equation $1-L(s)=0$ is

$$(1+sb)(1+sa)^{2}+A_{v}^{3}=0\tag{2}$$

$$s^{3}a^{2}b+s^{2}(a^{2}+2ab)+s(2a+b)+1+A_{v}^{3}=0\tag{3}$$

$$A_{3}s^{3}+A_{2}s^{2}+A_{1}s+A_{0}=0\qquad A_{i}>0$$

By Routh the c. c. is LHP iff

$$A_{2}A_{1}>A_{3}A_{0}\tag{4}$$

i. e.

$$\left(a^{2}+2ab\right)\left(2a+b\right)>a^{2}b\left(1+A_{v}^{3}\right)\tag{5}$$

$$2a^{2}+5ab+2b^{2}>ab\left(1+A_{v}^{3}\right) \tag{6}$$

$$2{b\over a}+5+2{a\over b}<1+A_{v}^{3} \tag{7}$$

for instability, i. e. for a pair of
poles in the RHP.  For $b=a$, ${C_{L}=0}$,

$$A_{v}^{3}>8\qquad A_{v}>2\tag{8}$$

in the normal way.  Eq.7 is the ordinary
Barkhausen condition in disguise.  Put
$s=j\omega $ in (1)

$$\eqalign{
|L(j\omega )|&=A_{v}^{3}\left[1+(\omega b)^{2}\right]^{-1/2}
\left[1+(\omega a)^{2}\right]^{-1}\cr
{\rm arg}L&=\pi -\tan ^{-1}\omega b-2\tan ^{-1}\omega a\cr}\tag{9}$$

Oscillation in the Barkhausen sense needs
${\rm arg}L=2k\pi $,

$$\tan ^{-1}\omega_{0}b+2\tan ^{-1}\omega_{0}a=\pi \tag{10}$$

$0<{\rm arg}<{3\pi /2}$, so (10) has a
solution for every $b$, nominally

$$\omega_{0}\approx {1\over a}\tag{11}$$

for $b\gg a$, because $\tan ^{-1}\omega_{0}b
\to \pi /2$ and $2\tan ^{-1}\omega_{0}a\to
\pi /2$.  At that $\omega_{0}$

$$|L(j\omega_{0})|\approx {A_{v}^{3}\over
\sqrt{1+(b/a)^{2}}\;2}\approx A_{v}^{3}{a\over 2b}
\tag{12}$$

so that

$$|L(j\omega_{0})|>1\iff A_{v}^{3}>2{b\over a}
\tag{13}$$

which is (7) for $b\gg a$.  In other words the
dominant pole compensation kills the loop gain
at the $0\,{\rm deg}$ crossover.  There is an

$$b_{c}\approx {1\over 2}A_{v}^{3}a\tag{14}$$

$$C_{Lc}\approx \left({1\over 2}A_{v}^{3}-1\right)C_{0}\tag{15}$$

${\cal O}(10^{2}-10^{3})C_{0}$ for a normal
$A_{v}\sim 10-20$, beyond which the small
signal pole pair is in the ${\rm Re}\,s<0$
half plane.  The meta stable $V_{A}=V_{B}=
V_{C}=V_{T}$ point becomes small signal stable.
For $b\to \infty $,

$$L(s)\to -{A_{v}^{3}\over sb(1+sa)^{2}}\tag{16}$$

a two pole amplifier dominant pole compensated,
which is stable; $C_{L}\to\infty $ shorts the
loop for $a.\,c.$  The normal $360^{0}$ linear
sinusoidal ring mode is extinguished and the
circuit will not start up from thermal noise.

That is the {\it linear\/} story.

Put the inverters back as large signal relays,
$I_{o}=I$ when on, $V_{T}=V_{DD}/2$,
$T_{d}=t_{p2}+t_{p3}$ the delay of the two
unloaded inverters.  With

$$C_{L}{{dV_{A}}\over {dt}}=I_{1}(V_{C})\tag{17}$$

$$V_{C}(t)= {\rm sgn}\left[V_{A}(t-T_{d})-V_{T}\right]\tag{18}$$

in the ideal relay approximation the circuit is
a first order plus delay relay.  Let $V_{A}$
cross $V_{T}$ upward at $t=0$.  $V_{C}=1$ for
$T_{d}$ more, so

$$V_{A}=V_{T}+I\,T_{d}/C_{L}\equiv V_{T}+\Delta
\tag{19}$$

at $t=T_{d}$ when $V_{C}$ flips to $0$ and
$V_{A}$ ramps down with $dV_{A}/dt=-I/C_{L}$,
recrosses $V_{T}$ at $t=2T_{d}$, continues to
$V_{T}-\Delta $ at $t=3T_{d}$ etc.  The system
has a limit cycle

$$\eqalign{
\Delta &= I\,T_{d}/C_{L}\cr
T_{0}&\approx 4T_{d}\cr}\tag{20}$$

for {\it any\/} finite $C_{L}$.  For $C_{L}$
small $\Delta \gg V_{DD}$ the relay saturates
and you get the ordinary rail to rail
$T_{0}\approx 2N\,t_{p}+k\,R_{o}C_{L}$ ring
oscillator.  For $C_{L}$ large

$$\Delta \propto 1/C_{L}\to 0\tag{21}$$

so the large signal swing collapses to an
infinitesimal triangle about $V_{T}$ of period
$\approx 4T_{d}$ and (20) ceases to be valid
as soon as $\Delta $ becomes of the order of the
linear transition width of the inverter,
${\cal O}(V_{DD}/A_{v})$.  Inside the transition
width the relay model has to be replaced by the
linear model (1) which, as we have seen, is
damped.  The infinitesimal limit cycle is then
damped to the stable $V_{T}$ DC point.

In text book digital language that is normally
phrased as {\it the circuit continues to oscillate
for any $C_{L}$, only more and more slowly\/}.
If oscillation is meant as a robust, self starting
rail to rail clock that grows out of noise, the
statement is: beyond (15) the conventional ring
mode disappears, the amplitude $\Delta \to 0$,
and for all engineering purposes the ring has
stalled at $V_{A}\approx V_{B}\approx V_{C}
\approx V_{DD}/2$.

With $C_{L}\to\infty $ {\it qua\/} $a.\,c.$
short the familiar $RC$ astable consisting of
one inverter loaded by $C_{L}$ buffered by the
other two is recovered as the $a.\,c.$
degenerate form of (20).  It is normally drawn
as the one inverter $RC$ relaxation oscillator
and, with ideal comparators, it does oscillate
for any $R\,C$.  With normal CMOS inverters the
oscillation is vanishingly small once (15) is
exceeded.

> {\it Remark:\/}  In most introductory treatments
> the ${\cal O}(1/C_{L})$ collapse of the swing
> is neglected and the circuit is said {\it not\/}
> to fail to oscillate: $f_{0}\approx
> \left[2Nt_{p}+0.7R_{o}C_{L}\right]^{-1}\to 0$ but
> $\ne 0$.  The linear, Barkhausen, start up
> failure described above is the correct analog
> description.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the dominant pole from the one-node load, the resulting loop-gain loss and small-signal stabilization beyond a load threshold, and concludes that a real CMOS ring can fail to start or sustain oscillation for arbitrarily large CL. The ideal-relay limit-cycle discussion is explicitly qualified and does not undermine that conclusion.

answers.question: If we double the widths of the NMOS and PMOS devices in the figure, what happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
With the usual ${\rm ideal~self~loaded}$ language
the circuit is the textbook Hajimiri Lee inverter ring.

Put $W_{p}/W_{n}$ so that the rise and the fall are
symmetric and change it with $W_{p}/W_{n}={\rm const}$

$${C_{L}\approx C_{g}+C_{d}\propto W\qquad 
R_{o}\approx 1/g_{m}\propto 1/W\qquad 
I_{av}\propto W}$$

so that to first order

$$t_{d}\approx 0.69R_{o}C_{L}\approx 
{{C_{L}V_{DD}}\over {I_{av}}}={\rm const.}$$

$$\omega _{0}\approx {1\over {2Nt_{d}}}={\rm const.}\tag{*}$$

for the $W$ dependent, intrinsic, load.
With a fixed wiring load $C_{\rm ext}$

$$C_{L}=C_{\rm ext}+Wc_{0}\qquad 
\omega _{0}\propto {W\over {C_{\rm ext}+Wc_{0}}}\tag{**}$$

and ($*$) is the $C_{\rm ext}\ll Wc_{0}$ limit.
The normal, saturated, short channel, current
is still $\propto W$ so that

$$P_{DC}=NC_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}\propto Wf_{0}\tag{***}$$

i. e. in the self loaded limit $f_{0}={\rm const.}$
and you burn twice the power.

For the Hajimiri-Lee ISF

$${\cal L}\{\Delta \omega \}=10\log \left[
{1\over {8\pi ^{2}\Delta f^{2}}}\,
{{{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}\,
{\Gamma _{rms}^{2}\over {q_{max}^{2}}}}\right] \tag{1}$$

$$q_{max}=C_{L}V_{DD}\propto W\tag{2}$$

$${{{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}=
4kT\gamma g_{d0}+K_{f}{{g_{m}^{2}}\over {WLC_{ox}} }{1\over f}
\propto W\tag{3}}$$

in white and in the normal $S_{v}=K_{f}/WLC_{ox}f$,
$S_{i}=g_{m}^{2}S_{v}$, flicker model.
$g_{d0}\propto g_{m}\propto W$ in the square law
or in the velocity saturated limit.
$\Gamma _{rms}$ and $c_{0}$, the rms and the
d.c. value of the impulse sensitivity function, depend
only on the normalized wave form and stay {\it pro
forma} constant if the symmetry $W_{p}/W_{n}$ is kept,
i. e. if the wave form stays symmetric the ${\rm 1/f}$
up conversion $c_{0}\approx 0$ stays suppressed.

Hence from (1)-(3)

$${\cal L}\propto {{{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}}\over
{q_{max}^{2}}}\propto {W\over {W^{2}}}={1\over W}\tag{4}$$

in power.  In the familiar Leeson form, for the
$N$ stage ring, Razavi,

$${\cal L}\{\Delta \omega \}\approx
{8\over {3\eta }}{{kT}\over {P_{DC}}}{{V_{DD}}\over
{V_{{\rm char}}}}\left({{\omega _{0}}\over {\Delta
\omega }}\right)^{2}\tag{5}$$

$$P_{DC}= {\rm (***)} $$

the same $1/P_{DC}\propto 1/W$ law.

I. e. in ($*$) $f_{0}$ does not move, $P_{DC}$ doubles
and the white, ${1\over {f^{2}}}$, side band power is
halved,

$${\cal L}_{w}\rightarrow {1\over 2}{\cal L}_{w}\;\;
-3\,{\rm dB~in~}{\cal L},-6\,{\rm dB~in~}{\cal L}^{1/2}
\tag{6}$$

$$\sigma _{J}^{2}= {{\kappa ^{2}}t}\qquad 
\kappa ^{2}\propto {{kT}\over {C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}}}\propto
{1\over W}\tag{7}$$

$$\kappa \propto {1\over {\sqrt{W}}}\qquad 
\sigma _{T}= \kappa \sqrt{T_{0}}\propto {1\over {\sqrt{W}}}$$

for the period jitter.  Colloquially you have put two
identical rings in parallel.

For the ${\rm 1/f}$ induced ${1\over {f^{3}}}$ skirt
(1) is normally written with the $c_{0}$ term,

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto c_{0}^{2}
{{{\overline{i_{n,1/f}^{2}}}}\over {q_{max}^{2}}}
{1\over {\Delta f^{3}}}\propto {1\over W}\tag{8}$$

in the $S_{i}\propto W$ model, i. e. another $3\,{\rm
dB}$ per octave of $W$.  Writing the flicker explicitly
as $K_{f}/WL$,

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto {{K_{f}}\over {WLC_{ox}}}
{{g_{m}^{2}}\over {q_{max}^{2}}}\propto
{1\over {W}}\,{{W^{2}}\over {W^{2}}}={1\over W}\tag{9}$$

and, if you count the $WL$ in the denominator as an
independent area factor, often quoted as

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto {1\over {W^{2}L}}\approx
{6\,{\rm dB~per~octave~of}~W}\tag{10}$$

and with $q_{max}^{2}\propto W^{2}$ as ${1\over {W^{3}}}$,
$9\,{\rm dB}$ per octave, in the current
$S_{i}=K_{f}I_{D}^{2}/WLC_{ox}f$ notation.  Any of (8)-(10)
is quoted as {\it the close in noise goes down
$6-9\,{\rm dB}$ per doubling of area.}

In Leeson FoM language

$${\rm FoM}={\cal L}\{\Delta f\}
-20\log \left({{f_{0}}\over {\Delta f}}\right)
+10\log \left({{P_{DC}}\over {1\,{\rm mW}}}\right)
\approx {\rm const.}\tag{11}$$

so that the ${\rm FoM}$ is to first order $W$
independent.  You buy the $3\,{\rm dB}$, $6\,{\rm dB}$
close in, at the price of twice the dissipation and,
in the ideal ($*$) limit, at the same $f_{0}$.
Normalised to $f_{0}$, i. e. at the same fractional
offset $\Delta f/f_{0}$ or the same jitter FoM,
there is no net improvement.

With ($**$) the absolute side band at a fixed absolute
$\Delta f$ is

$${\cal L}\{\Delta f\}\propto 
20\log f_{0}-10\log P_{DC}\tag{12}$$

so that with an extrinsic, $W$ independent, load the
$f_{0}$ increase $\propto 20\log f_{0}$ eventually
wins and the absolute ${\cal L}\{\Delta f\}$ gets
{\it worse} by $\approx +3\,{\rm dB}$ per octave of $W$
while ${\cal L}\{\Delta f/f_{0}\}$ and the jitter FoM
remain $\approx $ flat.  In deep sub $\mu$ the $g_{m}
\propto W^{\alpha }$, $\alpha <1$, wiring $C$ and
gate leakage make the $3\,{\rm dB}$ an upper bound.
Loosely phrased as {\it doubling the device has, to
first order, no effect on the oscillator FoM.}

> {\it Remark:} For a current starved, fixed $I_{SS}$,
> ring $P_{DC}={\rm const.}$, $f_{0}\propto 1/C_{L}\propto
> 1/W$ in ($*$) and (5) gives ${\cal L}\{\Delta f\}
> \propto f_{0}^{2}\propto 1/W^{2}$, $-6\,{\rm dB}$
> at fixed $\Delta f$, $-3\,{\rm dB}$ at fixed
> $\Delta f/f_{0}$, i. e. the same $1/W$ law for the
> fractional side band.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly gives the approximately 3 dB phase-noise reduction for the self-loaded ring and supports it with the right scaling: signal charge grows with width while device noise power grows only linearly. The extra discussion is not needed to answer the question and does not change that central result.

answers.question: If we double the widths of the NMOS and PMOS devices in the figure, what happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
With the (text book) ${\cal C}_{L}\propto W$
normalisation the ring is a constant ${\cal F}{\cal O}{\cal M}$
oscillator.  In Leeson's form

$$ {\cal L}(\Delta \omega )\propto 
{\overline {i_{n}^{2}}\over q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}
{1\over {\Delta \omega }^{2}}\propto 
{FkT\over P_{{\rm diss}}}{\omega _{0}^{2}\over {\Delta \omega }^{2}}\tag
{*}$$

$P_{{\rm diss}}$ is the D.C. plus the dynamic power

$$P_{{\rm diss}}\approx NP_{av}\approx Nf_{0}{\cal C}_{L}V_{DD}^{2}
+N I_{av}V_{DD}\propto {\cal C}_{L}\propto W \tag{1}$$

$$f_{0}\approx {1\over {2Nt_{d}}}\qquad 
t_{d}\approx {{\cal C}_{L}V_{DD}\over I_{av}}\approx 
{{\cal C}_{L}\over g_{m}}\tag{2}$$

$${\cal C}_{L}=N_{S}W{\cal C}_{{\rm ox}}+{\cal C}_{w}\propto W\qquad 
I_{av}\propto W\qquad g_{m}\propto W\tag{3}$$

$$\overline {i_{n}^{2}}=4kT\gamma g_{m}\propto W\tag{4}$$

$$q_{{\rm max}}={\cal C}_{L}V_{DD}\propto W\tag{5}$$

for the white noise and, for the conventional
${\overline {v_{n,1/f}^{2}}}=K_{F}/WLC_{{\rm ox}}f$,

$$\overline {i_{n,1/f}^{2}}=g_{m}^{2}{\overline {v_{n,1/f}^{2}}}
\propto W^{\alpha }\tag{6}$$

So that in the normal time domain language the
r.m.s. threshold jitter in one transition

$${\sigma _{t}^{2}}={{\overline {v_{n}^{2}}}\over S^{2}}
={{kT/{\cal C}_{L}}\over {\left(I_{av}/{\cal C}_{L}\right)^{2}}}
={{kT{\cal C}_{L}}\over {I_{av}^{2}}}\propto {1\over W}\tag{7}$$

$S=I_{av}/{\cal C}_{L}$ is the slew rate at the
threshold, and for the $N$ stage ring

$${\sigma _{T}^{2}}\approx N{\sigma _{t}^{2}}\tag{8}$$

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )\approx
{{\omega _{0}^{2}{\sigma _{T}^{2}}}\over {2T_{0}{\Delta \omega }^{2}}}
\approx {{\Gamma _{{\rm rms}}^{2}}\over {8\pi ^{2}{\Delta \omega }^{2}}}
{{\overline {i_{n}^{2}}}\over {q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}}\propto 
{{\overline {i_{n}^{2}}}\over {q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}}\tag{9}$$

cf. Hajimiri-Lee, {\it JSSC} {\bf 33}, 179 (1998)

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )={8\over 3\eta }N{{kT}\over P}
{{V_{DD}}\over {V_{{\rm char}}}}{{\omega _{0}^{2}}\over {\Delta \omega
^{2}}}\tag{10}$$

$$V_{{\rm char}}=E_{c}L/\gamma \tag{11}$$

for the $1/f^{2}$ region and with (6) for the
$1/f^{3}$ region.  I. e. to first order on a $W/L=$
const, $V_{DD}=$ const. basis

$$f_{0}\propto {g_{m}\over {\cal C}_{L}}={\rm const.}\tag{12}$$

$$ {\cal L}_{{\rm white}}\propto {1\over P}\propto {1\over W}
\qquad {\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto {1\over {W^{1\to 2}}}\tag{13}$$

The often quoted form is ($*$): the oscillator
figure of merit

$${\cal F}{\cal O}{\cal M}= {\cal L}(\Delta \omega )
+10\log {{P_{{\rm diss}}}\over {1{\rm mW}}}
-20\log {{\omega _{0}}\over {\Delta \omega }} ={\rm const.}\tag{14}$$

is (to first order) independent of $W$.  If you are
willing to burn the $\times 2$ power the absolute
(single side band) phase noise power ${\cal L}$,
${\rm dBcHz^{-1}}$, goes down by

$${{{\cal L}(2W)}\over {{\cal L}(W)}}\approx {1\over 2}\;\;
{\rm in\;power}\approx {1\over {\sqrt{2}}}\;\;{\rm in\;
voltage\;or\;jitter}\tag{15}$$

$10\log 2\approx 3\,{\rm dB}$ in power,
$20\log \sqrt{2}\approx 3\,{\rm dB}$ in amplitude, for
the normal $1/f^{2}$ thermal region, $\approx 3-6\,{\rm dB}$
for the $1/f^{3}$ region according as $A_{F}\approx
2\to 1$ in ${\overline {i_{n,1/f}^{2}}}\propto
I_{D}^{A_{F}}/WL$, at the expense of a $\times 2$ in
$I_{DD}$ and in $P_{{\rm diss}}$.  Normally quoted,
