$t_{p1}+t_{p2}+t_{p3}+t_{sw}$.

Let

$$A = {\rm input\;of\;}Inv_{1}$$
$$B = {\rm output\;of\;}Inv_{1}=\bar A$$
$$C = {\rm input\;of\;}Inv_{2}$$
$$D =\bar C$$
$$E =\bar D = C = Q$$

$$E =\bar{\bar C}=C$$

$Inv_{2}+Inv_{3}$ is a non inverting buffer.

* $CK=1,\;\bar{CK}=0$ : $S_{1}{\rm ON},S_{2}{\rm OFF}$

Transparent master, $S_{2}$ isolates slave.

$$A =E_{0}= Q_{0}$$
$$B =\bar A =\bar Q_{0}$$
$$C = C_{0}=Q_{0} {\rm \;held\;on\;}C_{C}$$
$$D =\bar Q_{0}$$
$$E = Q_{0}$$

Master samples the old slave output.

* $CK=0,\;\bar{CK}=1$ : $S_{1}{\rm OFF},S_{2}{\rm ON}$

Master holds on $C_{A}$, slave samples master.

$$A = A_{1}=Q_{0} {\rm \;held}$$
$$C =B =\bar A_{1}= \bar Q_{0}$$
$$D =\bar C = Q_{0}$$
$$E = \bar D =\bar Q_{0}= \bar A_{1}$$

$$E_{CK=0}= \bar A_{CK=0}$$

* Next $CK=1$:

$$A_{2}=E_{1}= \bar A_{1}$$
$$B_{2}= \bar A_{2}=A_{1}$$
$$E_{2}=E_{1}{\rm \;held}$$

$A$ changes on the $0\to 1$ edge, $E$
changes on the $1\to 0$ edge.

In discrete time at the active edge:

$$A_{n+1}=E_{n}= \bar A_{n}$$
$$E_{n+1}= \bar E_{n}$$

$$Q_{n+1}= \bar Q_{n}$$

i.e. $T$-flip flop with $T\equiv 1$.

| $CK$ | $S_{1}$ | $S_{2}$ | $A$ | $B$ | $C$ | $Q=E$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | C | O | $Q_{old}$ | $\bar Q_{old}$ |hold $Q_{old}$| $Q_{old}$ |
| 0 | O | C | hold $Q_{old}$ | $\bar Q_{old}$ | $\bar Q_{old}$| $\bar Q_{old}$ |
| 1 | C | O | $\bar Q_{old}$| $Q_{old}$ |hold $\bar Q_{old}$| $\bar Q_{old}$ |
| 0 | O | C | hold $\bar Q_{old}$| $Q_{old}$| $Q_{old}$| $Q_{old}$ |

> {\it Without the feedback} $D\to S_{1}$ the
> chain $D-S_{1}-Inv_{1}-S_{2}-Inv_{2}-Inv_{3}-Q$
> is a negative $D$ flip flop
> $$Q = \overline{D_{sampled}}$$
> latched on $CK$. With $D=Q$ you get
> $$Q(n+1)=\bar Q(n).$$

In the time domain, for a $50\%$ $CK$ of period
$T_{CK}$:

```
CK  _|‾|_|‾|_|‾|_|‾|_|‾|_|‾|_
A   ‾‾‾|_____|‾‾‾‾‾|_____|‾‾  f = fck/2  rising edge triggered
E   ___|‾‾‾‾‾|_____|‾‾‾‾‾|___  f = fck/2  falling edge triggered
B = ~A , D = ~C = ~Q
```

Tapping $A$ is a positive edge $T\,FF$, tapping $E$
is a negative edge $T\,FF$. Amplitude $2T_{CK}$,
$50\%$ duty, i. e. divide by $2$ prescaler.

This is the basic cell of the dynamic shift
register, $n$ cells in series $\times$ $2n$
Johnson counter/divider. In static form a weak
cross coupled keeper is added at $A$ and at $C$
to prevent leakage, becoming a fully static
master-slave TSPC divider at the cost of area
and speed.

Use: very small, very fast, very low power
$\propto C V^{2}f$, $1\,b$ memory, $:2$ prescaler
in PLL, counters, frequency synthesizers.
Must be clocked continuously within
$f_{min}\approx I_{leak}/C_{p}\Delta V < f < f_{max}
\approx 1/t_{p}$ with non overlapping $CK,\bar{CK}$,
otherwise data is lost - clock feedthrough,
charge sharing, skew and $t_{hold}$ violations.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the circuit as a divide-by-two built from two dynamic latches; the additional timing and device-level details are not required for full credit.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in the figure affect the performance?

answer.text:
It is the {\it keeper - trickle - bleeder}
for the $Inv_{1}$ {\it pseudo static}
master latch. Without it:

$$\eqalign{
CK=1~,{\bar {CK}}=0 &: A=E,I_{1}:A\rightarrow B ~{\rm open~at}~{\bar {CK}}\cr
CK=0~,{\bar {CK}}=1 &: A= {\rm floating}~,I_{1}:A\rightarrow B\rightarrow C\rightarrow D\rightarrow E }$$

i.e. the conventional {\it True Single Phase
Clock} $NORA$ dynamic divider/latch. In
first order ratio-less, minimum $C$, minimum
$I_{cc}$, minimum $t_{pLH},t_{pHL}$ and
maximum $f_{max}\sim 1/2\sum t_{p}$ ${\cal O}(1-2\,{\rm GHz}$ in 
$0.18\mu )$ but dynamic:

* $A$ is high impedance when $CK=0$
* has to stand the leakage $I_{j}+I_{sub}$,
clock feed-through, charge sharing, $dV/dt$
noise, $\alpha $ particle for $T_{L}>1/f_{min}$
* $dV_{A}/dt = I_{leak}/C_{A}$ so
$$V_{A}(t)=V_{A0}\exp -t/R_{leak}C_{A}$$
falls in ${\rm ms}$ to threshold and state is
lost. In practice it will not divide below
$\sim 100{\rm MHz}-10{\rm MHz}$ depending on
$T$ and will not tolerate slow $CK$
slew rate

With the red $I_{R}:B\rightarrow A$:

$$I_{1}+I_{R} : A\rightleftharpoons B$$

is a $>1$ loop gain cross coupled bistable.
For ${\bar {CK}}=1$, $I_{R}$ shorted at $A$ by
low $Z_{o}(I_{1})$, for $CK=0$, $SW_{CK}$
open, $I_{1}+I_{R}$ latches $A,B=\bar A$.

> staticizes the master. Pseudo static
> $TSPC$, St $TSPC$, $C^{2}MOS$ latch.

* no $f_{min}$ - DC to $f_{max}$ operation
* no charge retention problem
* large noise margin, no charge sharing
error, very much more tolerant to clock
overlap - skew - slow edge
* correct toggle divide by $2$ even with
gated clock

price:

* ratioed logic. $I_{R}$ contends with
$I_{1}$ and with the $2I$ slave feedback
$p/n$ through $SW_{CK}$ on a $0\rightarrow 1$
and $1\rightarrow 0$ write.
It must be made {\it weak} - small $W/L$, long
$L$, ${\cal O}(1/5-1/10)$ of $I_{1}$, i. e.
overpowerable, to be able to be written.
Normally $n$ weak $p$ weak inverter.
That is area, $C_{g}+C_{d}$ on the high
speed nodes $A,B$ and crow bar current
during the contention time.

$$\eqalign{
C_{A}^{\prime} &= C_{A}+C_{gR}+C_{dR}\cr
C_{B}^{\prime} &= C_{B}+C_{gR}+C_{dR}\cr
I_{eff} &= I_{1}-I_{R}~{\rm on~switching}}$$

so

* $t_{pMaster}\approx 0.69R_{1}(C_{B}+C_{R})$
increases $15-30\%$
* $t_{CK-Q}$ increases by same amount
* $I_{cc}=I_{dyn}+I_{sc}$ increases due to
$C_{R}$ and to $I_{1}\times I_{R}$ short
circuit current for $t_{cont}\sim t_{r,CK}$
* $P_{dyn}=C^{\prime}V_{DD}^{2}f$ increases
* $f_{max}=1/2\left[ t_{pM}^{\prime}+t_{pS}\right]$
decreases ${\cal O}(20-40\%)$
* large $I_{R}$ kills write, division failure,
small $I_{R}$ does not keep. $PVT$ ratio
critical.

In short: You buy DC, low frequency, leakage
and noise robustness with speed, power and area.
For a high speed prescaler without the $I_{R}$
is faster and lower power, with correctly
$k$ ratioed weak $I_{R}$ it becomes a robust
static $:2$ that will divide to DC. That is
normally quoted as ``static divider''.

> ***Remark:*** In text book form the red
> device is often drawn as a weak clocked
> feedback $p$ and $n$ or as a single weak
> $p$ pull up. Same function.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It misidentifies the red inverter as a keeper/feedback latch and claims it enables DC operation. The actual feedforward path improves high-speed operation but can raise the minimum usable clock frequency at low rates.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in the figure affect the performance?

answer.text:
With ${\rm Inv_{1}}$ it makes a so called
{\it keeper, bleeder, staticizer} and the {\it half}
{\it static} or {\it pseudo static} version of the
normally {\it fully dynamic} TSPC $C^{2}MOS$ master
slave $\,{:}\div 2$.

In normal drawing ${\rm Inv_{R}}$ is drawn upside
down with respect to ${\rm Inv_{1}}$:
$${\rm Inv_{1}}:E\to \bar E\qquad 
 {\rm Inv_{R}}:\bar E\to E$$
i. e. a cross coupled pair.

> {\it If you have really drawn it in parallel with
> ${\rm Inv_{1}}$, $E\to \bar E$, it is simply an
> increase of the transconductance of the master
> inverter, $\approx 1/2$ inverter delay less at
> $\approx 2\times $ capacitance $+$ power $+$ area.}

Logically no function. Normally $W_{R}/L_{R}\ll
W_{1}/L_{1}$ and in first order for logic the
functions are identical, a conventional positive
edge triggered $D$ with $D=\bar Q$, i. e. a $T$, i. e.
a $:2$ prescaler.

Physically it changes the master from capacitive
{\it dynamic} storage on $C_{par}$ at the input of
${\rm Inv_{1}}$ to {\it latched static} storage with
$\left |A_{v}\right |>1$ .

Without it:

* master node $M$ during $\overline{CK}=0$,
$CK=0$ - switch open - floats. It is kept only on

$$Q_{M}=C_{M}.V_{M}$$

$C_{M}$ the parasitic $C_{g}+C_{ov}+C_{j}$ at the
input of ${\rm Inv_{1}}$. For $t \gg R_{leak}C_{M}\approx
I_{leak}^{-1}C_{M}\Delta V$ the charge leaks away,
state is lost, the divider drops out. At ambient
$R_{leak}^{-1}\sim {\rm nA}$, at hot $\mu {\rm A}$ 
$R_{leak}C\sim {\rm  ns}-\mu {\rm s}$. I. e. a
{\it lower} limiting frequency $f_{min}\sim 10^{4}-10^{6}{\rm Hz}$
below which it does not work, it is not clock
stoppable, not gateable, very noise, $dV/dt$,
soft error, clock slope and $V_{DD}$, $T$ sensitive.
Clock must be free running with $f_{clk}>f_{min}$
and with small $t_{r},t_{f}$.

* in compensation it is fast, small and low
power. No DC contention, no extra $C_{g}$. For RF
this is the form used e. g. as $:2$ prescaler in a
PLL. E. g. in $65{\rm nm}$, $f_{max,dyn}\approx
8-10{\rm GHz}$ with $f_{min}\ne 0$.

With it ${\rm Inv_{R}}$ closes a regenerative loop
round ${\rm Inv_{1}}$ when $T_{G1}$ is open and holds
$M$ actively at $V_{DD}$ or $GND$.

$${\rm Inv_{1}}\parallel {\rm Inv_{R}}= {\rm latch}$$

* the node is no longer floating, low impedance
DC driven in both states. Noise margin is the normal
static noise margin of a $>1$ loop, $f_{min}=0$ to
DC, clock can be stopped indefinitely, gated,
slowed down, slope is immaterial. Charge sharing,
charge injection, clock feedthrough, $V_{T}$ loss
is restored to full swing. This is the normal
logic form of the divider. Price:

* $C_{M}\to C_{M}+C_{gR}+C_{jR}$ and $C_{\bar M}\to
C_{\bar M}+C_{dR}$, typically $10-30\%$ extra load
on the high speed loop {\it in addition} to the
active fight during the write phase $CK=1$.

During $CK=1$, $I_{in}=I_{Qb}$ through the two slave
inverters must {\it overpower} $I_{R}$ to force $M$
to the new value. For a time $\sim t_{p}$ there is a
crow bar current $I_{1}-I_{R}$ between $V_{DD}$ and
$GND$ and the effective $g_{m}$ driving $M$ is
$g_{m1}-g_{mR}$.

$$t_{p,stat}\approx t_{p,dyn}\left(1+\frac{C_{R}}{C_{M}}\right)
 \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}-g_{mR}} > t_{p,dyn}$$

$$t_{CQ,stat}>t_{CQ,dyn}\qquad f_{max,stat}<f_{max,dyn}$$

in the conventional $\sim 15-25\%$ for minimum
size keeper. Dynamic power $CV^{2}f$ goes up with
$C_{R}$ and short circuit power $I_{sc}V_{DD}t_{sc}f$
during the contention goes up. Area goes up.

For that reason ${\rm Inv_{R}}$ is always made
{\it weak}, long $L$, small $W$,

$$\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{R}\approx \frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{3}
 \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{1}$$

just strong enough to compensate $I_{leak}$ and
noise but weak enough to be overpowered with little
penalty. With correct ratioing the $f_{max}$ penalty can be
kept to $<10\%$ while $f_{min}$ is brought from
${\rm MHz}$ to $0$, e. g. $8{\rm GHz}$ dynamic to
$7.0-7.5{\rm GHz}$ pseudo static in $65{\rm nm}$,
at $\sim 10-20\%$ power and area cost.

Unratioed, $g_{mR}\ge g_{m1}$ the master cannot be
written, the divider sticks and/or draws large DC
current.

In the figure only the master is staticized, the
slave, the two inverters on the right, is still
dynamic, {\it half static} TSPC. With a second keeper
on the slave it becomes fully static.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It misidentifies the red inverter as a keeper/staticizer and claims it removes the low-frequency limit. The actual feedforward path bypasses part of the latch to improve speed, but can overwhelm the main path at low clock rates and raises the minimum usable frequency.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in the figure affect the performance?

answer.text:
It is the classical {\it weak keeper\/} ,
{\it staticizer\/} , {\it bleeder\/}
of the {\tt TSPC} $\div 2$.

$$D= \bar Q\;\;{\rm so}\;\;Q_{n+1}= \bar Q_{n}$$

with master made of $TG_{1}+{\rm Inv}_{1}$
and slave $TG_{2}+{\rm Inv}_{2}+{\rm Inv}_{3}$
closed in a ring is normally {\it all dynamic}.

In the ideal $CK/\bar {CK}$ non overlap case
with $C_{gs}$ alone:

* $CK=1\;,\;\bar {CK}=0$ : $Y=X$, $Z=\bar Y$,
$W=$ floating, $V=\bar W$, $X=\bar V$ holds

* $CK=0\;,\;\bar {CK}=1$ : $Y=$ floating, $Z=\bar Y$
holds, $W=Z$, $V=\bar W$, $X=\bar V=Z$ copied

so on every $0\to 1\to 0$ {\it full} period

$$Z_{n+1}= \bar Z_{n}\qquad X_{n+1}= \bar X_{n}$$

$\div 2$ only so long as the charge on the
floating node, $Y$ in $\Phi_{1}=0$ and $W$ in
$\Phi_{1}=1$, does not leak away. In normal
CMOS

$$\tau _{leak}\approx C_{node}V_{DD}/I_{leak}\approx
10^{-13}/10^{-9}\approx 10^{-4} {\rm s}$$

so

$$f_{min}\approx 10^{4}-10^{6}{\rm Hz},\;\;
f_{max}\approx 1/3t_{p}$$

any stop of the clock, any slow clock, any
coupling noise, clock feed through, charge
sharing on $Y,W$ destroys the state. It is
normally called {\it dynamic\/} and {\it
ratioless\/}:

$$P_{dyn}=C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f\;\;,\;\;t_{CQ}=t_{TG}+t_{Inv}$$
minimum.

Putting the red ${\rm Inv}$ in the master, in
sign as a {\it cross coupled latch} with
${\rm Inv}_{1}$

$$Y \xrightarrow{{\rm Inv}_{1}} Z
 \xrightarrow{{\rm red}}X \xrightarrow{TG_{1}}Y$$

in the drawing as a {\it parallel} driver
$$X\;\xrightarrow[{\rm red}]{{\rm Inv}_{1}}\;Z$$
it is the same thing {\it modulo} $TG_{1}$,
makes the master {\it pseudo static}, {\it
ratioed}.

In the transparent phase, $CK=1$, the two
${\rm Inv}$ drive $Z$ in {\it parallel}, {\it
a fortiori} faster. In the hold phase,
$CK=0$, $\bar {CK}=1$,

$$Z =\bar Y\;\;{\rm from\;Inv}_{1}\;\;{\rm with\;\;}
Y=Q_{n}={\rm floating\;capacitor}$$

is now held by

$$Z =\bar X\;\;{\rm from\;red\;\;with\;\;}
X= W = Z\;\;{\rm from\;slave}$$

{\it i. e.} the red ${\rm Inv}$ fights
${\rm Inv}_{1}$ on $Z$, or, if you draw it as
$Z\to X$, it fights the slave on $X$.

So for DC:

* Pro: the loop gain $>1$ holds $Y/Z$
for $f\to 0$. No $f_{min}$. The node is
low impedance, restored to $V_{DD}/V_{SS}$,
noise margin goes from $\approx 0$ dynamic
to $NM_{H,L}\approx V_{DD}/3$, clock feed
through and leakage insensitive, rail to
rail, can be stopped. In modern jargon the
conventional TSPC becomes the E-TSPC,
extended TSPC, and can even be made faster
because the series ${\rm MOS}$ in the
clocked ${\rm Inv}$ can be suppressed.

* Contra: ratioed logic. During the {\it
write} the driver must over power the keeper.

For the master to be writable

$$ \left({W\over L}\right)_{red}<<
   \left({W\over L}\right)_{Inv_{1}},
   \left({W\over L}\right)_{slave}$$

normally $1/3$ to $1/10$ and long $L$,
high $V_{t}$ if possible.  If that ratio is
not respected the latch cannot be flipped,
the divider is stuck, $Q_{n+1}=Q_{n}$, it
does not $\div 2$.

Even correctly ratioed:

* added $C_{g}+C_{d}$ on $X,Y,Z$, about
$20-30\%$ extra fan out, so

$$t_{CQ}^{stat}=t_{CQ}^{dyn}+ \Delta t_{red}
  +t_{fight}\approx 1.1-1.5\,t_{CQ}^{dyn}$$

$$f_{max}^{stat}\approx 0.7-0.9\,f_{max}^{dyn}$$

in $0.18\mu$ e. {\it g.} $5.0{\rm GHz}
\to 3.5-4.5{\rm GHz}$.

* a direct $V_{DD}\to V_{SS}$ short circuit
current during the fight

$$I_{sc}\approx {1\over 2}\mu C_{ox}{W\over L}
 \left(V_{DD}-V_{t}\right)^{2}\;\;{\rm for}\;\;
  t_{sc}\approx t_{r,f}$$

so

$$P =C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f +V_{DD}I_{sc}t_{sc}f$$

$10-30\%$ more power, static power
$\ne 0$ during transition, $PDP$ worse.

* $t_{setup},t_{hold}$ of the equivalent
$D\,{\rm FF}$ are degraded, essentially the
hold time must cover the fight time.

* process, $V_{DD}$, $T$ variation of the
ratio can make it fail at low $V_{DD}$ or
high $T$.

In one sentence: you buy DC, leakage and
noise robustness and rail to rail operation
for area, for a small to large, depending on
sizing, loss in $t_{p}$, $f_{max}$ and
$P_{dyn}+P_{sc}$ and you make the circuit
ratioed. Made weak enough it is a negligible
penalty, made as strong as ${\rm Inv}_{1}$
it kills the divider.

> {\it Remark:} In the literature the weak
> red ${\rm Inv}$ is normally gated with a
> $TG_{2}$ so that it is disconnected during
> the write, {\it e. g.} the conventional
> $TG$ static master-slave $D\,{\rm FF}$,
> to suppress the $I_{sc}$.  Unclocked as
> drawn it is the E-TSPC $\div 2$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It recognizes that the red inverter provides a parallel path that can speed the signal, but mischaracterizes it as a keeper/staticizer and reverses the key low-frequency effect: the unclocked branch raises, rather than removes, the minimum usable clock frequency. Its overall claim that the addition reduces maximum speed also conflicts with the intended feedforward speed benefit.

answers.question:
In the figure, somebody answers:

> The red inverter acts as a keeper, forming a cross-coupled latch with `Inv1`.
> This removes the minimum clock frequency requirement due to leakage.

Do you agree with this answer? What is the actual role of the red inverter?

answer.text:
This is the conventional CMOS ${\rm TG}/{\rm C^{2}MOS}$
{\it pseudo static} $T$ divide by 2 turned into the
conventional dynamic figure and somebody has tried to
``staticize" it. It is wrong in two ways.

Let

* $A$ = to the left of the $CK$ ${\rm TG}$
* $M$ = to the right of the $CK$ ${\rm TG}=$ input of
${\rm Inv}_{1}$
* $B$ = output of ${\rm Inv}_{1}=$ to the left of the
$\bar {CK}$ ${\rm TG}$
* $C$ = to the right of the $\bar {CK}$ ${\rm TG}$
  $=$ input of the slave ${\rm inv}$
* $E$ = output of the slave $=$ $A$ by the
global wiring.

Without colour the circuit is the dynamic
$T$~FF:

$$A\stackrel{CK}{\to}M\stackrel{{\rm Inv}_{1}}{\to}
B\stackrel{\bar {CK}}{\to}C\stackrel{{\rm Inv}}{\to}
\stackrel{{\rm Inv}}{\to}E=A\tag{*}$$

$3$ inversions round the loop. Closed on
$CK=1$ open on $\bar {CK}=0$ and vice versa.
It is an edge triggered $D$ with $D=\bar Q$.
$M$ and $C$ are {\it storage} nodes. On

* $CK=1$, $\bar {CK}=0$ $M=A=E$, $B=\bar A$,
$C$ is floating on $C_{C}$.
* $CK=0$, $\bar {CK}=1$ $M$ is floating on $C_{M}$,
$B={\rm Inv}_{1}(M)$, $C=B$, $E=\bar B=A$.

$C_{M}$ drives ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ and $C_{C}$ drives the
slave. In hold they leak with $I_{\rm off}$ so

$$ \Delta V = I_{\rm leak}T_{H}/C_{M,C} $$

must be $\ll V_{DD}/2$. I.e. $f_{CK}>f_{\min }
\approx I_{\rm leak}/C_{M,C}V_{DD}$, normally
${\rm kHz}$ to ${\rm MHz}$ with modern leakage.
That is the ``minimum frequency'' of a dynamic
divider.

A conventional weak keeper for a ${\rm TG}$
latch is

$${\rm Inv}_{1}:M\to B\,\;\;{\rm Keeper}:\;B\to M$$

with the ${\rm TG}$ {\it in series} with the loop.
With $CK=1$ the loop is transparent and $A$
overwrites it. With $CK=0$ the ${\rm TG}$ is
open and ${\rm Inv}_{1}+{\rm keeper}$ is a
cross coupled bistable holding $M/B$ statically.
It must be ratioed: keeper $W/L \ll {\rm Inv}_{1}$
and $\ll$ driver $E$ so it can be over written.

Normally you need {\it two} keepers: $B\to M$ for
the master and $E\to C$ or $D\to C$ for the slave.
With one keeper only the circuit is half static.
It still has a $f_{\min }$ for the other phase.

As drawn the {\it red} inverter is $A\to B$ in the
drawing, $B\to A$ if you reverse the symbol. In
either case it is {\it not} $B\to M$.

* If $A\to B$ it is a second feed forward
${\rm inv}$ in {\it parallel} with $CK+{\rm Inv}_{1}$.
With $\bar {CK}=1$ you have

$$A\stackrel{\rm red}{\to}B \to C \to\bar C\to E=A$$

$3$ inversions round a {\it combinational} loop:
a gated ring oscillator. With $\bar {CK}=0$ $B=
\bar A$ combinationally. There is no latch at
all.

* If $B\to A$, as normally intended as a keeper,
it goes to $A$, not to $M$.

$$ {\rm loop}: A\stackrel{CK}{\to} M\stackrel{{\rm Inv}_{1}}
{\to} B\stackrel{\rm red}{\to}A \tag{**}$$

i.e. ${\rm Inv}_{1}+{\rm red}$ is a latch {\it only}
with $CK=1$ closed. That is the {\it transparent}
phase, when you do {\it not} need it. With $CK=0$
open $M$ is disconnected. $(**)$ is open.
$M$ is left floating on $C_{M}$ driving ${\rm Inv}_{1}$.
${\rm Red}$ holds $A/B$ not $M/B$. $M$ still leaks and
will flip ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ after $T_{H}=C_{M}\Delta V/
I_{\rm leak}$.

In the other phase $\bar {CK}=1$

$$B\stackrel{\bar {CK}}{\to}E=B\;{\rm via\; slave}\qquad
B\stackrel{\rm red}{\to}A=E=\bar B\;{\rm via\; red}$$

the slave non inverting path $B\to E$ fights the
inverting path $B\stackrel{\rm red}{\to}E$ on the
same node $A=E$.

So at best ${\rm red}$ is a weak bus holder for the
{\it global} $A$ node. It will hold $A/B$ statically
when the slave is opaque, $CK=1$, but it does not
hold $M$ when the master is opaque and it does not
hold $C$ at all. The circuit stays dynamic.
$C$ is always dynamic. $M$ is dynamic for half
the period. The $f_{\min}$ for $T_{H}({\rm low})$
and for $f_{CK}$ is essentially unchanged.

What it does do is put a DC fight on $A=E$.
On $CK=0\to 1$ $E$ must overwrite the keeper to
write new data into the master and on $CK=1\to
0$ ${\rm red}$ must fight $E$ while the slave is
trying to toggle. If ${\rm red}$ is made with a
normal strong $W/L$ the divider will not toggle
at all - it is a ratioed latch stuck in the old
state. If made weak, long $L$ small $W$, the
divider can be made to work but with large crow
bar current during the write, degraded noise
margin, slower $f_{\max }$ and still dynamic
leakage on $M$ and $C$.

> {\it I.e. the conventional description ``red
> with ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ is a cross coupled keeper
> that makes the divider static and removes the
> $f_{\min}$'' is false as drawn. Correctly wired
> it would be $B\to M$, not $B\to A$, and even then
> it would make only the master static. You need a
> second keeper $E\to C$ to make the whole
> divider static. As drawn it is a miswired
> half keeper that leaves the critical storage node
> $M$ and the slave node $C$ floating, does not
> remove the leakage induced $f_{\min}$, makes the
> latch ratioed and can destroy the divide by two
> function if not made weak.} 

In textbooks this is exhibited as the classic
``keeper on the wrong side of the ${\rm TG}$''
mistake. The correct staticizer is to move the
left terminal of the red inverter from $A$ to $M$.
Then with a weak $W/L$ and a second weak
feredback inverter $E\to C$ you get the usual
``weak feedback'' pseudo static TSPC divider
with no $f_{\min }$ at the expense of ratioed
static power during switching.

With the wiring as shown it is at most a
pseudo static bus holder for $A$ that has to be
overpowered on every toggle.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly rejects the keeper interpretation and, in one case, identifies the A-to-B feedforward path and its gated-ring behavior. But the answer is internally inconsistent and concludes that the minimum-frequency requirement is essentially unchanged, missing the key tradeoff: the branch can help at high speed but overpower the intended latch at low clock rates and raise the minimum usable frequency.

answers.question:
In the figure, somebody answers:

> The red inverter acts as a keeper, forming a cross-coupled latch with `Inv1`.
> This removes the minimum clock frequency requirement due to leakage.

Do you agree with this answer? What is the actual role of the red inverter?

answer.text:
No. It is a {\it half} keeper.

$$CK~{\rm TG} + {\rm Inv}_{1} = {\rm master~~latch} \qquad 
\bar {CK}~{\rm TG}+2{\rm Inv} = {\rm slave~~latch}$$

with $Q=D\!=\!\bar Q$ i. e. $T$-FF/$\div 2$.

* With $CK=0$,$\bar {CK}=1$:

$$D_{M}\equiv B\;\;{\rm open}\;\;,
\;\;C\leftrightarrow B\;{\rm by\; Inv_{1}+red}$$
master opaque, stored on $B-C$.
$C$ drives $D$ drives $E$ drives $F$,
slave transparent:
$$F=C,\;\;E=\bar D, \;\;D=C\;{\rm driven}$$
whole ring closed $B-C-D-E-F$ and ${\rm DC}$
static.

* With $CK=1$,$\bar {CK}=0$:

$$D\;{\rm open},\;B\!-\!F\;{\rm closed}$$
master transparent $B=F$, $C=\bar B$,
slave opaque, $D$ high impedance

$$\eqalign{
B &=F \cr
C &=\bar B\cr
D &= {\rm float}\cr
E &=\bar D\cr
F &=\bar E = D\cr}$$

i. e. the master is still held by the
${\rm Inv}_{1}\leftrightarrow {\rm red}$ cross couple,
the slave storage node $D$, the input of the
slave inverter, is {\it dynamic}, on its
diffusion + gate $C_{p}$.

So ``red + ${\rm Inv}_{1}$'' is indeed a
cross coupled latch - normally drawn as a
{\it clocked} feedback inverter - here drawn
as a direct weak feedback inverter, a weak
keeper, trickle inverter, bleeder,
staticizer, level restorer, ``semi-static'',
``pseudo static'' latch.

When the master is opaque, $CK=0$, it is held
statically against leakage, charge sharing,
coupling noise, power supply droop, etc. by
the red inverter.

When the master is transparent, $CK=1$, the
red inverter is overdriven by the $F$ driver
through the $CK$ transmission gate.
I. e. it {\it must} be ratioed weak, long $L$
small $W$, high $R_{out}$, so it can be
overpowered for a correct write. While it is
being overpowered it draws $I_{sc}$ crowbar
current. It is a ratioed pseudo NMOS latch.
If it is made normal strength the divider
jams and will not toggle, $B=\bar F$ cannot be
written.

It does {\it not} make the whole master-slave
FF/divider static. For $CK=1$ the $D$ node is
floating. If you stop the clock with $CK=1$,
$\bar {CK}=0$, for

$$t_{H} > {C_{p}\Delta V\over I_{leak}} \approx
10^{-13}\times 0.5/10^{-9} \sim 10-100\mu {\rm s}$$

$D$ leaks to $V_{DD}$ or $V_{SS}$,
$E,F$ follow, the next $CK=0$ loads the
wrong $F$ and the $\div 2$ loses state.

So conventionally the circuit is still
regarded as {\it dynamic}. There is a maximum
allowable $CK=1$ pulse width, i. e. a minimum
operating frequency if the clock has $50\%$
duty cycle, or more precisely still a
minimum clock frequency for $DC$ high
operation. You can stop the circuit
indefinitely only with $CK=0$.

To make it truly single phase fully static,
$F_{min}=0$ for either phase, you need a
second, normally clocked, weak feedback
inverter round the slave, $F\rightarrow D$
or $E\rightarrow D$.

In text books the circuit as drawn is often
called the Yuan-Svensson True Single Phase
Clock, TSPC, pseudo static or half static
divide by two, master pseudo static, slave
dynamic, $T$-FF. The red inverter is the
master staticizer - it lets you run the
divider down to low frequency {\it and} holds
the master node while the master is opaque
so you do not have to refresh it every cycle -
but at the price of a ratioed contention write
and without staticizing the slave.

> {\it Remark:} With ordinary sizing the divider will
divide correctly as a dynamic divider even
without the red inverter. The red inverter is
not logically necessary, it is there for
robustness at low speed, noise, soft error
and start up.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer incorrectly treats the red inverter as a cross-coupled keeper/staticizer. It misses the actual feedforward path and its low-frequency failure mode, and reaches the opposite conclusion about low-frequency operation.

answers.question:
In the figure, somebody answers:

> The red inverter acts as a keeper, forming a cross-coupled latch with `Inv1`.
> This removes the minimum clock frequency requirement due to leakage.

Do you agree with this answer? What is the actual role of the red inverter?

answer.text:
It is ``keeper'' in name only. Let

* $N_{1}$ be the node to the {\it right} of the $CK$
  transfer gate $=$ input of $Inv_{1}$
* $N_{2}$ be the node to the {\it left} of the $\bar {CK}$
  transfer gate $=$ output of $Inv_{1}$
* $N_{3}$ be the node to the {\it right} of the $\bar {CK}$
  transfer gate $=$ input of the $slave$ $2\;Inv.$
* $N_{0}$ be the common node $=$ left of $CK$ $=$ output
  of the $slave$ $=Q$.

Without the red $Inv.$

* $CK=1$ , $\bar {CK}=0$: $N_{1}=N_{0}$, $N_{2}=\bar N_{1}$,
  transparent, $N_{3}$ $Z$
* $CK=0$, $\bar {CK}=1$: $N_{1}$ $Z$, $N_{2}= \bar N_{1}$
  memorised on $C_{N1}$, $C_{N2}$, $N_{3}=N_{2}$ transparent.
* $CK=1$, $\bar {CK}=0$: $N_{3}$ $Z$ memorised on $C_{N3}$.

So the toggle ${\rm DFF}$ with ${\rm D}=\bar Q$ is two
{\it dynamic} latches. The state is the charge on the
high $Z$ nodes $N_{1}$ and $N_{3}$ and to a lesser
extent $N_{2}$ which follows $N_{1}$. ${\rm d}V/{\rm d}t=
I_{leak}/C\sim $msec. The clock must be re-circulated
before that. There is a minimum $f_{ck}$.

A conventional weak keeper for the ${\rm M}$ latch is

$$N_{2} \rightarrow Inv_{w} \rightarrow N_{1}\tag{*}$$

with $Inv_{w}$ weak, so that when $CK=0$ the loop
$Inv_{1}+Inv_{w}$ is {\it closed} and isolated from $N_{0}$.
$N_{1}$ is always driven, either by $N_{0}$ through $CK=1$ or
by $Inv_{w}$ through $(*)$ for $CK=0$. $Inv_{1}$ can
overpower $Inv_{w}$ when $CK=1$ to write. Ditto for
the ${\rm S}$ latch $N_{5}\rightarrow Inv_{w}\rightarrow N_{3}$.

What is drawn in red is {\it not} $(*)$. Up to orientation,

$$\;N_{2}\; {\rm or}\; N_{0} \rightarrow Inv_{red} \rightarrow
  N_{0}\; {\rm or}\; N_{2}\; \tag{**}$$

in the drawing the left plate of the red $Inv.$ is
$N_{0}$ , the right plate, bubble, is $N_{2}$. So at
best

$$N_{0}\rightarrow Inv_{red}\rightarrow N_{2} $$

or vice versa $N_{2}\rightarrow Inv_{red}\rightarrow N_{0}$.
In either case the left plate is {\it not} $N_{1}$.

In particular the often quoted $N_{2}\rightarrow Inv_{red}
\rightarrow N_{1}$ ``cross coupled latch with $Inv_{1}$''
does not exist. $N_{1}$ and $N_{0}$ are the same node
only when $CK=1$. When the latch is supposed to hold,
$CK=0$, $N_{1}$ is open. The red loop is open. The
charge on $N_{1}$ is still left on a $Z$ node and will
leak through the $n$ - or $p$ - diffusion of the $TG$
and of $Inv_{1}$ with time constant $C_{N1}/I_{off}$.

$$N_{1}\;\;{\rm is\;still\;dynamic}$$

The only thing the red $Inv.$ does keep is $N_{2}$.
For $CK=0$, $N_{1}$ $Z$, $Inv_{1}$ is driving $N_{2}$
to $\bar N_{1}$ on the basis of a leaking input, $N_{2}$
would follow the leak. The red $Inv.$ now drives $N_{2}$
from $N_{0}=Q$ which is low impedance. So $N_{2}$ is
never $Z$, it is always driven either by $Inv_{1}$ or
by $Inv_{red}$. But it is driven to the {\it wrong}
value in hold.

Normal hold: with $CK=0$, $\bar {CK}=1$, $Q=N_{2,old}$,
$N_{3}=N_{2,old}$.

With $N_{0}\rightarrow N_{2}$ red: $N_{2,red}= \bar N_{0}
= \bar Q = \bar N_{2,old}$. The red $Inv.$ fights the
value the ${\rm M}$ latch is supposed to hold. Normal
operation is only possible as {\rm ratioed} logic: the
red $Inv.$ must be made weak $W/L \ll W/L_{Inv1}$,
$W/L_{Q\;driver}$ so that during the phase in which it
fights it is overpowered. We get

* $CK=1$: $CK$ closed, $Inv_{1}$ and $Inv_{red}$ both drive
$N_{2}$ to $\bar N_{0}$ - no fight.
* $CK=0$: $CK$ open, $Inv_{1}$ drives $N_{2}$ to the
old $\bar N_{1,old}$, $Inv_{red}$ drives $N_{2}$ to
$\bar N_{0}= \bar N_{2,old}$, opposite, $Inv_{1}$ must win
if the leak has not yet moved $N_{1}$.

The complementary case $N_{2}\rightarrow N_{0}$ is the
dual: the loop $N_{1}-CK-Inv_{1}-Inv_{red}$ is a latch
{\it closed when $CK=1$}, i.e. precisely when the ${\rm M}$
latch should be transparent. It holds when it should sample
and is open when it should hold. Again it only works
ratioed.

In either description it is not a conventional keeper/
cross coupled bistable isolated when $CK=0$. It is a
weak feed through, half keeper, pseudo-NMOS, contention
latch. It gives a DC path $V_{DD}-V_{SS}$ through
$Inv_{1}/Inv_{red}/Q$ driver for half the cycle and
static power.

Even if you accept to call the $N_{0}-N_{2}$ loop a
weak pseudo latch that keeps $N_{2}$ defined, the
circuit {\it as a frequency divider} is still dynamic:

* $N_{1}$ still $Z$ for $CK=0$
* $N_{3}$ still $Z$ for $\bar {CK}=0\;(CK=1)$

One weak inverter on the master can at most pseudo-
staticize the master intermediate node $N_{2}$, it cannot
staticize the true storage node $N_{1}$ nor the slave
storage node $N_{3}$. The divider will still lose state
if $\bar {CK}=0$ is kept too long, $C_{N3}$ leaking, and
if $CK=0$ is kept too long $C_{N1}$ leaking will flip
$Inv_{1}$ and, even though $N_{2}$ is weakly held, the
contention current will eventually be won by the leak if
you wait long enough. So a minimum $f_{ck}$ remains,
at best moved by the ratio.

A truly static toggle ${\rm DFF}$ needs {\it two}
keepers, $(*)$ for the master and the equivalent for the
slave, both weak and isolated behind the $TG$, e.g. clocked
feedback inverter. Moving the left plate of the red
$Inv.$ from $N_{0}$ to $N_{1}$ and adding the missing
slave keeper, properly ratioed $\sim 1/5-1/10$, is the
text book static TSPC/C$^{2}$MOS latch.

Without that the 3 $Inv.$ + $2\;TG$ + global $\bar Q\rightarrow D$
connection is just the well known dynamic divide by $2$.
Adding the red $Inv.$ as drawn does not make it static,
it makes it a ratioed pseudo static divider with contention,
degraded swing, noise margin and power, and is normally
quoted as the classic {\it wrong place for the keeper}
mistake. Remove it and you recover the correct low power
dynamic divider operation.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly rejects a conventional cross-coupled keeper and identifies the N0-to-N2 path, but mischaracterizes it as a weak pseudo-keeper and attributes the frequency limit mainly to leakage. It misses the key role as an unclocked feedforward bypass, which can speed high-rate operation yet dominate the latch path at low rates and raise the minimum usable clock frequency.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit shown in the figure for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
With the bias choke ${\rm C}_{1}\to {\rm s.c.}$
for ${\rm a.c.}$ put

$${G_{F}=1/R_{F}\;\;G_{s}=1/R_{s}\;\;G_{o}=1/r_{o}\;\;
r_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\;\;g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}\;\;
i_{n}^{2}=4kT\gamma g_{m}\;{\rm A^{2}/Hz}\;\;0.7<\gamma <2$$

$$\eqalign{
i_{nF}^{2}&=4kTG_{F}\cr 
v_{ns}^{2}&=4kTR_{s}\cr}$$

$${\rm at\;\;input:}\;(V_{i}-V_{s})G_{s}+(V_{i}-V_{o})G_{F}+i_{nF}=0 \tag{1}$$
$${\rm at\;\;output:}\;(V_{o}-V_{i})G_{F}-i_{nF}+V_{o}G_{o}+g_{m}V_{i}
+i_{n}=0 \tag{2}$$

$$\left| {{V_{o}}\over {V_{i}}}\right| _{0}=
{{g_{m}-G_{F}}\over {G_{F}+G_{o}}}\approx g_{m}r_{o}\parallel R_{F}=|A_{v}|$$

$$\left| {{V_{o}}\over {V_{s}}}\right| =
{{G_{s}(g_{m}-G_{F})}\over {G_{s}(G_{F}+G_{o})+G_{F}(G_{o}+g_{m})}}
\equiv A_{vs} \tag{3}$$

$${{I_{x}}\over {V_{x}}}= {{1+ g_{m}r_{o}}\over {R_{F}+r_{o}}}\equiv
{{1}\over {R_{in}}}\tag{4}$$

$$R_{in}={{R_{F}+r_{o}}\over {1+g_{m}r_{o}}}
      ={{G_{o}+G_{F}}\over {G_{F}(G_{o}+g_{m})}}\approx
      {1\over {g_{m}}}+{{R_{F}}\over {g_{m}r_{o}}}\tag{5}$$

for $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$.

With $V_{s}=0$ from (1)(2)

$$V_{o}={{i_{nF}(g_{m}+G_{s})-i_{n}(G_{s}+G_{F})}\over {D}}\tag{6}$$

$$D=G_{s}(G_{F}+G_{o})+G_{F}(G_{o}+g_{m})$$

so that, $i_{nF}$ and $i_{n}$ uncorrelated

$$\eqalign{
H_{F}&={{V_{o}}\over {i_{nF}}}={{g_{m}+G_{s}}\over {D}}\cr
H_{m}&={{V_{o}}\over {i_{n}}}=-{{G_{s}+G_{F}}\over {D}}\cr}
\tag{7}$$

and, from (3),

$$S_{o,s}=A_{vs}^{2}4kTR_{s}\tag{8}$$
$$S_{o,F}=H_{F}^{2}4kTG_{F}\tag{9}$$
$$S_{o,m}=H_{m}^{2}4kT\gamma g_{m}\tag{10}$$

$${\cal F}={{S_{o,s}+S_{o,F}+S_{o,m}}\over {S_{o,s}}}
        =1+{{S_{o,F}}\over {S_{o,s}}}+{{S_{o,m}}\over {S_{o,s}}}\tag{11}$$

As $D$ cancels

$${\cal F}=1+{{G_{F}(g_{m}+G_{s})^{2}}\over
                {G_{s}(g_{m}-G_{F})^{2}}}
           +\gamma {{g_{m}(G_{s}+G_{F})^{2}}\over
                {G_{s}(g_{m}-G_{F})^{2}}}\tag{12}$$

$$\approx 1+{{G_{F}}\over {G_{s}}}{{  
            \left(1+G_{s}/g_{m}\right)^{2}}\over
            {\left(1-G_{F}/g_{m}\right)^{2}}}
           +\gamma {{g_{m}}\over {G_{s}}}
             {{ \left(1+G_{F}/G_{s}\right)^{2}}\over
              {g_{m}^{2}\left(1-G_{F}/g_{m}\right)^{2}}}(G_{s}+G_{F})^{2}/g_{m} $$

For the usual $g_{m}\gg G_{F}$

$${\cal F}\approx 1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}
          \left(1+{{G_{s}}\over {g_{m}}}\right)^{2}
          +\gamma {{(1+R_{s}/R_{F})^{2}}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}\tag{13}$$

and, for $r_{o}\to \infty $, $R_{in}=1/g_{m}$,

$${\cal F}\approx 1+4{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}+ 
      \gamma\left(1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}\right)^{2}
       \;\;{\rm for}\;\;g_{m}=G_{s}\tag{14}$$

$${\cal F}\approx 1+\gamma \;\;{\rm for}\;\;R_{F}\gg R_{s}\tag{15}$$

$g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$,
$\gamma g_{m}=\gamma _{n}g_{m1}+\gamma _{p}g_{m2}$ for
different $\gamma $.

Eq.14 makes the trade off evident:

* $4kTR_{F}$ wants $R_{F}$ as large as possible,
$ \propto R_{s}/R_{F}$
* $4kT\gamma g_{m}$ wants $g_{m}$ as large as possible,
$\propto 1/g_{m}R_{s}$.

$$S_{o,F}/S_{o,s}\propto 1/R_{F}\;\;,\;\;S_{o,m}/S_{o,s}\propto 1/g_{m}$$

With $R_{in}$ fixed the two are not independent.
From (5)

$$R_{s}=R_{in}={{R_{F}+r_{o}}\over {1+g_{m}r_{o}}}\tag{16}$$

$$R_{F}=R_{s}(1+g_{m}r_{o})-r_{o}=r_{o}(g_{m}R_{s}-1)+R_{s}
      \approx g_{m}r_{o}R_{s}\;\;g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1 \tag{17}$$

$$g_{m}= {{R_{F}+r_{o}-R_{s}}\over {R_{s}r_{o}}}
        =R_{s}^{-1}+{{R_{F}-R_{s}}\over {r_{o}R_{s}}} \tag{18}$$

I. e. for a given $r_{o}$ to keep $R_{in}=R_{s}=50\;\Omega $,
$R_{F}$ and $g_{m}$ must be increased together.
Put (17) in (13):

$${\cal F}-1 \propto {1\over {g_{m}r_{o}}}+{1\over {g_{m}}}$$

so ${\cal F}$ is monotonically decreasing with $g_{m}$ and
with $R_{F}$. There is no finite optimum: in the limit

$$R_{F}\to \infty \;\;,\;\;g_{m}\to \infty \;\;,\;\;
{\cal F}\to 1\tag{19}$$

In practice the limit is power, area, bandwidth and
stability:

* Choose the smallest $L$ that still gives acceptable
$\gamma \approx 2/3-1.0$ and $1/f$ and acceptable $r_{o}$.
$s.c.$ $\gamma \approx 1.5-2$ has to be traded for
$f_{T}$. Often $L\approx 1.2-1.5\,L_{min}$ is used.

* For a given bias current $I_{D}$, $g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$,
$g_{mi}\propto \sqrt{\mu C_{ox}(W/L)I_{D}}$.
$W$ is increased, multi finger to keep $R_{g}$ small,
until the $C_{gs}+C_{gd}+C_{db}$ pole

$$\omega _{p}\approx {1\over {(R_{F}\parallel r_{o}\parallel R_{L})C_{L}}}$$

and the input pole $\omega _{in}\approx 1/R_{s}C_{in}$
still satisfies the band and
$$|A_{v}|=g_{m}r_{o}\parallel R_{F}< {\rm stability\;limit}.$$
$g_{m}/I_{D}$ is maximum in weak-moderate inversion,
so low $V_{ov}\approx 100-200\,{\rm mV}$ is normal.

* With that $g_{m,{\max }}$ allowed by the power budget,
put

$$R_{F,opt}=R_{in}(1+g_{m,{\max }}r_{o})-r_{o}\tag{20}$$

Numerically for $r_{o}=0.5-1\,{\rm k\Omega }$

$$\eqalign{
R_{in}=50\;\Omega &: g_{m}\approx 20\,{\rm mS}+{{R_{F}-50}\over {r_{o}50}}\cr
R_{F}=0.2-0.5\,{\rm k\Omega }&: g_{m}\approx 25-40\,{\rm mS}\cr
R_{F}=1-2\,{\rm k\Omega }&: g_{m}\approx 60-100\,{\rm mS}\cr}$$

and

$$|A_{vs}|\approx {{g_{m}r_{o}\parallel R_{F}}\over 2}\tag{21}$$
$${\cal F}\approx 1+\gamma {{1}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}+{\cal O}(R_{s}/R_{F})$$

i. e. with $r_{o}\to \infty $, $R_{in}=1/g_{m}=R_{s}$,
$R_{F}$ can be made arbitrarily large and

$${\cal F}_{min}\approx 1+{{\gamma }\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}\to 1+\gamma
\tag{22}$$

$\approx 2.2\,{\rm dB}$ for long channel $\gamma =2/3$,
$3-4\,{\rm dB}$ for short channel $\gamma \approx 1-1.5$,
limit $0\,{\rm dB}$ for $g_{m}\to \infty $.
Increasing the intrinsic gain $g_{m}r_{o}$ by cascoding,
long $L$, or using a $r_{o}$ enhancing load allows a
larger $R_{F}$ for the same $R_{in}$ and therefore the
same $g_{m}$ to give lower ${\cal F}$.

That is the conventional resistive shunt-feedback inverter
LNA. To break the $R_{in}-{\cal F}$ trade off the usual
cures are, to first order noiseless feedback:

* inductive or capacitive feedback $Z_{F}=1/sC_{F}$ or
$sL_{F}$, transformer feedback,
* $L_{g}$ series peaking at the input to resonate $C_{in}$,
so $R_{in}$ is not $1/g_{m}$,
* Bruccoleri noise cancelling: an auxiliary $g_{m,A}$
senses the noise voltage on $R_{in}$ and adds it out of
phase at the output, cancelling to first order the noise
of $R_{F}$ and of the matching device. With ideal
cancellation ${\cal F}\to 1+{\rm noise\;of\;}g_{m,A}$,
$<2\,{\rm dB}$ is routinely obtained with $R_{in}=50\;\Omega $.

In its simplest form: maximize $g_{m}$, maximize
$R_{F}$ with (16) satisfied, maximize $g_{m}r_{o}$,
use large, fingered devices with low $R_{g}$, large $C_{1}$,
and accept the power-bandwidth penalty. Any further
improvement requires a noiseless feedback element or a
noise cancelling auxiliary amplifier and power-noise
matching $R_{opt}\ne R_{in}$ with tolerable $S_{11}\approx
-10\,{\rm dB}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Uses the finite-output-resistance match relation and explains that increasing gm above 1/Rs requires increasing RF to keep Rin at 50 Ω; along that match, NF falls below 1+gamma. This satisfies the golden solution’s full-credit rule.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit shown in the figure for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
This is the self biased shunt-shunt inverter, Fig 3.14
in Razavi. 

$$\eqalign{
g_{m}&=g_{m1}+g_{m2}\cr
r_{o}&=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\cr
A_{0}&=-g_{m}r_{o}}$$

$$C_{1}\approx {\rm short}$$

$$\eqalign{
G_{m}v_{i}+{{v_{o}-v_{i}}\over {R_{F}}}+{{v_{o}}\over {r_{o}}}=0\cr
{\rm for}\;v_{i}= {\rm input}\;,v_{o}={\rm output}}$$

$$A_{v}\equiv {{v_{o}}\over {v_{i}}}={{1/R_{F}-g_{m}}\over {1/R_{F}+1/r_{o}}}
\approx -g_{m}r_{o}\parallel R_{F}\tag{1}$$

With $R_{s}$ at the input

$$\eqalign{
{{v_{i}-v_{s}}\over {R_{s}}}+{{v_{i}-v_{o}}\over {R_{F}}}&=0\cr
-g_{m}v_{i}+{{v_{o}-v_{i}}\over {R_{F}}}+{{v_{o}}\over {r_{o}}}&=0}$$

$$R_{in}\equiv {{v_{i}}\over {i_{in}}}={{v_{i}}\over {(v_{i}-v_{o})/R_{F}}}
={{R_{F}}\over {1-A_{v}}}= {{r_{o}+R_{F}}\over {1+g_{m}r_{o}}}\tag{2}$$

$$R_{in}\approx {{R_{F}}\over {1+g_{m}r_{o}}}\approx 
{{1}\over {g_{m}}}+{{R_{F}}\over {g_{m}r_{o}}}\qquad g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$$

i. e. $R_{in}$ is no longer $R_{F}$ and no longer
$1/g_{m}$. For $R_{F}\gg r_{o}$ $R_{in}\to 1/g_{m}$, for
$R_{F}\ll r_{o}$ $R_{in}\to R_{F}/g_{m}r_{o}$.
Normally $50\Omega $ is obtained with $g_{m}R_{s}\ne 1$.

Let $\overline{i_{n,R_{F}}^{2}}=4kT/R_{F}$ in parallel
with $R_{F}$ and 
$\overline{i_{n,D}^{2}}=4kT\gamma g_{m1}+4kT\gamma g_{m2}
=4kT\gamma g_{m}$ at the output.

Writing nodal equations with $v_{s}$, $i_{n,R_{F}}$, $i_{n,D}$

$$\left[ \matrix{
1/R_{s}+1/R_{F} &-1/R_{F}\cr
g_{m}-1/R_{F} &1/R_{F}+1/r_{o}}\right]
\left[ \matrix{v_{i}\cr v_{o}}\right] =
\left[ \matrix{v_{s}/R_{s}-i_{n,R_{F}}\cr i_{n,R_{F}}-i_{n,D}}\right] $$

$D=(1/R_{s}+1/R_{F})(1/R_{F}+1/r_{o})+(1/R_{F})(g_{m}-1/R_{F})$

$$\eqalign{
v_{o}\vert_{v_{s}}&=-{{g_{m}-1/R_{F}}\over {R_{s}D}}v_{s}\cr
v_{o}\vert_{R_{F}}&={{g_{m}+1/R_{s}}\over {D}}i_{n,R_{F}}\cr
v_{o}\vert_{D}&=-{{1/R_{s}+1/R_{F}}\over {D}}i_{n,D}}$$

$$\eqalign{
S_{vo,R_{s}}&={{(g_{m}-1/R_{F})^{2}}\over {R_{s}^{2}D^{2}}}4kTR_{s}\cr
S_{vo,R_{F}}&={{(g_{m}+1/R_{s})^{2}}\over {D^{2}}}{{4kT}\over {R_{F}}}\cr
S_{vo,D}&={{(1/R_{s}+1/R_{F})^{2}}\over {D^{2}}}4kT\gamma g_{m}}$$

$$F\equiv {{S_{vo,R_{s}}+S_{vo,R_{F}}+S_{vo,D}}\over {S_{vo,R_{s}}}}$$

$$F=1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}
\left({{g_{m}+1/R_{s}}\over {g_{m}-1/R_{F}}}\right)^{2}
+\gamma g_{m}R_{s}
\left({{1/R_{s}+1/R_{F}}\over {g_{m}-1/R_{F}}}\right)^{2}\tag{3}$$

$D$ and $r_{o}$ drop out. For the usual
$g_{m}\gg 1/R_{F},1/R_{s}$

$$F\approx 1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}+{{\gamma}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}
\left(1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}\right)^{2}
\approx 1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}+{{\gamma}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}\tag{4}$$

and with $\gamma _{1}\ne \gamma_{2}$

$$\gamma g_{m}\to \gamma_{n}g_{m1}+\gamma_{p}g_{m2}\tag{5}$$

$$F\approx 1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}+
{{\gamma_{n}g_{m1}+\gamma_{p}g_{m2}}\over {g_{m}^{2}R_{s}}}$$

$R_{s}=R_{in}=50\Omega $ when matched.
The familiar $F\approx 1+\gamma$ for
$1/g_{m}=R_{s}$, $R_{F}\to \infty$ is recovered.

With the match constraint (2)

$$R_{F}=R_{in}(1+g_{m}r_{o})-r_{o}=R_{s}+r_{o}(g_{m}R_{s}-1)\tag{6}$$

So $R_{F}$ and $g_{m}$ are not independent once
$R_{in}=50\Omega$ is imposed. Putting (6) in (4)

$$F\approx 1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{s}+r_{o}(g_{m}R_{s}-1)}}
+{{\gamma}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}} \tag{7}$$

For $A_{0}=g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$

$$R_{F}\approx R_{s}g_{m}r_{o}=R_{s}A_{0}$$

$$F\approx 1+{{1}\over {g_{m}r_{o}}}+{{\gamma}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}
=1+{{1}\over {g_{m}}}\left({{1}\over {r_{o}}}+{{\gamma}\over {R_{s}}}\right)\tag{8}$$

I. e. for fixed $R_{in}$

* {\it increasing $R_{F}$ without increasing loop gain
destroys the match.}
* decreasing $F$ needs {\it increasing loop gain $A_{0}=g_{m}r_{o}$},
i. e. increasing $R_{F}$ {\it and} $g_{m}r_{o}$
together according to (6).

In (8) $F\to 1$ monotonically for $g_{m}\to \infty$ and
for $r_{o}\to \infty$. In practice:

* Maximise $g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ for the power you can
afford.  $g_{m}\propto \sqrt{W I_{D}}$ in strong inversion,
$\propto I_{D}$ in weak inversion, so weak-moderate inversion
is $g_{m}/I_{D}$ optimum.  Increase $W_{1},W_{2}$ and $I_{D}$
until the input pole

$$\omega_{in}\approx {1\over {R_{s}C_{in}}},\qquad
C_{in}\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+(1+|A_{v}|)C_{gd}$$

falls on the band edge, Miller effect included.
Multi finger layout to keep $R_{g}\ll R_{s}$.

* Maximise $r_{o}$ at that current: longer $L$, cascode the
inverter - $r_{o}\to g_{m,cas}r_{o,cas}r_{o}$ - retro-cascode
self biased LNA. This lets you use a much larger $R_{F}$ for
the same $50\Omega $, cf. (6), and kills the $R_{s}/R_{F}$
term. Short channel $A_{0}\approx 8-15$, cascoded $A_{0}\approx 30-50$.

Then set

$$R_{F}=50(1+g_{m}r_{o})-r_{o}$$

for the $g_{m},r_{o}$ you have. E. g. $r_{o}=300\Omega $,
$g_{m}=20\,{\rm mS}$, $A_{0}=6$, $R_{F}\approx 50\Omega $,
$F\approx 1+0.17+0.67\approx 1.84=2.6\,{\rm dB}$ for
$\gamma\approx 1$.  Doubling $g_{m}$ to $40\,{\rm mS}$ with
$r_{o}=250\Omega $, $A_{0}=10$, $R_{F}\approx 300\Omega $,
$F\approx 1+0.17+0.33\approx 1.5=1.8\,{\rm dB}$.

* Optimise the split $g_{m1}$ vs $g_{m2}$,
Eq.5.  For $\gamma_{n}\approx \gamma_{p}$ the split cancels to
first order.  Usually $W_{p}\approx (\mu_{n}/\mu_{p})W_{n}$ for
symmetrical inverter $V_{o,DC}\approx V_{DD}/2$ maximum
swing and $g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$.  If $\gamma_{p}<\gamma_{n}$
weight to the p-device.

With unbounded $g_{m}r_{o}$ the only limit is power and
$C_{in}$ bandwidth and $R_{g}$, induced gate noise. Power
constrained optimum is

$${\rm min}\;F\;{\rm s.t.}\;R_{in}=50,\;P_{DC}=V_{DD}I_{D}=const.,
\;C_{in}<1/R_{s}\omega_{0}$$

swept with $g_{m}/I_{D}$ methodology in simulation.

In a narrow band design $R_{F}$ can be made noiseless by
replacing it by $L_{F}$ or transformer feedback. In wide band
the $R_{s}/R_{F}$ vs $R_{in}$ trade off is fundamentally broken
by {\it noise cancelling}: sense the noise voltage at the
matching node with an auxiliary amplifier $A_{aux}=-1-R_{F}/R_{s}$
and add it in phase to the signal so that $i_{n,R_{F}}$ and
$i_{n,D}$ cancel, Bruccoleri et al. JSSC 2005. Then $R_{in}$
can be $50\Omega $ with $F\approx 1+\gamma/g_{m}R_{s}$ with no
$R_{s}/R_{F}$ penalty, $<2\,{\rm dB}$ in deep sub micron CMOS.

> {\it In short: keep $R_{in}=50$ by keeping
> $R_{F}=R_{in}(1+g_{m}r_{o})-r_{o}$. The only way to lower
> $F\approx 1+R_{s}/R_{F}+\gamma/g_{m}R_{s}$ without
> changing $R_{in}$ is to raise the open loop gain.
> Raise $g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ and $r_{o}$ - larger $W$, larger
> $I_{D}$, longer $L$ or cascodes - and raise $R_{F}$
> proportionally. In the limit $F=1+(1/r_{o}+\gamma/R_{s})/g_{m}$.
> Practically 20-40 mS total $g_{m}$ with $A_{0}>10$ gives
> $R_{F}=200-500\Omega $ and $NF=2-3\,{\rm dB}$ wideband,
> $<2\,{\rm dB}$ with cascoding or noise cancellation. The
> optimum power constrained $W$ is the largest $W$ that still meets
> the $1/R_{s}C_{in}$ bandwidth.}

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It uses the finite-r_o match relation and adjusts R_F as g_m rises, showing how g_m can exceed 1/R_s and reduce NF below 1+\gamma. Minor asymptotic and numerical imprecision does not change the core recommendation.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit shown in the figure for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
For a first order it is the :

$${\cal T}_{v}={\cal T}_{i}={\cal R}_{m}
\sim  -R_{F}$$ inverting shunt-shunt amplifier.

$$R_{in}= {V_{t}\over I_{t}}\approx 
{R_{F}+r_{o}\over 1+g_{m}r_{o}}\approx {R_{F}\over 1+g_{m}r_{o}\parallel R_{F}}
\approx {1\over g_{m}}\;\;,\;g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}\;\;,\;\;
r_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\tag{1}$$

in the normal high gain limit $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$ and
$r_{o}\gg R_{F}$ and

$$A_{v0}=-g_{m}r_{o}\parallel R_{F}\approx -g_{m}R_{F}\tag{2}$$

$$R_{in}\approx {R_{F}\over 1-A_{v0}}\tag{3}$$

$A_{v}$ is the open loop voltage gain of the
inverter.

> {\it I.E. $R_{in}$ is $R_{F}$ divided by the amount of
> feed back. For $r_{o}\rightarrow \infty$ $R_{in}\rightarrow
> 1/g_{m}$ independent of $R_{F}$ to first order.}

With (1) the matching condition ``50 Ohm'' {\it fixes}
$g_{m}$ and $R_{F}$ to one relation, for $r_{o}\rightarrow
\infty$ it fixes $g_{m}$ itself:

$$R_{in}=R_{s}=50\;\;\to\;\; g_{m}\approx 1/R_{s}=20{\rm mS}
\tag{4a}$$

$$R_{F}=R_{s}\left( 1+g_{m}r_{o}\right)-r_{o}\approx g_{m}r_{o}R_{s}
\;\;,\;\;r_{o}<\infty \tag{4b}$$

Small signal nodal with $G_{s}=1/R_{s}\;,\;G_{F}=1/R_{F}\;,\;
G_{o}=1/r_{o}$ :

$$\eqalign{
\left(G_{s}+G_{F}\right)V_{in}-G_{F}V_{out}&=G_{s}V_{s}\cr
\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)V_{in}+\left(G_{o}+G_{F}\right)V_{out}&=0}$$

$${\cal D}=G_{s}\left(G_{o}+G_{F}\right)+G_{F}\left(G_{o}+g_{m}\right)$$

$$A_{v}={V_{out}\over V_{s}}=-G_{s}\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)/{\cal D}
\tag{5}$$

Put noise current sources in parallel with $R_{F}$ and in
parallel with $r_{o}$

$$\eqalign{
\overline{I_{nF}^{2}}&=4kTG_{F}\cr
\overline{I_{nD}^{2}}&=4kT\gamma g_{m}\cr
&\gamma \approx {2\over 3}-2-3\;{\rm in\;short\;ch.}\cr
\overline{V_{nRs}^{2}}&=4kTR_{s}}$$

$$\eqalign{
\left(G_{s}+G_{F}\right)V_{in}-G_{F}V_{out}&=-I_{nF}\cr
\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)V_{in}+\left(G_{o}+G_{F}\right)V_{out}&=
+I_{nF}} \tag{6a}$$

$$\eqalign{
\left(G_{s}+G_{F}\right)V_{in}-G_{F}V_{out}&=0\cr
\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)V_{in}+\left(G_{o}+G_{F}\right)V_{out}&=
-I_{nD}} \tag{6b}$$

$$\eqalign{
{|V_{out}|^{2}_{F}&=|I_{nF}|^{2}\left(G_{s}+g_{m}\right)^{2}/{\cal D}^{2}\cr
|V_{out}|^{2}_{D}&=|I_{nD}|^{2}\left(G_{s}+G_{F}\right)^{2}/{\cal D}^{2}\cr
|V_{out}|^{2}_{Rs}&=|V_{nRs}|^{2}G_{s}^{2}\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)^{2}
/{\cal D}^{2}}$$

i. e. with $F$ the conventional $SNR_{in}/SNR_{out}$

$$F=1+{ |V_{out}|^{2}_{F}+|V_{out}|^{2}_{D}\over
|V_{out}|^{2}_{Rs}} \tag{7}$$

$$F=1+{G_{F}\left(G_{s}+g_{m}\right)^{2}\over
G_{s}\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)^{2}}+
\gamma g_{m}{\left(G_{s}+G_{F}\right)^{2}\over
G_{s}\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)^{2}} \tag{8}$$

For $g_{m}\gg G_{F}$

$$F\approx 1+{G_{F}\over G_{s}}\left(1+{G_{s}\over g_{m}}\right)^{2}
+\gamma {1\over g_{m}G_{s}^{-1}}\left(1+{G_{F}\over G_{s}}\right)^{2}
\tag{8a}$$

$$F\approx 1+{R_{s}\over R_{F}}\left(1+{1\over g_{m}R_{s}}\right)^{2}+
{\gamma\over g_{m}R_{s}}\left(1+{R_{s}\over R_{F}}\right)^{2}
\approx 1+{\gamma\over g_{m}R_{s}}+{R_{s}\over R_{F}}\tag{8b}$$

up to factors $2-4$ depending on the exact definition of
matching. In the literature you will find often quoted in the
very high gain limit $g_{m}R_{s}\gg 1$

$$F\approx 1+{4R_{s}\over R_{F}}+{\gamma\over g_{m}R_{s}}\tag{9}$$

and, with the matching constraint enforced, e. g. $G_{o}\to 0$,
$R_{in}=1/g_{m}=R_{s}$:

$$F_{|matched, r_{o}\to \infty}=
1+{G_{F}\over G_{s}}\left(1+1\right)^{2}+
\gamma \left(1+{G_{F}\over G_{s}}\right)^{2}
\approx 1+\gamma +4{R_{s}\over R_{F}}\tag{10}$$

* the $R_{s}/R_{F}$ term is the $4kTR_{F}$ noise divided
by the loop gain. It is made small by making $R_{F}$ large.

* the $\gamma /g_{m}R_{s}$ term is the channel noise of the
inverter referred to the source. For the usual inverter
$\gamma g_{m}= \gamma_{n}g_{m1}+\gamma_{p}g_{m2}$.
It is made small by making $g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ large.

Under the constraint (4) $R_{F}$ and $g_{m}$ are not
independent. Imposing $R_{in}=R_{s}$ :

$${\cal D}_{|match}=2G_{s}\left(G_{o}+G_{F}\right)=
2G_{F}\left(G_{o}+g_{m}\right) \tag{11}$$

$$G_{F}=G_{s}{G_{o}\over G_{o}+g_{m}-G_{s}}=
{R_{s}^{-1}r_{o}^{-1}\over r_{o}^{-1}+g_{m}-R_{s}^{-1}}\tag{12}$$

Put it in (8):

$$F_{|match}=1+{x(1+y)^{2}+\gamma y(1+x)^{2}\over (y-x)^{2}}\tag{13}$$

$$x={G_{F}\over G_{s}}={R_{s}\over R_{F}}\;\;,\;\;
y={g_{m}\over G_{s}}=g_{m}R_{s}\;\;,\;\;z={G_{o}\over G_{s}}=
{R_{s}\over r_{o}}$$

with $z+x=x(z+y)$ from the match. For $z\to 0$,
$y\to 1$. I.E. to first order fixing the match
fixes $g_{m}$. Then (13) $\to 1+\gamma$ for
$x\to 0$, $R_{F}\to \infty$.

For $z\ne 0$ you can let $x\to 0$ and

$$y\approx 1+z/x\gg 1\tag{14}$$

$$F_{|match}\approx 1+ x +{\gamma\over y}\to 1\tag{15}$$

I.E. in principle $F\to 1$, $NF\to 0\,{\rm dB}$ for
$y=g_{m}R_{s}\to \infty$, $R_{F}\to \infty$ with (4b)
satisfied.

Physically: increase the open loop gain $|A_{v0}|=
g_{m}r_{o}\parallel R_{F}$ . Then for the same
$R_{in}=R_{F}/(1+|A_{v0}|)=R_{s}$ you can afford a
larger $R_{F}$ - less $R_{F}$ noise - and a larger
$g_{m}$ - less $g_{m}$ noise referred to input.

So the recipe for the topology as drawn - a self
biased shunt-shunt current reuse inverter - is:

* current reuse is already optimum: $g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$
for the same $I_{D}$. So for a given power you get
$\times 2$ $g_{m}$. Size $M_{1},M_{2}$ so that
$g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$. I. e. $W_{p}\approx 2-3\,W_{n}$
for equal $g_{m}$.

* make $g_{m}R_{s}$ as large as power allows and make
$R_{F}$ as large as (4b) allows. In practice for
$r_{o}=\infty$, $R_{F}$ is free to first order and
$$NF_{min}\approx 10\log\left[1+{\gamma\over g_{m}R_{s}}\right]
\approx 10\log\,(1+\gamma)\approx 2-3.5\,{\rm dB}
\tag{16}$$
for $g_{m}R_{s}=1$, $\gamma =0.7-1.5$.

With finite $r_{o}$

$$R_{F}=R_{s}+r_{o}\left(g_{m}R_{s}-1\right) \tag{17}$$

so every increase of $g_{m}$ must be accompanied by an
increase of $R_{F}$ to keep $R_{in}=50\,{\rm \Omega}$.

Typical $0.18\mu$, $1.8\,{\rm V}$, $2-5\,{\rm mA}$:
$g_{m}\approx 20-40\,{\rm mS}$, $r_{o}\approx 0.5-2\,{\rm k\Omega}$,
$|A_{v0}|\approx 10-20$, $R_{F}\approx 200-800\,{\rm \Omega}$,
$|A_{v}|\approx R_{F}/R_{s}\approx 4-16$, $NF\approx 2.5-4\,{\rm dB}$.
Doubling $g_{m}$ to $40\,{\rm mS}$ and putting
$R_{F}\approx 500-1k$ brings (8) down by $\approx 1\,{\rm dB}$
at the price of $\approx \times 2$ power and
$\propto W_{g}C_{gs}$ input capacitance.

The limits are:

* power $P=V_{DD}I_{D}$, $g_{m}\propto I_{D}/V_{ov}$,
$g_{m}/I_{D}$ max. $\approx 15-20\,{\rm S/A}$ in
moderate inversion.

* $r_{o}\propto 1/\lambda I_{D}\propto L/I_{D}$, cascode
to boost $r_{o}$ and allow larger $R_{F}$ for the same
$g_{m}$ without extra power.

* bandwidth / stability. Input pole
$\omega_{in}\approx \left(1+g_{m}r_{o}\right)/R_{F}C_{in}$,
$C_{in}=C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+C_{gd}(1+g_{m}R_{F})+C_{pad}$,
output pole $\omega_{out}\approx 1/r_{o}C_{out}$.
Large $R_{F},g_{m},W_{g}$ quickly make the two pole
system unstable. Add $C_{F}$ compensation or series
peaking $L_{g}$.

* headroom: the self biased inverter $V_{in,DC}=V_{out,DC}$
$\approx V_{DD}/2$ for $ \beta_{n}\approx \beta_{p}$,
set by $R_{F}$. Large $R_{F}$ makes bias very
sensitive.

If $2-3\,{\rm dB}$ is not enough, the shunt $R_{F}$
topology cannot be noise and power matched simultaneously
with a noiseless match. You have to resort to
transformer, inductive degeneration, capacitive
noiseless feedback or, most common today, noise
cancelling: sense the $R_{F}$ and $M_{1,2}$ noise at
the input node with an auxiliary $g_{mA}$ stage and
subtract it at the output. In ideal cancellation the
$R_{s}/R_{F}$ and a large part of $\gamma/g_{m}R_{s}$
terms are cancelled, $R_{in}$ remaining $\approx 1/g_{m}$
while $NF\to 1+\gamma_{A}/g_{mA}R_{s}$, $<2\,{\rm dB}$
is routinely achieved.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer uses the finite-output-resistance input-match relation, shows that gm can exceed 1/Rs when RF is increased to preserve Rin = 50 Ω, and explains that this can reduce NF below 1 + γ. This matches the golden solution’s full-credit rule.

answers.question: Compute the input impedance of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
With the conventional notations put
$r_{o1}=g_{ds1}^{-1},r_{o2}=g_{ds2}^{-1},r_{o3}=g_{ds3}^{-1}$
$R_{SS}=r_{s{\rm s}}$, $R_{D1}^{\prime }=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}$,
$R_{D2}^{\prime }=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o3}$ and for the
sake of writing $g_{m2}=g_{m3}=g_{m}^{{\prime }}$,
$g_{m}^{{\prime }}=g_{m}+g_{mb}$ if the bulk effect is
kept, the feedback is voltage shunt.

Put $V_{DD}=0$ for the signal.
For $r_{ss}\to \infty $ and with $R_{F}$ removed

$${\rm M}_{1}:\qquad i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{ds1}v_{X}
\tag{1}$$
$$v_{X}=-i_{d1}R_{D1}=-g_{m1}v_{P}R_{D1}^{\prime }
\qquad R_{D1}^{\prime }={1\over {1\over R_{D1}}+g_{ds1}}\tag{2}$$

${\rm M}_{2}-{\rm M}_{3}$ is a $p$ diff. pair, ${\rm S}$ the
common source.  For the $p$ device

$$i_{d}=g_{m}v_{sg}+g_{ds}v_{sd}\;\;,
\qquad v_{sg}=v_{S}-v_{G}\tag{3}$$

$$\eqalign{
i_{d2}&=g_{m2}(v_{S}-v_{X})+g_{ds2}v_{S}\cr
i_{d3}&=g_{m3}v_{S}+g_{ds3}(v_{S}-v_{o})\tag{4}}$$

$${v_{S}\over R_{SS}}+i_{d2}+i_{d3}=0\tag{5}$$

so that

$$\left[{1\over R_{SS}}+g_{m2}+g_{m3}+g_{ds2}+g_{ds3}\right]v_{S}
-g_{m2}v_{X}-g_{ds3}v_{o}=0 \tag{6}$$

$$v_{S}={{g_{m2}v_{X}+g_{ds3}v_{o}}\over {G_{S}}}\tag{7}$$

$$G_{S}={1\over R_{SS}}+g_{m2}+g_{m3}+g_{ds2}+g_{ds3}
\qquad A={g_{m3}+g_{ds3}\over G_{S}}\tag{8}$$

At the output

$$i_{d3}={v_{o}\over R_{D2}}+{v_{o}-v_{P}\over R_{F}}\tag{9}$$

i. e.

$$(g_{m3}+g_{ds3})v_{S}-g_{ds3}v_{o}
-{v_{o}\over R_{D2}}-{v_{o}-v_{P}\over R_{F}}=0\tag{10}$$

With (2)(7)

$$A\left[g_{m2}v_{X}+g_{ds3}v_{o}\right]-g_{ds3}v_{o}
-{v_{o}\over R_{D2}}-{v_{o}-v_{P}\over R_{F}}=0\tag{11}$$

$$v_{o}\left[{1\over R_{D2}}+{1\over R_{F}}+g_{ds3}(1-A)\right]
+A\,g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}^{\prime }v_{P}-{v_{P}\over R_{F}}=0\tag{12}$$

i. e. with the sign $v_{o}=-K\,v_{P}$, $K>0,$

$$K={{A\,g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}^{\prime }-{1/R_{F}}\over
{1\over R_{D2}}+{1\over R_{F}}+g_{ds3}(1-A)}}>0\tag{13}$$

In the usual $g_{ds}R_{D}\ll 1$, $R_{SS}\to \infty $

$$A\approx {g_{m3}\over g_{m2}+g_{m3}}\;,\qquad 
G_{S}\approx g_{m2}+g_{m3}\tag{14}$$

and, with $g_{ds}\to 0$,

$$\;v_{o}\approx -v_{P}\,
{A\,g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}\over {1\over R_{D2}}+{1\over R_{F}}}\; \tag{15}$$

For the matched pair $g_{m2}=g_{m3}=g_{m}$,

$$A={1\over 2}\;,\qquad 
v_{o}\approx -v_{P}\,
{g_{m1}R_{D1}\,g_{m}\over 2\left({1\over R_{D2}}+{1\over R_{F}}\right)}
=-v_{P}g_{m1}R_{D1}{g_{m}\over 2}R_{D2}\!\parallel\!R_{F}\tag{15a}$$

With $R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$

$$A_{v0}={v_{o}\over v_{P}}\approx -{1\over 2}g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}
\qquad {\rm without\; }R_{F}{\rm \;loading}\tag{16}$$

If the $1/R_{F}$ and $R_{D2}\parallel R_{F}$ loading is kept it is
normal to write

$$A_{vL}= -g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\prime }\,{g_{m2}g_{m3}\over g_{m2}+g_{m3}}
\left(R_{D2}^{\prime }\parallel R_{F}\right) \tag{16a}$$

and $g_{m}\to g_{m}+g_{mb}$ if the body effect is included.
For a conventional resistive loaded $n$ pair with a current
mirror load the $1/2$ is absent, $A_{v0}=-g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}R_{D2}$.

$R_{F}$ is the ${\cal R}$ feedback network.  For the shunt
mixing put $I_{in}$ at the $P$ node,

$$I_{in}=v_{P}\left({1\over R_{in}}+sC_{in}\right)
+{v_{P}-v_{o}\over R_{F}}+i_{g1}\tag{17}$$

$i_{g1}\approx 0$, $i_{g1}=sC_{gs1}v_{P}+sC_{gd1}(v_{P}-v_{X})$
if the MOS caps. are kept.  Neglecting $i_{g1}$,

$$I_{in}=v_{P}\left({1\over R_{in}}+sC_{in}+{1\over R_{F}}\right)
-{v_{o}\over R_{F}}\tag{18}$$

With $v_{o}=-K\,v_{P}$

$$I_{in}=v_{P}\left[{1\over R_{in}}+sC_{in}+{1+K\over R_{F}}\right]
\tag{19}$$

so that the impedance seen by the source $I_{in}$

$$Z_{in}(s)={v_{P}\over I_{in}}=
{1\over {1\over R_{in}}+sC_{in}+{1+K(s)\over R_{F}}}\tag{20}$$

in parallel of $R_{in}$, $C_{in}$ and the impedance seen
looking into the gate itself,

$$Z_{P}(s)={R_{F}\over 1+K(s)}\tag{21}$$

i. e. the familiar $R_{F}/(1-A_{v})$ shunt--shunt result.
Explicitly, from (13),

$${1\over Z_{P}}={1\over R_{F}}+
{A\,g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}^{\prime }\over
R_{F}\left[{1\over R_{D2}}+{1\over R_{F}}+g_{ds3}(1-A)\right]}\tag{22}$$

and with (14)(15)

$$Z_{P}\approx {R_{F}\over 1+
\displaystyle {A\,g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}\over {1\over R_{D2}}+{1\over R_{F}}}}
\approx {R_{F}\over 1+|A_{vL}|}\tag{23}$$

For the matched $g_{m}$ pair and $g_{ds}\to 0$, $R_{SS}\to
\infty $,

$$Z_{P}(0)\approx
{R_{F}\over 1+g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}\!\parallel\!R_{F}/2}\tag{24}$$

so that, to first order,

$$Z_{in}(s)\approx
R_{in}\parallel {1\over sC_{in}}\parallel
{R_{F}\over 1+g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}\!\parallel\!R_{F}/2}
\tag{25}$$

At low frequency $s\to 0$ and with the $R_{F}$ loading
normally $R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$,

$$Z_{in}(0)\approx R_{in}\parallel
{R_{F}\over 1+{1\over 2}g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}}\approx
R_{in}\parallel {2R_{F}\over g_{m1}g_{m}R_{D1}R_{D2}}\tag{26}$$

for $g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}\gg 1$.  Without the $1/2$, e. g.
with a current mirror load,

$$R_{P}\approx {R_{F}\over g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}R_{D2}}\tag{27}$$

is often quoted.

In particular the amplifier becomes a transresistance

$${v_{o}\over I_{in}}=-{K\over {1\over R_{in}}+sC_{in}+{1+K\over R_{F}}}
\approx -R_{F}{K\over 1+K}\xrightarrow[K\gg 1]{}-R_{F}\tag{28}$$

and the conventional input pole is at

$$p_{in}\approx {1+K\over R_{F}C_{in}}\approx
{|A_{v0}|\over R_{F}C_{in}}={g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}\over 2R_{F}C_{in}}\tag{29}$$

Any $C_{gs1},C_{gd1},C_{gs2}$ etc. add in parallel and are
Miller multiplied by $1+|A_{v}|$, e. g. $C_{in,{\rm eff}}\approx
C_{in}+C_{gs1}+C_{gd1}(1+g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\prime })+\cdots $.
Putting $R_{D1}\to R_{D1}\!\parallel\!r_{o1}$,
$R_{D2}\to R_{D2}\!\parallel\!r_{o3}$ and
$g_{m}\to g_{m}+g_{mb}$ gives the result with finite
$r_{o}$ and bulk effect.  With finite $R_{SS}$ replace
$A=g_{m3}/(g_{m2}+g_{m3})$ by (8).  In Blackman form
$Z_{in}=R_{F}(1+T_{sc})/(1+T_{oc})$ with return ratio
$T_{0}\approx g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\prime }(g_{m}R_{D2}^{\prime }\parallel
R_{F})/2$.

In round numbers $Z_{P}\ll R_{in}$ so that
$|Z_{in}|_{LF}\approx R_{P}\sim {\rm a\;few}\;10\,{\rm \Omega}
-{\rm k\Omega}$, capacitive $\approx 1/sC_{in}$ beyond
$p_{in}$.

> *Remark:*  Many texts drop the $1/2$ and write
> $|A_{v0}|=g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}R_{D2}$; the $1/2$ is the
> single ended loss of the resistive loaded diff. pair.
> With an $n$ mirror load $A\to 1$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies shunt feedback and gives the right high-gain, low-frequency approximation; its equations for K and ZP can also be combined to recover the exact result. However, it never states that result correctly, and the explicit simplification in Eq. 22 drops the output-side RD2 contribution and is inconsistent with the preceding equations.

answers.question: Compute the input impedance of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
With $R_{D1}\rightarrow R_{D1}^{\prime }=R_{D1}\Vert 
r_{o1}$,
$R_{D2}\rightarrow R_{2}^{\prime }=R_{D2}\Vert r_{o3}\Vert r_{ISS}$
and, for simplicity ${\rm  PMOS}\;M_{2}\equiv M_{3}$,

$$g_{m2}=g_{m3}=g_{m}\qquad r_{o2}=r_{o3}=r_{o}\tag*{}$$
${\rm NMOS}\;g_{m1}$ the feedback is

$${\rm sample}\;V_{o}\qquad {\rm mix}\;I_{p}\tag*{}$$

shunt at the input, shunt at the output.
${\cal R}_{M}=V_{o}/I_{p}$ transresistance.
Put ${\bf V}_{DD}=0$ for $a.c.$ and $V_{b}=0$.

$$\eqalign{
P:&I_{in}=V_{p}Y_{in}+{{V_{p}-V_{o}}\over {R_{F}}} \cr
   &Y_{in}={1\over {R_{in}}}+sC_{in}+sC_{gs1}+sC_{gd1}(1-A_{1})+\cdots \cr
X:&{{V_{x}}\over {R_{D1}^{\prime }}}+g_{m1}V_{p}+g_{o1}V_{x}=0 \cr
S:&g_{m2}(V_{s}-V_{x})+g_{o2}V_{s}+g_{m3}V_{s}+g_{o3}(V_{s}-V_{o})=0\cr
O:&g_{m3}V_{s}+g_{o3}(V_{s}-V_{o})={{V_{o}}\over {R_{D2}}}+{{V_{o}-V_{p}}
\over {R_{F}}} \tag{1}}$$

$g_{o}=1/r_{o}$.  For $g_{o}R_{D}\ll 1$, $g_{o}R_{F}\ll 1$,
$g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$ and an ideal $I_{SS}\to \infty $,

$$\eqalign{
V_{x}&=-g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\prime }V_{p}
{{1}\over {1+sR_{D1}^{\prime }C_{x}}}\cr
V_{s}&={{g_{m2}V_{x}+g_{o3}V_{o}}\over {g_{m2}+g_{m3}}}\approx
{{V_{x}}\over 2}\qquad g_{m2}=g_{m3}\cr
g_{m}V_{s}&=V_{o}\left({1\over {R_{2}^{\prime }}}+{1\over {R_{F}}}\right)
-{{V_{p}}\over {R_{F}}}} \tag{2}}$$

i. e. with $Z_{Di}(s)=R_{Di}^{\prime }/(1+sR_{Di}^{\prime }C_{i})$

$$A_{v}(s)={{V_{o}}\over {V_{p}}}{\Bigl |}_{R_{F}\to \infty }=
-g_{m1}Z_{D1}(s){{g_{m3}Z_{D2}(s)}\over {g_{m2}+g_{m3}}}
\left[ 1+{\cal O}(g_{o}R)\right] \tag{3}$$

and, with the conventional $r_{o}\to \infty $,

$$\;A_{v}(s)\approx -g_{m1}R_{D1}{{g_{m}R_{D2}}\over 2}
{1\over {(1+s/\omega _{x})(1+s/\omega _{o})}}\; \tag{4}$$

$$\omega _{x}^{-1}=R_{D1}C_{x}\;,\qquad 
\omega _{o}^{-1}=R_{D2}C_{o}\;, \qquad 
A_{0}=|A_{v}(0)|={{g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}}\over 2}\tag{5}$$

including the $R_{F}$ loading on (2)

$$\eqalign{
g_{m}V_{s}&=-{{g_{m}g_{m1}R_{D1}}\over 2}V_{p}
      =V_{o}\left({1\over {R_{2}^{\prime }}}+{1\over {R_{F}}}\right)
        -{{V_{p}}\over {R_{F}}}\cr
A_{vF}&={{V_{o}}\over {V_{p}}}
      ={{-{{g_{m}g_{m1}R_{D1}}\over 2}+{1\over {R_{F}}}}\over 
            {{1}\over {R_{2}^{\prime }}}+{1\over {R_{F}}}}
      =-A_{0}{{R_{F}}\over {R_{F}+R_{2}^{\prime }}}
        +{{R_{2}^{\prime }}\over {R_{F}+R_{2}^{\prime }}}\approx 
        -{{g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}(R_{2}^{\prime }\Vert R_{F})}\over 2}
        \tag{6}}$$

For $R_{F}\gg R_{2}^{\prime }$, $A_{vF}\to -A_{0}$.
In the general mis--matched case replace $1/2$ by
$g_{m3}/(g_{m2}+g_{m3})$.

Put (6) in the $P$ equation,

$$I_{in}=V_{p}Y_{in}+{{V_{p}-A_{vF}V_{p}}\over {R_{F}}}
       =V_{p}\left[\,Y_{in}+{{1-A_{vF}}\over {R_{F}}}\,\right] \tag{7}$$

so that the impedance that the source $I_{in}$ sees at the
terminal $P$ is

$$\;Z_{in}(s)={{V_{p}}\over {I_{in}}}
      ={1\over {Y_{in}(s)+{{1-A_{vF}(s)}\over {R_{F}}}}}\;
      \approx {1\over {{1\over {R_{in}}}+sC_{in}+{{1+|A_{v}(s)|}
      \over {R_{F}}}}}\tag{8}$$

$Y_{in}=1/R_{in}+sC_{in}$ is the ordinary bias-- and
capacitance that is in $\,\Vert $ with the gate.  The gate
itself is $Z_{g}\to \infty $.  Neglecting $Y_{in}$ the
impedance looking into the gate through the feedback is

$$\;Z_{gF}(s)={{R_{F}}\over {1-A_{vF}(s)}}\; \tag{9}$$

the normal Miller result $R_{F}/(1+|A_{v}|)$.
With (6) for $r_{o}\to \infty $ and at $d.c.$

$$Y_{gF}(0)={{1-A_{vF}(0)}\over {R_{F}}}
        ={{1+A_{0}}\over {R_{F}+R_{D2}}}\tag{10}$$

i. e.

$$\;R_{gF0}={1\over {Y_{gF0}}}={{R_{F}+R_{2}^{\prime }}
      \over {1+A_{0}}}=
      {{R_{F}+R_{D2}\Vert r_{o3}}\over 
      {1+{{g_{m1}(R_{D1}\Vert r_{o1})g_{m}(R_{D2}\Vert r_{o3})}\over 2}}}\; \tag{11}$$

For $g_{o}R\ll 1$, $r_{o}\to \infty $

$$\;R_{gF0}\approx {{R_{F}+R_{D2}}\over {1+g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}/2}}
      \xrightarrow[R_{F}\gg R_{D2}]{}{{R_{F}}\over {1+A_{0}}}
      \approx {{2R_{F}}\over {g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}}}\; \tag{12}$$

In general $g_{m}\to g_{m}+g_{mb}$ for the $p$ devices if the
$n$ well is returned to $V_{DD}$.

The total $d.c.$ resistance seen by $I_{in}$ is $R_{gF0}$ in
parallel with the explicit bias resistor,

$$\;R_{in}^{c}=R_{in}\Vert R_{gF0}\approx R_{gF0}\;\;{\rm for}\;\;
      A_{0}\gg 1\tag{13}$$

normally a few $10\,{\rm \Omega }$ to a few $10^{2}{\rm\Omega }$,
the conventional virtual earth of the transimpedance
amplifier.  For $A_{0}\to \infty $, $R_{in}^{c}\to 0$.

Including $C_{in}$,

$$\;Z_{in}^{c}(s)\approx {1\over
      {{1\over {R_{in}}}+sC_{in}+{{1+A_{0}/(1+s/\omega _{x})
      (1+s/\omega _{o})}\over {R_{F}+R_{D2}}}}\; \tag{14}$$

which for $|A_{v}|\gg 1$ is

$$Z_{in}^{c}(s)\approx {{R_{F}+R_{D2}}\over {A_{0}}}
      (1+s/\omega _{x})(1+s/\omega _{o})
      \Vert R_{in}\Vert {1\over {sC_{in}}}\tag{15}$$

inductive with an apparent inductance $\approx
(R_{F}+R_{D2})C_{o}/A_{0}$, etc. The dominant input pole
$1/R_{in}C_{in}$ is pushed out to

$$\omega _{in}^{c}\approx {{1+A_{0}}\over {(R_{F}+R_{D2})C_{in}}}
      \approx {{1}\over {R_{gF0}C_{in}}}\gg \omega _{in}^{o} \tag{16}$$

so that the $d.c.$ transresistance is

$$R_{M}^{c}={{V_{o}}\over {I_{in}}}\approx -R_{F}{{A_{0}}\over {1+A_{0}}}
      \approx -R_{F}\qquad A_{0}\gg 1 \tag{17}$$

the usual shunt--shunt feedback result
$Z_{in}^{c}=Z_{in}^{o}/(1+\beta A)$,
$\beta \approx -1/R_{F}$, $A\approx {\cal R}_{M}^{o}\approx
-A_{0}R_{F}/(1+A_{0})$ and loop gain
$T_{0}= -\beta A\approx A_{0}R_{F}/(R_{F}+R_{D2})$.
Any explicit Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$,
$C_{in,{\rm eff}}=C_{in}+C_{gs1}+C_{gd1}(1+g_{m1}R_{D1})+\cdots $,
is to be added to $C_{in}$ in $Y_{in}$.

> *Remark:* With $g_{mb}\ne 0$ put $g_{m}\to g_{m}+g_{mb}$,
> with $r_{o}$ finite put $R_{Di}\to R_{Di}\Vert r_{oi}$ in
> $A_{0}$.  Up to the $g_{o}R$ corrections Eq.\,8--11 is the
> exact low frequency small signal result from Eq.\,1.  To first
> order $Z_{gF}\approx R_{F}/|A_{v}|$ is a low resistance to
> ground at $P$ which in parallel with $R_{in},C_{in}$ forms the
> closed loop input impedance of the TIA.  The sign in (9) is
> $1-A_{v}=1+|A_{v}|$ for the inverting amplifier.

For example $g_{m1}R_{D1}=5$, $g_{m}R_{D2}=5$,
$A_{0}=12.5$, $R_{F}=10\,{\rm k\Omega }$, $R_{D2}=5\,{\rm k\Omega }$,
$R_{gF0}=(15\,{\rm k\Omega })/13.5\approx 1.1\,{\rm k\Omega }$,
$\approx R_{F}/A_{0}=0.8\,{\rm k\Omega }$ for $R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Gives the exact low-frequency Miller result, including the output-side resistance: RgF0 = (RF + RD2)/(1 + A0), with the correct two-stage unloaded gain A0. The added finite-ro and capacitance discussion does not alter the essential result.

answers.question: Compute the input impedance of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
With the conventional notation let the input probe be
${\cal E}$ at $P$, ${\cal E}=V_{p}$, ${\cal I}=I_{p}$ ${\cal E}/{\cal
I}=Z_{p}$ and put $V_{b}=0$ for the signal.  Put for the
signal $V_{DD}=0$.  Neglect $C_{gs}$, $C_{gd}$ for the
low frequency calculation and put

$$g_{1}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}\qquad g_{2}=g_{m2}\qquad g_{3}=g_{m3}\qquad 
G_{D1}=R_{D1}^{-1}+g_{o1}\;\;,\;\;G_{D2}=R_{D2}^{-1}+g_{o3} \;\;, \;\;
G_{F}=R_{F}^{-1}\;\;,\;\;G_{in}=R_{in}^{-1}\;\;, \;\;
Y_{in}=G_{in}+sC_{in}$$

the conventional small signal circuit is Fig.1.  For a
$p$ channel ${\cal M}_{2}-{\cal M}_{3}$,

$$\eqalign{
I_{2}&=g_{2}(V_{s}-V_{x})+g_{o2}V_{s}\cr
I_{3}&=g_{3}V_{s}+g_{o3}(V_{s}-V_{o})\cr}
\tag{1}$$

$I_{SS}=0$ for the signal so that, for $g_{o2,3}\ll g_{2,3}$,

$$(g_{2}+g_{o2}+g_{3}+g_{o3})V_{s}-g_{2}V_{x}-g_{o3}V_{o}=0 \tag{2}$$

$$V_{s}={{g_{2}V_{x}+g_{o3}V_{o}}\over {g_{2}+g_{3}}}+O(g_{o}/g)
\approx {{g_{2}}\over {g_{2}+g_{3}}}V_{x}\tag{2a}$$

and for the matched pair $g_{2}=g_{3}=g_{p}$

$$V_{s}\approx {\textstyle{1\over 2}}V_{x}\tag{2b}$$

At the high impedance node $X$,

$$(G_{D1}V_{x}+g_{1}V_{p}=0\tag{3}$$

i. e.

$$V_{x}=-{{g_{1}}\over {G_{D1}}}V_{p}=-g_{1}R_{D1}^{\ast }V_{p}\tag{3a}$$

$$R_{D1}^{\ast }=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\approx R_{D1}\tag{3b}$$

for $g_{o1}R_{D1}\ll 1$.  At the output node, Fig.1,

$$G_{D2}V_{o}+G_{F}(V_{o}-V_{p})-I_{3}=0\tag{4}$$

with (1),

$$(G_{D2}+G_{F}+g_{o3})V_{o}-G_{F}V_{p}-(g_{3}+g_{o3})V_{s}=0\tag{4a}$$

With (2) and (3a)

$$V_{o}{{D}}\approx V_{p}\left[G_{F}-
{{g_{1}R_{D1}^{\ast }g_{2}(g_{3}+g_{o3})}\over {g_{2}+g_{3}}}\right]
\tag{5}$$

$$D=G_{D2}+G_{F}+g_{o3}-{{g_{o3}(g_{3}+g_{o3})}\over {g_{2}+g_{3}}}
      =G_{D2}+G_{F}+O(g_{o}) \tag{5a}$$

so that, to $O(g_{o}/g)$,

$$A_{v}^{\ast }\equiv {{V_{o}}\over {V_{p}}}\Bigl|_{G_{F}=0}
      =-{{g_{1}R_{D1}^{\ast }g_{2}g_{3}}\over {g_{2}+g_{3}}}
        {{1}\over {G_{D2}}}=-g_{1}R_{D1}^{\ast }{{g_{2}}\over {g_{2}+g_{3}}}
          g_{3}R_{D2}^{\ast } \tag{6}$$

$$R_{D2}^{\ast }=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o3}\parallel r_{o2}\approx R_{D2}$$

and with the $G_{F}$ loading the usual loaded voltage gain of
the forward amplifier is

$$A_{vL}= -g_{1}R_{D1}^{\ast }{{g_{2}}\over {g_{2}+g_{3}}}g_{3}
        \left(R_{D2}^{\ast }\parallel R_{F}\right) \tag{6a}$$

For the matched $p$ pair

$$A_{vL}\approx -{\textstyle{1\over 2}}g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\ast }g_{p}
        \left(R_{D2}^{\ast }\parallel R_{F}\right)\tag{6b}$$

and for $R_{F}\gg R_{D2}^{\ast }$

$$A_{v0}\approx -{\textstyle{1\over 2}}g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{p}R_{D2}\tag{6c}$$

apart from the sign.  ${\cal M}_{2}$ is a source follower,
${\cal M}_{3}$ a common gate device, the differential pair is a
follower $+$ CG stage with the well known $g_{m}R_{D}/2$ gain.
If the $R_{D2}$ gain is counted as part of the buffer it is
conventional to write

$$A_{v0}^{\prime }\approx -g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\ast }\tag{6d}$$

for the core $CS$ stage.

At the input node

$${\cal I}=Y_{in}V_{p}+G_{F}(V_{p}-V_{o})\tag{7}$$

so that with (5)

$${{{\cal I}}\over {V_{p}}}=Y_{in}+G_{F}-G_{F}{{V_{o}}\over {V_{p}}}
 =Y_{in}+G_{F}{{D-G_{F}+g_{1}R_{D1}^{\ast }g_{2}(g_{3}+g_{o3})/(g_{2}+g_{3})}
        \over {D}} \tag{8}$$

i. e. $O(g_{o}/g)$,

$${{1}\over {Z_{p}}}\approx Y_{in}+
        G_{F}{{G_{D2}+g_{1}R_{D1}^{\ast }g_{2}g_{3}/(g_{2}+g_{3})}\over
                {G_{D2}+G_{F}}}\tag{9}$$

For the matched pair and $g_{o}R_{D}\ll 1$, $r_{o}\to \infty $,

$$\eqalign{
{{1}\over {Z_{p}}}&\approx {{1}\over {R_{in}}}+sC_{in}
        +{{1}\over {R_{F}}}{{1+R_{F}/R_{D2}+{\textstyle{1\over 2}}
                g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{p}R_{D2}}\over {1+R_{F}/R_{D2}}}\cr
&\approx {{1}\over {R_{in}}}+sC_{in}
        +{{1}\over {R_{F}}}\left[1+|A_{vL}|\right]{{R_{D2}^{\ast }\over
                {R_{D2}^{\ast }+R_{F}}}+O(1) \cr}\tag{10}$$

In the conventional $R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$ large gain approximation

$${{1}\over {Z_{p}}}\approx {{1}\over {R_{in}}}+sC_{in}+
        {{|A_{v0}|}\over {R_{F}}}\tag{10a}$$

$$|A_{v0}|={\textstyle{1\over 2}}g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{p}R_{D2}\tag{10b}$$

so that the impedance seen looking into the gate itself,
$Z_{p0}=Z_{p}|_{R_{in}\to \infty ,C_{in}\to 0}$, is the
familiar shunt--shunt result

$$Z_{p0}\approx {{R_{F}}\over {1+|A_{vL}|}}
      \approx {{R_{F}\parallel R_{D2}}\over {1+|A_{v0}|}}\,
      |A_{v0}|\gg 1\tag{11}$$

i. e.

$$Z_{p0}\approx {{2R_{F}}\over {g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{p}R_{D2}}}\,
      {{R_{F}+R_{D2}}\over {R_{D2}}}\approx 
      {{2R_{F}}\over {g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{p}R_{D2}}}\qquad 
      R_{F}\gg R_{D2}\tag{11a}$$

in parallel with $R_{in}$ and $1/sC_{in}$,

$$Z_{in}(s)={{1}\over {Y_{in}+1/Z_{p0}(s)}}=
      {{1}\over {sC_{in}+1/R_{in}+1/Z_{p0}(s)}}\tag{12}$$

At low frequencies $s\to 0$

$$R_{in,CL}=R_{in}\parallel Z_{p0}\approx 
      R_{in}\parallel {{R_{F}}\over {1+|A_{vL}|}}\tag{13}$$

For the circuit often quoted as a unity gain buffer after the
$CS$ stage, $g_{p}R_{D2}/2\to 1$,

$$Z_{p0}\approx {{R_{F}}\over {1+g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\ast }}}\tag{14}$$

$$R_{in,CL}\approx R_{in}\parallel {{R_{F}}\over {1+g_{m1}R_{D1}}}
      \qquad {\rm ``buffer''\;approx.}\tag{14a}$$

In (11)--(14) $R_{D1}^{\ast }=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}$,
$R_{D2}^{\ast }=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o3}$ and $g_{m}\to g_{m}+g_{mb}$
if body effect is retained.

With frequency the dominant poles are at $X$ and at the output,

$$A_{vL}(s)\approx {{A_{vL}(0)}\over 
        {\left(1+sR_{D1}^{\ast }C_{X}\right)\left(1+sR_{D2L}^{\ast }C_{L}
                \right)}}\tag{15}$$

$$R_{D2L}^{\ast }=R_{D2}^{\ast }\parallel R_{F}\qquad 
  C_{X}=C_{db1}+C_{gs2}+C_{gd1}+C_{gd2}\qquad 
  C_{L}=C_{db3}+C_{gd3}+C_{L,ext}$$

so that

$$Z_{p0}(s)\approx {{R_{F}}\over {1-A_{vL}(s)}}\approx 
      {{R_{F}}\over {|A_{vL}(s)|}}\;\;|A_{vL}|\gg 1\tag{16}$$

and

$$Z_{in}(s)\approx \left[sC_{in}+{{1}\over {R_{in}}}+
      {{1-A_{vL}(s)}\over {R_{F}}}\right]^{-1}\tag{17}$$

which is $\approx 1/sC_{in}$ for $|s|C_{in}\gg G_{in}+R_{F}^{-1}
|A_{vL}(s)|$ and $\approx R_{in,CL}$ for $s\to 0$.
Writing $|A_{vL}(s)|=|A_{v0}|/{\cal D}(s)$,

$$Z_{in}(s)\approx {{R_{F}}\over {|A_{v0}|}}{\cal D}(s)
      \parallel R_{in}\parallel {{1}\over {sC_{in}}}\tag{18}$$

so that beyond the loop unity gain frequency the input looks
inductive, $|Z_{in}|\propto |s|$, before $C_{in}$ takes over.
Any $C_{F}$ in parallel with $R_{F}$ adds a zero at
$1/R_{F}C_{F}$.

Numerically, e. g. $g_{m1}=1\,{\rm mS}$, $R_{D1}=5\,{\rm k}$,
$g_{p}=2\,{\rm mS}$, $R_{D2}=5\,{\rm k}$, $R_{F}=50\,{\rm k}$,
$|A_{v0}|\approx 25$, $Z_{p0}\approx R_{F}/25\approx 2\,{\rm k}$,
$R_{in,CL}\approx 2\,{\rm k}\parallel R_{in}$.  With
$r_{o}$ finite replace $R_{D}$ by $R_{D}\parallel r_{o}$ and
$g_{m}$ by $g_{m}+g_{mb}$ for the usual $\sim 10$--$30\%$
correction.  The closed loop transimpedance is
$V_{o}/I_{in}\approx -R_{F}A_{vL}/(1+A_{vL})\approx -R_{F}$ for
$|A_{vL}|\gg 1$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Equation (9) gives an input admittance equivalent to the exact Miller result, with the output-side resistance included and the correct unloaded gain identifiable. However, the later simplification and loaded-gain formulas are inconsistent with that result, so the final answer is muddled.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in the figure generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
In general a voltage can only $FM$ an
autonomous circuit where the common mode to
differential mode rejection is finite:

$${\cal L}_{LDO}(\Delta \omega )\approx 
{{S_{\phi}(\Delta \omega )}\over {2}}$$

$${{S_{\phi}(\Delta \omega ) {\rm rad^{2}/Hz} }\over 
{S_{Vout}(\Delta \omega ){\rm V^{2}/Hz}}}=
\left| H_{\phi V}(\Delta \omega)\right|^{2}$$

where $H_{\phi V}$ is the {\it supply pushing}
{\it frequency modulation} transfer function.
For $S_{Vout}\approx S_{th}$ white, $H\propto 1/\Delta \omega $
is an ideal integrator.

For the topology of the figure:

* $V_{out}$ is the RF common mode $V_{cm}=(V_{X}+V_{Y})/2$
  through the $R_{p}+j\omega L_{1}$ impedance.
  For $\Delta \omega \ll \omega _{0}=1/\sqrt{L_{1}C_{t}}$

$$Z_{cm}\approx j\Delta \omega L_{1}\rightarrow 0$$

so low frequency noise on $V_{out}$ appears
undivided on $V_{cm}$. For high frequencies
it is divided by

$$V_{cm}(\Delta \omega)=V_{out}(\Delta \omega)
{{Z_{cm}}\over {Z_{cm}+Z_{LDO}(\Delta \omega)}}=
 V_{out}H_{LPF}(\Delta \omega)$$

$$H_{LPF}= {1\over {1+j\Delta \omega R_{LDO}C_{dec}}}
{1\over {1+j\Delta \omega L_{1}/R_{p}}}+...$$

Normally put a $C_{dec}\sim 10-100{\rm pF}$ to $>{\rm nF}$
off chip on that node so:

$${\rm PSD}_{Vcm}(\Delta \omega)=
S_{th}(\Delta \omega)\left| H_{LDO}(\Delta \omega)\right|^{2}
\left| H_{LPF}(\Delta \omega)\right|^{2}$$

$$S_{th}=S_{BG}G^{2}+S_{EA}+4kTR_{on}+4kT\gamma g_{m}^{-1}+...\;{\rm V^{2}/Hz}$$

usual LDO white $+$ $K_{F}/f$ , $H_{LDO}$ is the
closed loop $V_{out}/v_{n}$ transfer function,
$\approx 1$ for $\Delta \omega <\omega _{u,LDO}$ and
$1/\Delta \omega $ above.

It $FM$'s the oscillator:

$$\omega _{0}(V_{cm})={1\over {\sqrt{L_{1}C_{t}(V_{cm})}}}$$

$$C_{t}=C_{B1}+C_{B2}+C_{v}(V_{cm}-V_{cont})+C_{M1,2}(V_{cm})+C_{p}$$

$$d\omega _{0}= {\partial \omega _{0}\over{\partial V_{cm}}}dV_{cm}
+{\partial \omega _{0}\over{\partial V_{cont}}}dV_{cont}$$

$${\partial \omega _{0}\over{\partial V_{cm}}}=
-{1\over 2}{\omega _{0}\over{C_{t}}}{\partial C_{t}\over{\partial V_{cm}}}
\;\;{\rm rad/s/V}$$

$${K_{VDD}}={1\over{2\pi}}{\partial \omega _{0}\over{\partial V_{out}}}
\;\;{\rm Hz/V}\approx -{1\over 2}{f_{0}\over{C_{t}}}
{\partial C_{v}\over{\partial V_{cm}}}~~{\rm dominant}$$

is the {\it supply pushing coefficient}. Can be
extracted small signal from a

* dc sweep of $V_{out}$ vs $f_{0}$ in PSS
* $p_{ss}+p_{ac}$ : $FM$ sideband on $V_{out}$
  $\delta V_{out}\cos \Delta \omega t\rightarrow 
  \delta \omega \cos \Delta \omega t$

Typical $10-500{\rm MHz/V}$. In a perfectly balanced
tank without $V_{cont}$ dependence $K_{VDD}=0$ to first
order and pushing is second order ${\cal O}(\Delta C/C)$
mismatch and ${\rm AM-PM}$ via the Groszkowski effect,
but with the MOS varactor $M_{v}$ of the figure
$C_{v}=C_{v}(V_{GS}=V_{X}-V_{cont})$ it is first order:

$$\Delta \omega (t)=K_{0}v_{n}(t)\;\;\;K_{0}=2\pi K_{VDD}$$

$$\theta(t)=\int^{t} \Delta \omega(\tau)d\tau$$

for the usual $|\Delta \omega |\ll \omega_{0}$
narrow band $FM$:

$$v_{out}(t)=V_{0}\cos [\omega_{0}t+\phi_{n}(t)]+{\rm AM}$$

$$\phi_{n}(t)=\int^{t} K_{0}v_{n}(\tau)d\tau$$

In the Fourier domain $j\Delta \omega \Phi_{n}=K_{0}V_{n}$

$$\left| \Phi_{n}(\Delta \omega)\right|^{2}=
{{K_{0}^{2}}\over{\Delta \omega^{2}}}\left| V_{n}(\Delta \omega)\right|^{2}$$

I. e. $PSD$ sense:

$$ {\cal S_{\Delta \omega}(\Delta \omega)=K_{0}^{2}{\cal S}_{Vcm}(\Delta \omega)
\;{\rm (rad/s)^{2}/Hz}} $$

$${\cal S}_{\Delta f}(\Delta \omega)=K_{VDD}^{2}{\cal S}_{Vcm} \;
{\rm Hz^{2}/Hz}}$$

$${\cal S}_{\phi}(\Delta \omega)={{{\cal S}_{\Delta \omega}}\over{\Delta \omega^{2}}}
={{K_{0}^{2}}\over{\Delta \omega^{2}}}{\cal S}_{Vcm}(\Delta \omega)
={{K_{VDD}^{2}}\over{\Delta f^{2}}}{\cal S}_{Vcm}(\Delta f)
\;{\rm rad^{2}/Hz}} \tag{1}$$

Single sideband to carrier ratio normally quoted:

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega)=10\log_{10}{{{\cal S}_{\phi}(\Delta \omega)}\over 2}
\;{\rm dBc/Hz} $$

$$ {\cal L}_{LDO}(\Delta \omega)\approx 
10\log_{10}\left[ {{K_{VDD}^{2}S_{th}(\Delta \omega)
\left| H_{LDO}H_{LPF}\right|^{2}}\over{2\Delta f^{2}}}\right]} $$

$$=10\log_{10}\left[ {{K_{0}^{2}S_{th}(\Delta \omega)
\left| H_{LDO}H_{LPF}\right|^{2}}\over{2\Delta \omega^{2}}}\right]
\tag{2}$$

with $K_{0}=2\pi K_{VDD}$ if $K_{VDD}$ in ${\rm Hz/V}$.

Eq.1 is the linearized {\it Hajimiri-Lee} result.
Rigorously

$$\phi_{n}(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma_{cm}(\tau)v_{n}(\tau)d\tau$$

where $\Gamma_{cm}(t)$ is the impulse sensitivity
function from the common mode node. Expanding
$\Gamma_{cm}=c_{0}/2+\sum c_{n}\cos n\omega_{0}t+...$

$$c_{0}={1\over{\pi}}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\Gamma_{cm}d\theta
\approx {{K_{0}}\over{\omega_{0}}}$$

$$ {\cal S}_{\phi}(\Delta \omega)\approx 
{{c_{0}^{2}}\over{4\Delta \omega^{2}}}{\cal S}_{Vcm}(\Delta \omega)
+\sum_{n\ge 1}{{c_{n}^{2}}\over{4}}\,{\cal S}_{Vcm}(n\omega_{0}\pm\Delta \omega) $$

The $n=0$ term is Eq.1, the frequency translation
of noise around $n\omega_{0}$, in particular $2\omega_{0}$
for tail noise, is normally negligible for supply
common mode if $c_{n\ge 1}\ll c_{0}$. That is evaluated
