in ${\rm PSS}+pnoise/pxf$ as the periodic transfer
function ${\rm PXF}_{Vout\rightarrow \phi}$.

In words: White $S_{th}$ becomes $1/\Delta\omega^{2}$,
i.e. $-20{\rm dB/dec}$ phase noise. $1/f$ noise of the
LDO

$$S_{th}=S_{th,0}\left(1+{{f_{c}}\over{f}}\right)$$

becomes $1/f^{2}$ and $1/f^{3}$ phase noise after the
integration:

$${\cal L}\propto {1\over{\Delta f^{2}}}\;\;{\rm for}\;\Delta f>f_{c}$$

$${\cal L}\propto {1\over{\Delta f^{3}}}\;\;{\rm for}\;\Delta f<f_{c}$$

unfiltered. The $H_{LPF}$ eventually restores $-20{\rm dB/dec}$
roll off above the $R_{LDO}C_{dec}$ pole.

> Example: $S_{th}^{1/2}=30{\rm nV/\sqrt{Hz}}$,
> ${\cal S}_{th}=9\times 10^{-16}{\rm V^{2}/Hz}$,
> $K_{VDD}=100{\rm MHz/V}$,
> $\Delta f=1{\rm MHz}$,
> ${\cal S}_{\phi}=K_{VDD}^{2}{\cal S}_{th}/\Delta f^{2}
> =9\times 10^{-12}{\rm rad^{2}/Hz}$,
> ${\cal L}\approx 10\log 4.5\times 10^{-12}
> \approx -113{\rm dBc/Hz}$,
> to be added power wise to the intrinsic tank/MOS
> Leeson phase noise. With $C_{dec}=100{\rm pF}$,
> $R_{LDO}=100\Omega$, $f_{p}=16{\rm MHz}$, no attenuation
> at $1{\rm MHz}$.

That is observable and usually requires $C_{dec}$,
$RC$ filtering on $V_{out}$ or a high ${\rm PSRR}$
regulated cascode between $L_{1}$ and $V_{out}$,
or regulation of the tail current instead of the
tank top, to meet e.g. GSM $-165{\rm dBc/Hz}$ at
$20{\rm MHz}$. In simulation simply replace $V_{out}$
by $V_{out}+v_{n}$, run ${\rm pss+pnoise}$ with
$v_{n}$ as input and observe ${\rm pnoise}$ sideband
at $\omega_{0}\pm\Delta\omega$. The sum of intrinsic
and supply induced:

$${\cal L}_{tot}=10\log_{10}\left(10^{{\cal L}_{VCO}/10}
+10^{{\cal L}_{LDO}/10}\right)$$

is filtered by any subsequent $PLL$ loop
$|1/(1+G_{PLL})|^{2}$ inside the loop bandwidth.

AM sidebands ${\cal S}_{AM}=
\left|H_{AM}\right|^{2}{\cal S}_{Vcm}$ are at the same
$\Delta\omega$ but do not contribute to zero crossing
jitter to first order.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly derives the supply-pushing sensitivity, converts LDO noise to phase noise with the required 1/Δf² dependence, and identifies the direct varactor modulation that links supply pushing to the tuning sensitivity. The additional filtering and spectral details do not undermine the core result.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in the figure generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
In the narrow band sense the ${\rm VCO}$
is a {\it frequency modulator} with

$${\omega_{osc}}(t)=\omega _{0}+ {\cal K}_{DD}v_{n}(t) \tag{1}$$

$$v_{n}(t)=V_{out}(t)-V_{out, D.C.}\qquad 
{\cal K}_{DD}={{\partial \omega_{0}}\over {\partial V_{out}}}
  =2\pi {{\partial f_{0}}\over {\partial V_{DD}}}=2\pi K_{DD}$$

so that

$$\phi _{n}(t)=\int {\cal K}_{DD}v_{n}(t)dt\;\;\;,\;\;H_{FM}(s)={\cal K}_{DD}/s \tag{2}$$

modulo the low pass filtering between the physical
noise source and the $V_{out}$ node.
For $f_{m}\ll f_{0}$, $L_{1}$ is a short and
$V_{n}$ is a common mode $D.C.$ shift of $X$ and $Y$.
I. e. $S_{th}(f_{m})$, one sided, ${\rm V^{2}Hz^{-1}}$,
is impressed unattenuated on the tank common mode
unless deliberately decoupled

$$S_{th}^{eff}(f_{m})=S_{th}(f_{m})
\left| {{Z_{dec}}\over {Z_{o,LDO}+Z_{dec}}}\right|^{2}
\left| H_{LDO}(f_{m})\right|^{2} \tag{3}$$

$H_{LDO}\approx 1/[1+jf_{m}/f_{p,LDO}]$ and
$Z_{o,LDO}\parallel 1/sC_{dec}$ otherwise $S_{th}^{eff}
\approx S_{th}$ in the usual $10{\rm kHz}<f_{m}<10{\rm MHz}$
band.

${\cal K}_{DD}$ is the normally simulated supply pushing

$${\cal K}_{DD}= {{\Delta \omega_{0}}\over {\Delta V_{out}}}$$

and can be obtained by a $D.C.$ sweep
${\rm PSS}/{\rm PAC}$ {\it a.c.} injection of $1{\rm V}$
at $V_{out}$ or analytically to first order.
E. g. for the dominant varactor ${\rm AM{\hbox{-}}PM}$
conversion

$$V_{var}=V_{X,D.C.}-V_{cont}\approx V_{out}-V_{cont}$$

$$C_{tot}=C_{fix}+C_{av}(V_{var})+C_{par}(V_{X})$$

$$f_{0}= {1\over {2\pi\sqrt{L_{1}C_{tot}}}}$$

$$\eqalign{
K_{DD}&={{\partial f_{0}}\over {\partial V_{out}}}
 =-{{f_{0}}\over {2C_{tot}}}{{\partial C_{tot}}\over {\partial V_{out}}} \cr
 &\approx -{{f_{0}}\over {2C_{tot}}}
\left[{{\partial C_{av}}\over {\partial V_{var}}}
+{{\partial C_{par}}\over {\partial V_{X}}}\right]_{Q} } \tag{4}$$

i. e. to varactor accuracy

$$|K_{DD}|\approx |K_{VCO}|\qquad 
K_{VCO}={{\partial f_{0}}\over {\partial V_{cont}}}$$

up to a sign. The conventional varactor tuning gain is
a measure of supply pushing.  Any other
${\rm AM{\hbox{-}}PM}$ via the Groszkowski effect
$C_{eff}(A(V_{out}))$ and $C_{gd,db}(V_{X})$ is
included in the simulated

$$K_{DD}= \left.{{\Delta f_{0}}\over {\Delta V_{out}}}\right|_{sim} \tag{5}$$

in ${\rm HzV^{-1}}$.  For one varactor per side,
two sides,

$$\Delta f_{0}\approx -{{f_{0}}\over {C_{tot}}}{{dC_{av}}\over {dV}} \Delta V_{out}$$

For a sinusoidal $v_{n}=V_{m}\cos \omega _{m}t$

$$v_{o}(t)=V_{0}\cos \left[\omega _{0}t+
{{{\cal K}_{DD}V_{m}}\over {\omega _{m}}}\sin \omega _{m}t\right] \tag{6}$$

narrow band ${\cal K}_{DD}V_{m}/\omega _{m}\ll 1$

$$v_{o}\approx V_{0}\cos \omega _{0}t-
V_{0}{{{\cal K}_{DD}V_{m}}\over {2\omega _{m}}}
\left\{ \cos (\omega _{0}+\omega _{m})t
-\cos (\omega _{0}-\omega _{m})t\right\}$$

side band / carrier $= {\cal K}_{DD}V_{m}/2\omega _{m}$.
For a random $v_{n}$ with one sided power
spectral density $S_{th}(f_{m})$ ${\rm V^{2}/Hz}$

frequency noise:

$$S_{f}(f_{m}) = K_{DD}^{2}S_{th}^{eff}(f_{m})\;\;{\rm Hz^{2}Hz^{-1}} \tag{7a}$$
$$S_{\omega}(f_{m})={\cal K}_{DD}^{2}S_{th}^{eff}(f_{m})
\;\;{\rm (rad/s)^{2}Hz^{-1}} \tag{7b}$$

phase noise. With $\Phi _{n}(s)={\cal K}_{DD}V_{n}(s)/s$ :

$$S_{\phi}(f_{m}) = {{{\cal K}_{DD}^{2}}\over {\omega _{m}^{2}}}
S_{th}^{eff}(f_{m})
= {{K_{DD}^{2}}\over {f_{m}^{2}}}S_{th}^{eff}(f_{m})
\;\;{\rm rad^{2}Hz^{-1}}\;\;{\rm DSB}\tag{8}$$

$${\cal L}(f_{m})=10\log {{S_{\phi}(f_{m})}\over 2}
=10\log \left[ {{K_{DD}^{2}S_{th}^{eff}(f_{m})}
\over {2f_{m}^{2}}}\right]
=10\log \left[ {{{\cal K}_{DD}^{2}S_{th}^{eff}(f_{m})}
\over {2\omega _{m}^{2}}}\right]\;{\rm dBcHz^{-1}}\tag{9}$$

SSB. For a white $S_{th}=S_{0}=4kTR_{o,LDO}+S_{a}/g_{m}+\cdots$
constant to $f_{p,LDO}$ this is $1/f_{m}^{2}$,
$20{\rm dB/dec}$, added in power to the intrinsic
VCO phase noise $S_{\phi ,VCO}$ given by Leeson/Hajimiri.
For a $1/f$ LDO noise $S_{th}\propto 1/f_{m}$ it gives
$1/f_{m}^{3}$, $30{\rm dB/dec}$, close in.

In ISF language eq. 8 is $|H(j\omega _{m})|^{2}S_{th}$
with $H={\cal K}_{DD}/j\omega _{m}= \Gamma_{DD,DC}\omega_{0}
/\omega_{m}$ and $\Gamma_{DD}$ the supply ISF.
More generally from ${\rm PSS}+{\rm PNOISE}$ you inject
$1{\rm V\>a.c.}$ in series with $V_{out}$ and
$H(j\omega _{m})= \Delta \Phi /\Delta V_{out}$ is the
p.m. transfer function, so $S_{\phi}=|H|^{2}S_{th}$.

> {\it Rigorously the periodic transfer function
> $H(j\omega _{m},t)=\sum_{k}H_{k}e^{jk\omega _{0}t}\)
> upconverts $S_{th}$ at $k\omega _{0}\pm \omega _{m}$
> with $H_{k}\propto \Gamma_{k}$.  For the supply node
> $H_{0}$ i.e. ${\cal K}_{DD}/j\omega _{m}$ dominates.}

In practice: get $K_{DD}\sim 50-500{\rm MHz/V}$ from
simulation/measurement and apply (8)-(9).
E. g. $S_{th}^{1/2}=10{\rm nVHz^{-1/2}}$,
$S_{th}=1.0\times 10^{-16}{\rm V^{2}Hz^{-1}}$,
$K_{DD}=100{\rm MHz/V}$:

$$S_{\phi}(1{\rm MHz}) =10^{16}\times 10^{-16}/10^{12}
=10^{-12}{\rm rad^{2}Hz^{-1}}$$

$${\cal L}(1{\rm MHz})\approx -123{\rm dBcHz^{-1}}$$

low pass filtered for $f_{m}>f_{p,LDO}$ or $f_{m}>1/2\pi R_{o}C_{dec}$.

That is the {\it excess} phase noise due to the
regulator.  Total ${\cal L}_{tot}= {\cal L}_{VCO}
\oplus {\cal L}_{LDO}$ on a linear power basis.
Suppression requires large $C_{dec}$, high
$PSRR_{LDO}$ at $f_{m}$, low $K_{DD}$ by
differential design, low $K_{VCO}$, and low
$R_{o,LDO}$ noise. This is why a noiseless
$V_{out}$ is normally decoupled with nF to $\mu$F
on chip or board.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies supply pushing, converts the LDO voltage-noise spectrum through the VCO sensitivity to phase noise with the required 1/offset-frequency-squared dependence, and notes that direct varactor modulation makes the pushing sensitivity closely related to KVCO. Extra modeling details do not undermine the essential answer.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in the figure generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
In general that is a {\it quasi static}
frequency modulation, the differential mode being
in first order insensitive to it, and a second order
Groszkowski - AM/PM conversion. For $f_{m}<< f_{0}$
you can treat it ${\rm LTI}$.

>$$\eqalign{
&V_{out}=V_{out0}+v_{n}(t) \cr
&v_{n}^{2}/\Delta f = S_{th}(f)\ {\rm in\ } {\rm V^{2}Hz^{-1}}\cr
&S_{V_{out}} = S_{th}|Z_{out}||H_{LDO}|^{2}\cr
&{\rm if\ } S_{th} {\rm\ is\ in\ A^{2}Hz^{-1}\;\;
S_{V_{out}}=S_{th}|Z_{out}|^{2}\;\;,
Z_{out}=R_{out}||1/sC_{out}}}$$

Let

$${\omega}_{0}= {\omega}_{0}(V_{out},V_{cont},...)$$

be the {\it large} signal oscillation frequency.
Put $V_{cont}={\rm const}$ and

$$K_{push}={{\partial {\omega}_{0}}\over {\partial V_{out}}}
  =2\pi {{\partial f_{0}}\over {\partial V_{out}}}
  \approx -{{\omega}_{0}\over {2C_{T}}}{{\partial C_{T}}\over
  {\partial V_{out}}}\quad {\rm rad\,s^{-1}V^{-1}} \tag{1}$$

$$K_{push}^{Hz} =K_{push}/2\pi \;\;{\rm Hz\,V^{-1}}$$

$C_{T}=C_{B}+C_{v}(V_{cont}-V_{X})+C_{M1,2}(V_{out})$.
For the circuit as drawn $C_{T}$ is dominated by
${\rm B_{1,2}}$ and the MOS varactor ${\rm M_{v}}$ so that
with $V_{X,dc}\approx V_{out}$

$${{\partial C_{T}}\over {\partial V_{out}}}
      \approx {{\partial C_{v}}\over {\partial V_{X}}}
      =-{{\partial C_{v}}\over {\partial V_{cont}}}$$

so that to first order

$$\left|K_{push}\right|\approx \left|K_{VCO}\right|
      =\left|{{\partial {\omega}_{0}}\over {\partial V_{cont}}}\right| \tag{2}$$

In general (1) is obtained by a ${\rm PSS}$ sweep
$${\omega}_{0}\;{\rm vs\;}V_{out}$$ or by a small
sinusoidal modulation

$$V_{out}=V_{out0}+\Delta V\cos {\omega}_{m}t$$

$${\rm FM\ sideband\ }: \;\Delta f = K_{push}^{Hz}\Delta V$$

and includes the Groszkowski shift

$${{\Delta {\omega}}\over {{\omega}_{0}}}\approx
  {1\over {2Q}}{{ {\rm Im\;} \{Y_{1}\}}\over {{\rm Re\;} \{Y_{1}\}}}$$

due to the change of the harmonic content, {\it i. e.}
of the amplitude

$$A(V_{out})\approx \cases{
I_{VCO}R_{p} & current limited \cr
V_{out} & voltage limited}$$

and the ${\rm AM\!\to\! PM}$ conversion through
$C_{v}(A)$ and $C_{gd}(A)$. In practice $K_{push}$
in (1) is taken as the {\it effective} including
AM$\to$PM, $K_{push}=K_{FM}+K_{AM}K_{AM-PM}$ and is
normally $10-100\,{\rm MHz/V}$ for a ${\rm GHz}$ $LC$
$VCO$.

For ${\omega}_{m}=2\pi f_{m}<< {\omega}_{0}$ :

$${\omega}(t) ={\omega}_{0}+K_{push}v_{n}(t) \tag{3}$$

$${\phi}_{n}(t)=\int^{t} K_{push}v_{n}(\tau)d\tau \tag{4}$$

in the frequency domain ${\cal F}\{ \phi_{n}\}=K_{push}
V_{n}(s)/s$. I. e. a voltage noise $v_{n}$ FM modulates
the oscillator. In power spectral language
double sided:

$$S_{\phi}(\omega_{m}) = {{K_{push}^{2}}\over {\omega_{m}^{2}}}
     S_{V_{out}}(\omega_{m})\left|H_{cm}(\omega_{m})\right|^{2}
     \qquad {\rm rad^{2}Hz^{-1}} \tag{5}$$

$$S_{\phi}(f_{m})={{K_{push}^{Hz\,2}}\over {f_{m}^{2}}}
     S_{V_{out}}(f_{m})\left|H_{cm}(f_{m})\right|^{2} $$

$H_{cm}$ is the low pass from the $LDO$ to the
common mode of the tank,

$$H_{cm}(s)\approx {1\over {1+sR_{out}C_{out}}}\,
      {Z_{cm}(s)\over {Z_{cm}(s)+sL_{1}/2}} \approx
      {1\over {1+sR_{out}C_{out}}}\;\;{\rm for\;}f_{m} < f_{0}$$

$$Z_{cm}= \left[ sC_{T,cm}+1/s(L_{1}/2)+G_{p,cm}\right]^{-1}$$

So that the conventional {\it single sideband to carrier}
phase noise $L=10\log {\cal L}$,
${\cal L}(f_{m})=S_{\phi}(f_{m})/2$ single sided, is
for white $S_{th}=S_{0}=4kTR_{n}$ at the output of the
$LDO$:

$${\cal L}(f_{m}) =10\log \left[
  {{K_{push}^{2}S_{0}}\over {2\omega_{m}^{2}\left[1+(\omega_{m}/
  \omega_{p})^{2}\right]}} \right]\;\;{\rm dBcHz^{-1}} \tag{6}$$

$$\approx 10\log \left[
  {{K_{push}^{Hz\,2}S_{0}}\over {2f_{m}^{2}\left[1+(f_{m}/
  f_{p})^{2}\right]}} \right]$$

${\omega}_{p}=1/R_{out}C_{out}$ is the $LDO$ dominant
pole, $f_{p}={\omega}_{p}/2\pi $. Normally we quote in
${\rm dBcHz^{-1}}$

>$$ {\cal L}_{LDO}(f_{m})\approx 20\log {{K_{push}^{Hz}}\over {f_{m}}}
      +10\log S_{Vout}(f_{m}) -3{\rm dB} -20\log \sqrt{1+(f_{m}/f_{p})^{2}} $$

{\it i.e.} white supply noise becomes $1/f_{m}^{2}$,
$20{\rm dB/dec}$, phase noise. $1/f$ noise of the
$LDO$ becomes $1/f_{m}^{3}$, $30{\rm dB/dec}$.

With $K_{push}^{Hz}=50\,{\rm MHz/V}$,
$S_{Vout}^{1/2}=10\,{\rm nV\,Hz^{-1/2}}$,
$S_{0}=10^{-16}{\rm V^{2}Hz^{-1}}$,

$${\cal L}(1\,{\rm MHz})\approx 10\log{{(5\times 10^{7})^{2}
  10^{-16}}\over {2\times 10^{12}}}\approx -96{\rm dBcHz^{-1}}$$

at $100{\rm kHz}$, $-116+20= -76{\rm dBcHz^{-1}}$ before
filtering. The intrinsic $VCO$ noise must be added in
power.

Eq. 5 is the ${\rm LTI}$ approximation. Rigorously the
$LDO$ noise is a cyclostationary input to a linear
periodically time variant system. With Hajimiri-Lee
impulse sensitivity function $\Gamma_{DD}(x)$,
$q_{max}=C_{T}V_{max}$ the maximum charge swing,
$i_{n,DD}=v_{n}/R_{out}$:

$$\Gamma_{DD}(\theta) = \Gamma_{0}+ \Gamma_{2}\cos 2\theta+\cdots$$

common mode, essentially zero at $\omega_{0}$. The
injection of a charge $\Delta q$ at phase $\theta$
at the $V_{out}$ node produces an asymptotic phase
shift $\Delta \phi =\Gamma_{DD}(\theta)\Delta q/q_{max}$.
Expanding $\Gamma_{DD}$ in Fourier series $c_{n}$:

$$S_{\phi}(f_{m})={1\over {8\pi^{2}f_{m}^{2}q_{max}^{2}}}
   \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}c_{n}^{2}S_{i,n}(f_{m}-nf_{0}) \tag{7}$$

For supply noise the dominant terms are $n=0$,
low frequency noise converted to $1/f_{m}^{2}$, and
$n=\pm 2$, noise at $ \approx 2f_{0}$ down converted
to phase noise at $f_{0}\pm f_{m}$.

$c_{0}$ is the ${\rm DC}$ value of $\Gamma_{DD}$ and

$$c_{0}/q_{max}= K_{push}/{\omega}_{0}$$

so that (7) reduces to (5) for $f_{m}<<f_{0}$.

In a simulator: ${\rm PSS}+{\rm PXF}$ or ${\rm PSS}+{\rm PNOISE}$
with the perturbation projection vector ${\bf p}^{T}(t)$,
Demir {\it et al.}, extraction of ${\bf p}^{T}{\bf B}v_{n}$
gives directly (7). In SpectreRF put a small voltage
source in series with $V_{out}$, run $pnoise$ modulated,
PM, the result is ${\cal L}_{LDO}(f_{m})$ within the
Leeson factor.

In design it is the reason for a large $C_{out}$
on the $LDO$, $f_{p}<<f_{m,{\rm min}}$, and for a
low $K_{push}$, {\it i.e.} low $K_{VCO}$ and large
fixed $C_{B}$ compared to $C_{v}$, and for a high
$Q$ tank, low $K_{AM-PM}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies supply pushing, converts the LDO output-noise spectrum to phase noise with the expected 1/Δf² dependence, and notes that the direct varactor sensitivity makes Kpush closely related to KVCO, so reducing KVCO reduces the conversion. Extra modeling details and factor conventions do not undermine the essential answer.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in the figure. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
In the sense of Hajimiri that is the
{\it Hegazi} filter, Fig.2 {\tt JSSC 12/01}
and Samori {\it et al.}, in first order,
with a dimensioning

$${\vert Z_{T}(2\omega _{0})\vert \ll {\vert Z_{T}(0)\vert
\over 1+q_{max}} \qquad Z_{T}={1\over j\omega C_{T}}\parallel
r_{0T}}$$

it {\it filters} the ${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )$.
In more detail

$$ {\cal L}(\Delta \omega )=10\log
\left\{ {2FkT\over P_{s}}\left[1+\left({\omega_{0}\over
2Q\Delta \omega}\right)^{2}\right]\left(1+{\omega_{1/f^{3}}\over
\vert\Delta \omega\vert}\right)\right\}$$

$$F= 1+ \gamma {4\over 9}g_{m}R + \gamma g_{mT}R\,
{{c_{0}^{2}+c_{2}^{2}+ \cdots }\over 4}
{S_{I_{SS}}(n\omega_{0}\pm \Delta \omega)\over 4kT}+\cdots $$

is normally dominated, close and far from carrier,
by the bias.  $\Gamma _{T}(t)$ is the ISF from the
common source, $P$ in the figure.  For the conventional
inductive loaded cross coupled pair

$$\Gamma _{T}(t)=c_{0}+c_{2}\cos 2\omega_{0}t+\cdots
\qquad c_{0}\sim 0.5-0.8\;\;,\;\;c_{2}\sim 0.3-0.5$$

and $c_{0}^{2}$ up converts the ${\rm flicker}$,
$1/f$, noise of $I_{SS}$ to $1/f^{3}$ close in
by AM-FM, Groszkowski, varactor, $C_{gs,nl}$,
modulation, and $c_{2}^{2}$ down converts the {\it white}
power around $2\omega_{0}$ to $\omega_{0}\pm \Delta\omega$
{\it etc.}
$I_{SS}(t)=I_{SS}+i_{n,T}(t)$,
$i_{n,T}(\Delta \omega )$ mixes with $\omega_{0}$,
$i_{n,T}(2\omega_{0}\pm \Delta \omega )$ mixes with
$\omega_{0}$ to $\Delta \omega$ according to

$$i_{D1}+i_{D2}= I_{SS}+i_{n,T}(t) + {\cal O}(v_{X,Y}^{2})$$
$$v_{P}(t)=V_{P0}+V_{P2}\cos 2\omega_{0}t+\cdots$$

so that $S_{\phi}(\Delta \omega )\propto 
\Gamma_{T,rms}^{2}S_{I_{SS}}(\Delta \omega )$.

$C_{T}$ shunts $i_{n,T}$ to ground at
$\vert \omega \vert \gg (r_{0T}C_{T})^{-1}$,
in particular

$${\vert i_{n,T}(2\omega_{0})\vert^{2}\over \vert 1+j2\omega_{0}
r_{0T}C_{T}\vert^{2}}\approx 
{\vert i_{n,T}(2\omega_{0})\vert^{2}\over (2\omega_{0}r_{0T}C_{T})^{2}}$$

and suppresses the $c_{2}^{2}S_{I_{SS}}(2\omega_{0})$ term
and to a large extent the $c_{0}^{2}S_{I_{SS}}(\Delta\omega)$
UPSIDE low frequency $1/f$ by decreasing $V_{P2}$
and the effective NMF, Samori, {\it et al}, and
decreasing the {\it impulse sensitivity} during the
zero crossing when $M_{1}-M_{2}$ are both on.

In the normal $1-5\,{\rm GHz}$ range that is:

* $1/f^{2}$ thermal floor $\propto c_{2}^{2}
S_{I_{SS}}(2\omega_{0})/P_{s}$ is reduced by
$\vert Z_{T}(2\omega_{0})\vert^{2}\propto (2\omega_{0}C_{T})^{-2}$.
Typically $2-6\,{\rm dB}$ with $C_{T}$ alone
for $C_{T}\approx (2\omega_{0}R_{T})^{-1}$ to
$10\times$ that, {\it i. e.} ${\cal O}({\rm pF})$
to ${\cal O}(10\,{\rm pF})$.

* $1/f^{3}$, $1/f$ up conversion, $\propto
c_{0}^{2}S_{I_{SS},1/f}(\Delta\omega )$, is drastically
reduced because $V_{P}(t)$ no longer follows
$i_{n,T}(\Delta\omega )$ via the $2\omega_{0}$
rectification and the AM-FM conversion

$$\Delta \omega_{0}\approx
{K_{0}\over 2}{\Delta I_{SS}\over I_{SS}}\approx
{K_{0}\over 2}{v_{P}\over V_{ov}}$$

with $K_{0}=\partial \omega_{0}/\partial V_{P}$ via the
non linear $C(V)$ of the tank, is suppressed.
Hegazi reports $\sim 7-10\,{\rm dB}$ at
$\Delta\omega = 2\pi\times 1\,{\rm MHz}$ and
$\omega_{1/f^{3}}$ moving from $\sim 2\times 10^{5}\,{\rm Hz}$
to $\sim 3\times 10^{4}\,{\rm Hz}$ in $1.1\,{\rm GHz}$
bipolar and $5\,{\rm GHz}$ CMOS, Andreani {\it et al}
similar.

Formally $C_{T}$ narrows the NMF and lowers
$\Gamma_{T,rms}$.

> {\it Remark:} With $C_{T}$ alone the circuit
> shunts its own $2\omega_{0}$ common mode current
> generated by the $M_{1}-M_{2}$ commutation to ground.
> I. e. the $Q$ at $2\omega_{0}$ is killed,
> $V_{P2}\to 0$, the pair loads the tank during
> the cross over with $2/g_{m}$ and the swing
> $V_{X,Y}\approx I_{SS}R_{p}$ drops.
> The $F$ due to the $M_{1}-M_{2}$ pair itself then
> goes up.
> So the improvement saturates and for $C_{T}\to\infty$,
> a. c. ground at $P$, it reverses.  There is an
> optimum $C_{T,opt}\approx 2-5\times (2\omega_{0}
> R_{T})^{-1}$ for the bare circuit of the figure.
> The full ``filtering technique'' interposes a
> choke $L_{T}$ between $P$ and $I_{SS}$ so that
> $L_{T}\parallel C_{T}$ is a {\it high} impedance
> $\approx \omega_{T}L_{T}Q_{T}$ for the oscillator's
> own $2\omega_{0}$ current, preserving $V_{P2}$ and
> the hard commutation, but a {\it low} impedance to
> ground for the $I_{SS}$ noise, {\it i. e.} it is made
> to resonate,

> $$\omega_{T}={1\over \sqrt{L_{T}C_{T}}}\approx 2\omega_{0}$$

> $L_{T}$ can be the parasitic bond wire or an
> explicit ${\cal O}({\rm nH})$ inductor and/or the
> tail device capacitance. In that tuned form the
> Hegazi filter gives the quoted $8-15\,{\rm dB}$
> close in and $3-6\,{\rm dB}$ far out lower
> ${\cal L}$, essentially for the price of the
> area of $C_{T}$ and $L_{T}$ and a somewhat larger
> start up $g_{m}R>1$ requirement and cm settling time
> $\sim r_{0T}C_{T}$.  $kT/C_{T}$ itself mixed down is
> normally negligible.  See E. Hegazi {\it et al},
> {\it IEEE JSSC} {\bf 36}, 1928 (2001);
> P. Andreani {\it et al}, {\it JSSC} {\bf 37}, 342
> (2002); C. Samori {\it et al}, {\it JSSC} {\bf 37},
> 244 (2002).

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It recognizes an optimum and that excessive CT can worsen phase noise, but mainly attributes the improvement to filtering tail-current noise. It misses the class-C peak-current mechanism and Razavi's key degradation mechanisms; its tank-loading explanation does not capture them.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in the figure. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
With ${\rm T}={\rm tail}$ distinguish
$$i_{nT}({\rm th.})~~{\rm at}~~2\omega _{o}~~
{\rm and}~~i_{nT}({\rm LF},1/f)~{\rm at}~\Delta \omega $$
the so called {\it Hegazy} filter {\it a la}
Hajimiri for the cyclostationary ${\mit \Gamma }(t)$.

In a normally balanced way, with ${r_{oT}\to \infty }$ the
tail is a common mode.  To first order $v_{nT}$ does not
produce ${\rm FM}$.
To second order it does

* a current $I_{SS}+i_{nT}$ at $2\omega _{o}$ develops a
voltage

$$v_{nP}=i_{nT}Z_{P}\qquad 
Z_{P}^{-1}=g_{oT}+j\omega C_{P0}+j\omega C_{T}\tag{1}$$

at $2\omega _{o}$ which is mixed by the
${f_{p}}(t)=I_{1}(t)/I_{SS}$ {\it i.~e.} the
commutating function of the pair, whose second Fourier
coefficient is $c_{2}\ne 0$, down to $\omega _{o}$ and
appears as additive ${\rm AM}$ and, trough the
${\rm Am}\to {\mit \Phi}{\rm m}$ conversion of the
non linear ${\rm C}$'s, of the varactor, of the
Groszkowski effect and of any ${\rm C}_{gs}-{\rm C}_{gd}$
modulation as ${\mit \Phi}{\rm m}$

$$S_{{\mit \Phi}}(\Delta \omega )=
 \left|c_{2}Z_{P}(2\omega _{o})\right|^{2}
  S_{i_{nT}}(2\omega _{o}\pm \Delta \omega )\tag{2}$$

so that with $C_{T}=0$, $|Z_{P}|\approx 1/\omega C_{P0}$,
normally a ${\rm k\Omega }$ at $2\omega _{o}$, the
white noise of the tail at $2\omega _{o}$ is normally
the dominant contribution to the $1/f^{2}$ ${\cal L}$;

* the ${\rm LF}$ noise $i_{nT}(\Delta \omega )$ is
up converted by the same $c_{2}$,

$$S_{{\mit \Phi}}(\Delta \omega )=
 c_{0}^{2}S_{i_{nT}}(\Delta \omega ),\qquad 
 c_{0}={1\over {T_{o}}}\int_{0}^{T_{o}}{\mit \Gamma }
 (t){{I_{S}(t)}\over {I_{SS}}}\,dt \tag{3}$$

${\mit \Gamma }(t)$ the Hajimiri impulse sensitivity
function and $I_{S}(t)=I_{1}(t)+I_{2}(t)$
the cyclostationary noise modulating function.  $c_{0}$
is the ${\rm dc}$ value of the effective ${\rm ISF}$
${\mit \Gamma }_{{\rm eff}}={\mit \Gamma }(t)I_{S}(t)/I_{SS}$.
For $C_{P0}=0$, $I_{S}=I_{SS}={\rm const.}$ and
$c_{0}={1\over {T_{o}}}\int {\mit \Gamma }dt\ne 0$ if
${\mit \Gamma }$ is asymetric, {\it i.~e.} if the
wave form is asymetric.  Close to commutation both
$M_{1,2}$ are on, $C_{P0}$ must be charged/discharged
by $\Delta Q=C_{P0}\Delta V_{P}$. The charge comes
from the tank.  The wave form becomes asymetric,
$\int{\mit \Gamma }dt\ne 0$ and large, and (3) up
converts the very large $1/f$ noise of $I_{SS}$ and of
$M_{1,2}$ to $1/f^{3}$ close in ${\cal L}$.

$$\begin{aligned}
{\cal L}(\Delta \omega )&\approx 
10\log \left[{1\over {8}}{\omega _{o}^{2}\over {\Delta \omega }^{2}}
{{\mit \Gamma }_{{\rm rms}}^{2}\over {q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}}
{{{\overline {i_{n}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}\over {\Delta \omega }^{2}}
\left(1+{\omega _{1/f}\over {\Delta \omega }}c_{0}^{2}\right)\right] \\
&\propto {FkT\over {2Q^{2}}}{{\omega _{o}^{2}}\over {\Delta \omega }^{2}}
{P_{{\rm sig}}^{-1}}
\end{aligned}\tag{4}$$

$C_{T}$ {\it shorts} (1) at $2\omega _{o}$,

$$\left|Z_{P}(2\omega _{o})\right|\approx {1\over {2\omega _{o}C_{T}}}
\ll \left|Z_{P0}\right|\tag{5}$$

and, if $1/r_{oT}C_{T}\ll \omega _{o}$ filters the
$2\omega _{o}$ thermal noise (2).  In the limit
$C_{T}\to \infty $, $P$ is an ${\rm a.c.}$ ground,
${{dV_{P}}\over {dt}}\to 0$, $I_{S}(t)=I_{SS}+C_{T}\dot V_{P}$
follows the commutation instantaneously, the memory
associated with $C_{P}$ disappears, the wave form can
be made symmetric, ${\mit \Gamma }(t)=-\,{\mit \Gamma }
(t+T_{o}/2)$,

$$\int_{0}^{T_{o}}{\mit \Gamma }_{{\rm eff}}dt=c_{0}\to 0\tag{6}$$

and (3) is suppressed.  In Samori {\it et al.},
Hegazy {\it et al.} $JSSC\;12/01$ language $C_{T}$
{\it linearises} the operation of the pair and suppresses
the ${\rm Am}\to {\mit \Phi}{\rm m}$ conversion due to
${\rm C}_{gs},{\rm C}_{gd},{\rm C}_{db}$ and varactor
modulation by $V_{P}$.  The normal result is for a
correctly dimensioned, {\it i.~e.} $C_{T}$ large enough
that

$$\omega _{p}={1\over {r_{oT}C_{T}}}\ll 2\omega _{o}\tag{7}$$

and normally large with respect to the ordinary parasitic
$C_{P0}\sim 0.2-0.5\,{\rm pF}$, $C_{T}=2-20\,{\rm pF}$
for a ${\rm GHz}$ oscillator,

* $5-10\,{\rm dB}$ lowering of the $1/f^{2}$ plateau
due to (2) and to the increase of the tank swing,
because the pair stays in saturation for a larger
fraction of the period,
* more than one order of magnitude lowering of the
$1/f^{3}$ corner, typically from $200-500\,{\rm kHz}$
to $20-50\,{\rm kHz}$, and $10-15\,{\rm dB}$ lowering
of ${\cal L}$ close in due to (6).  The published
{\it filtering} technique is $C_{T}\parallel L_{T}$
resonating at $2\omega _{o}$ in series with $I_{SS}$,
Fig.1, so that the source of $M_{1,2}$ sees

$$\eqalign{
Z_{P}({\rm LF})&\approx 0\cr
Z_{P}(2\omega _{o})&\to \infty {\rm \;for\;the\;core}\cr
Z_{P}(2\omega _{o})&\approx 0 {\rm \;for\;}I_{SS}}$$

so that the noise of $I_{SS}$ is shorted to ground
while the tank is not loaded at $2\omega _{o}$.

> {\it In text book form: $C_{T}$ is a tail noise
> filter.  Ideally ${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )$ goes down.
> The $1/f^{3}$ ${\cal L}$ is essentially removed.}

With $C_{T}$ alone the loading effect can dominate.
For $Z_{P}\to 0$ the impedance looking into the drain
of the on device goes to $1/g_{m}\parallel r_{o}$ and
the pair loads the tank for the whole conduction angle,
$2{\mit \Phi}_{c}\propto \sqrt{I_{SS}/C_{T}}$,
where both devices are on.  The effective $Q$ is
degraded as

$${1\over {Q_{{\rm eff}}}}={1\over Q_{0}}+
{2{\mit \Phi}_{c}\over {2\pi}}{g_{m}R_{p}\over Q_{0}}$$

and the swing is reduced.  So ${\cal L}$ {\it vs} $C_{T}$
is not monotonic.  From $C_{T}=0$ to $C_{T}\approx
(2-5)C_{P0}$ ${\cal L}$ often goes {\it up}} by $1-2\,{\rm dB}$,
it goes down to a minimum for $C_{T}$ satisfying (7)
or, with $L_{T}$, for

$$\omega _{T}={1\over {\sqrt{L_{T}C_{T}}}}=2\omega _{o}
\tag{8}$$

the {\it optimum} {\it Hegazy} filter, and goes up
again for $C_{T}\to \infty $ because of tank loading,
Groszkowski frequency pulling

$${\Delta \omega \over {\omega _{o}}}\approx
-{1\over {2Q}}{{I_{2}}\over {I_{1}}}\tag{9}$$

which is ${\rm Am}\to {\rm Fm}$ converted to ${\mit \Phi}{\rm m}$,
and ultimately squegging and start up failure if the
common mode resonance

$$\omega _{{\rm CM}}\approx {1\over {\sqrt{(L_{1}\parallel L_{2})C_{T}}}}
\tag{10}$$

is pulled below $\omega _{o}$.  In a normal design the
optimum is broad and the improvement quoted above is
readily obtained.  With $C_{T}$ alone, no $L_{T}$,
the improvement is $3-6\,{\rm dB}$ at the expense of a
somewhat reduced tuning range and a reduced supply
pushing.  The circuit with $C_{T}\to \infty $, {\it i.~e.}
no tail, is the well known low $1/f$ ${\rm FM}$ topology.

See E. Hegazy {\it et al.} {\it A filtering technique to
lower LC oscillator phase noise} J. Solid State Circuits
36, 1928-1934, Dec.2001; Samori {\it et al.} {\it ibid}
35, 244-246, 2000; Hajimiri-Lee {\it JSSC} 33, 179-194,
1998.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly describes a nonmonotonic effect: tail-noise filtering can improve phase noise, while excessive CT can cause tank loading and low-frequency instability/squegging. It omits the class-C peak-current mechanism required for full credit.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in the figure. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
With the usual hand waving the so called {\it
filtering} technique it is a noise filter.Say $X=-Y=
V_{0}\cos \omega _{0}t$.
$$V_{P}=V_{P0}+V_{P2}\cos 2\omega _{0}t+...$$
The tail source $I_{SS}$ with $S_{I}(f)=4kT\gamma
g_{mT}+K_{f}I_{SS}/f$ is normally high $Z$ and all of
its current, current noise included, is forced through
$M_{1}-M_{2}$ into $L_{1},L_{2}$. In the
${\cal L}\left( \Delta \omega \right)$ of
Leeson-Cutler

$${\cal L}\sim 10\log \left[\left(1+
\left({\omega _{0}\over 2Q\Delta \omega }\right)^{2}
\right){F kT\over 2P_{s}}\left(1+{\omega _{1/f^{3}}\over
\Delta \omega }\right)\right]$$

$F=F_{R}+F_{M_{1,2}}+F_{T}$
is dominated, in a properly designed $LC$, by the tail.

In particular in the Hajimiri formulation

$${\cal L}\propto 
\overline {\Gamma _{{\rm eff}}^{2}}\;\;,\;\;
\Gamma _{{\rm eff}}=\Gamma (t)\times \alpha (t)$$

$\Gamma (t)$ is the impulse sensitivity function,
$\alpha (t)=g_{m}(t)/g_{m,max}$ is the cyclostationary
noise modulating function, the tail contributes through
the $2\omega _{0}$ component of $\alpha (t)\Gamma (t)$.

Its low frequency $1/f$ noise, $S_{I}(\Delta \omega )$,
mixed with the $2\omega _{0}$ component of the large
signal operation appears as $S_{\phi }(\omega _{0}\pm
\Delta \omega )$ - the $1/f^{3}$ skirt - and its white
noise $S_{I}(2\omega _{0}\pm \Delta \omega )$ mixed
down with the $2\omega _{0}$ large signal appears as
$S_{\phi }(\omega _{0}\pm \Delta \omega )$ - the
$1/f^{2}$ skirt. I. e. to first order only the noise
of $I_{SS}$ in a band $\Delta \omega$ about $2\omega
_{0}$ and about DC matters, c. f. Samori {\it et al.},
Hegazi {\it et al.} {\sl JSSC 36, 1928, 2001}, Razavi,
{\sl RF Microelectronics}.

Putting $C_{T}$ from $P$ to {\it a.c.} ground puts, for

$$\left| Z_{T}(\omega )\right| =\left| R_{T}\parallel
{1\over j\omega C_{T}}\right| \ll R_{T}$$

a shunt for $\omega \sim 2\omega _{0}$ so that
$i_{n,T}(2\omega _{0}\pm \Delta \omega )$ does not
develop a voltage at $P$ which can frequency modulate
the tank through

* the $C_{gs}-C_{gd}-C_{db}$ non linearity at $P$
* the Groszkowski effect $\Delta \omega _{0}/
\omega _{0}\propto (I_{2}/I_{1})^{2}/Q^{2}$
* the $AM-PM$ of the varactor, if any,
  $K_{V}=d\omega _{0}/dV_{P}$.

In more conventional terms it {\it low pass} filters the
tail source. For $C_{T}\gg C_{p,P}$, the parasitic at
$P$,

$$Z_{P}(j\omega )\approx {1\over j\omega C_{T}}\;\;{\rm for
}\;\; \omega \gg (R_{T}C_{T})^{-1}$$

so that for {\it large} $C_{T}$ the $1/f^{3}$ corner

$$\omega _{1/f^{3}}\propto 
{\overline {\Gamma _{dc,{\rm eff}}^{2}}\over
 \overline {\Gamma _{rms,{\rm eff}}^{2}}}\;
 \omega _{1/f,T} \tag{*}$$

goes nominally $\propto C_{T}^{-1}$ to zero and

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{2}}\propto 
F_{T}\propto {S_{I}(2\omega _{0})\over I_{SS}^{2}}
\left| Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})\right|^{2}$$

goes as $|Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})|^{2}\propto
(\omega _{0}C_{T})^{-2}$.

In round numbers for a $1-2\,{\rm GHz}$ $LC$ with
$L\sim 2-5\,{\rm nH}$, $I_{SS}\sim 2-5\,{\rm mA}$

* $C_{T}=0$ :  ${\cal L}(1\,{\rm MHz})\approx -110$
  ${\rm dBc/Hz}$ , $\omega _{1/f^{3}}/2\pi \approx
  200-500\,{\rm kHz}$
* $C_{T}\sim 2-10\,{\rm pF}$ to ground: $\Delta {\cal
  L}_{1/f^{2}}\approx 3-6\,{\rm dB}$, $\Delta {\cal
  L}_{1/f^{3}}\approx 5-10\,{\rm dB}$, $\omega
  _{1/f^{3}}$ reduced by $2-5\times$, the Hegazi
  {\it et al.} result.

That is the textbook result normally quoted: {\it
a large $C_{T}$ to ground filters the tail and the
phase noise goes down, essentially the $1/f$ induced
$1/f^{3}$ phase noise.}

With the usual caveats that make $C_{T}$ alone
normally a bad idea in detail:

With $C_{T}$ the circuit has a {\it common mode}
tank. For $L_{1}=L_{2}=L$, $C_{D}$ the tank $C$,

$$\omega _{0}^{2}={1\over LC_{D}}\;\;{\rm diff.\;mode}$$

$$\omega _{CM}^{2}\approx {1\over L_{CM}C_{T}}\approx
{2\over LC_{T}}\;\;{\rm com.\;mode}$$

with finite $Q_{CM}=R_{CM}/\omega _{CM}L_{CM}$.
If, as $C_{T}$ is increased from $0$,

$$\omega _{CM}(C_{T})\approx \omega _{0}\;\;{\rm or}\;
2\omega _{0}$$

the common mode $Q$ will magnify the tail noise and
${\cal L}$ {\it peaks} by $10-20\,{\rm dB}$.

$$\left| Z_{P}(j\omega )\right| =
\left| {j\omega L_{CM}\over 1-\omega ^{2}L_{CM}C_{T}}
\right|$$

Hence the customary ${\cal L}$ versus $C_{T}$ curve,
Fig. 2 of Hegazi, goes through a pronounced maximum
for $C_{T}\sim C_{D}/2$ where $\omega _{CM}=\omega
_{0}$ and for $C_{T}\sim C_{D}/8$ where $\omega _{CM}=
2\omega _{0}$. Only for

$$C_{T}\gg C_{D}\;\;,\;\;\omega _{CM}\ll \omega _{0}\tag{**}$$

i. e. $C_{T}\sim 10-40\,{\rm pF}$ on chip or nF off
chip, do you get the filtering action above.

Moreover, made $P$ a.c. ground the sources of $M_{1,2}$
can no longer follow $2\omega _{0}$. The pair spends
a larger fraction of the period in triode, the tank
is loaded by $R_{on}=1/g_{ds}(t)$ during the zero
crossing, $Q_{L}$ falls, and in the rigorous
Hajimiri $\Gamma _{{\rm eff}}$ analysis the {\it
d.c.} value $\Gamma _{dc,{\rm eff}}\ne 0$ that
controls $(*)$ is no longer zero. I. e. the large
signal waveform is made more asymmetric and the
cyclostationary $\alpha (t)$ peaks where $\Gamma (t)$
peaks. For moderate $C_{T}$ the net $\overline
{\Gamma _{{\rm eff}}^{2}}$ and $\Gamma _{dc,{\rm
eff}}$ {\it increase} and the $1/f^{3}$ noise
increases although $Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})$ has
decreased. This is why Andreani, {\it et al.},
Hajimiri, Razavi quote $C_{T}$ alone as {\it
increasing} the close in phase noise.

The robust remedy is the so called Hegazi filter,
Fig. 3 of {\sl JSSC 36,1932}: $C_{T}$ to ground {\it
plus} a $L_{T}$ in series with $I_{SS}$,

$$Z_{P}(j\omega )={1\over j\omega C_{T}+1/(j\omega
L_{T}+R_{T})}$$

tuned so

$$\omega _{p}={1\over \sqrt{L_{T}C_{T}}}=2\omega _{0}$$

At $2\omega _{0}$ $Z_{P}$ is high, $\approx Q_{p}^{2}
R_{T}$, so the $2\omega _{0}$ current of the pair is
preserved - no triode loading, $\Gamma _{dc}=0$ - and
the second harmonic is allowed to resonate in phase
with the fundamental to make the waveform more square,
$\Gamma _{rms}$ smaller. At all other frequencies
$Z_{P}\approx 1/j\omega C_{T}$ small, so the broadband
thermal and $1/f$ noise of $R_{T}$ is still shorted.
Then

$$\Delta {\cal L}\approx 8-15\,{\rm dB}$$

with $\omega _{1/f^{3}}$ reduced an order of
magnitude can be obtained reliably and is the
conventional tail filtered $LC$ VCO. With $C_{T}$ alone
you get nominally $\sim 1/2$ of that improvement for
$(**)$ and a degradation for intermediate $C_{T}$,
commonly loosely described as $C_{T}$ {\it increases
phase noise} unless resonated with $L_{T}$ at
$2\omega _{0}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It recognizes a non-monotonic effect and describes transistor-waveform/triode-related degradation, but attributes the improvement to tail-noise filtering and misses the class-C mechanism of peak tank currents exceeding ISS. It also omits the instability possible at very large CT.

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
In the small signal sense the {\it cold} circuit is
a parallel $G\parallel L\parallel C_{T}$ with

$$C_{T}=C_{MIM}+C_{db}+C_{gd}+C_{gs}+...$$

the total capacity to ground at $X_{i},Y_{i}$ and
$G=1/R_{p}=1/Q\omega _{0}L$, $B=\omega C_{T}-1/\omega L$,
$\omega _{0}^{2}=1/LC_{T}$ in the differentiated form
$L_{d}=2L$, $C_{d}=C_{T}/2$ so that $L_{d}C_{d}=LC_{T}$.
Put

$$V_{1}=X_{1}-Y_{1}\qquad V_{2}=X_{2}-Y_{2}$$

and, with the usual square law normalisation,
$g_{m}\propto I_{SS}$, $g_{m1}\propto I_{1}$,
$g_{m1}/g_{m}=I_{1}/I_{SS}$ for equal geometries,
the small signal KCL at the two tanks is, to within a
sign which is the $\pm 90^{0}$ wiring of the figure,

$$\eqalign{
YV_{1}&=g_{m}V_{1}+g_{m1}V_{2}\cr
YV_{2}&=g_{m}V_{2}\mp g_{m1}V_{1}\cr}\qquad 
Y=G+jB\tag{1}$$

with the upper sign for the in phase wiring and the
lower sign for the cross wiring in Fig.1.  In matrix form

$$\left[ \matrix{Y-g_{m}&-g_{m1}\cr 
\pm g_{m1}&Y-g_{m}\cr}\right]\left[\matrix{V_{1}\cr V_{2}\cr}
\right]=0 \tag{2}$$

so that, for $V_{1,2}\ne 0$,

$${\rm Det}=0\;\;:\;\;(Y-g_{m})^{2}+g_{m1}^{2}=0\tag{3}$$

$${\rm i.e.}\;\;Y=g_{m}\pm jg_{m1}\tag{4}$$

and, with $Y=G+jB$, the Barkhausen
${\rm Re\,}Y=g_{m}$, ${\rm Im\,}Y=\pm g_{m1}$,

$$\eqalign{
G&=g_{m} \tag{5a}\cr
B&=\omega C_{T}-{1\over{\omega L}}=\pm g_{m1}\tag{5b}}$$

(5a) is the ordinary start up condition

$$g_{m}R_{p}\ge 1\qquad R_{p}=Q\omega _{0}L={1\over G}
\tag{6}$$

the core pair has to cancel the tank loss.  (5b) is the
frequency condition.  With $\omega _{0}^{2}=1/LC_{T}$,

$$\omega ^{2}LC_{T}\mp g_{m1}L\omega -1=0 \tag{7}$$

$$\omega _{1,2}= \mp {{g_{m1}}\over{2C_{T}}}
+\sqrt{\omega _{0}^{2}+\left({{g_{m1}}\over{2C_{T}}}\right)^{2}}
 \tag{8}$$

$${\omega _{1,2}\approx \omega _{0}\mp {{g_{m1}}\over{2C_{T}}}
\qquad g_{m1}\ll \omega _{0}C_{T}\tag{9}$$

The two roots are the two normal modes of the coupled
system.  For the straight wiring $B=0$ is a solution,
$V_{2}=V_{1}$, the conventional in phase mode

$$\omega _{ip}= \omega _{0}={1\over{\sqrt{LC_{T}}}}
\qquad f_{ip}={1\over{2\pi \sqrt{LC_{T}}}} \tag{10}$$

differential inductance $2L$ with differential capacity
$C_{T}/2$, in single ended notation (10).  For the cross
wiring $|V_{2}|=|V_{1}|$,

$$V_{2}= \pm jV_{1}\tag{11}$$

the two tanks oscillate in quadrature.  The susceptance
$g_{m1}$ injected by the {\it coupling} pair in quadrature
with $V_{1}$ pulls the oscillation off $\omega _{0}$ by

$$\Delta \omega =\pm {{g_{m1}}\over{2C_{T}}}\tag{12}$$

i. e. in compact form, with (8),

$$f_{q}= {1\over{2\pi }}\left[
\sqrt{{1\over{LC_{T}}}+\left({{g_{m1}}\over{2C_{T}}}\right)^{2}}
\pm {{g_{m1}}\over{2C_{T}}}\right]
\approx f_{0}\pm {{g_{m1}}\over{4\pi C_{T}}}\tag{13}$$

For equal device geometries $g_{m1}/g_{m}=I_{1}/I_{SS}$ so
that with $g_{m}=G=1/R_{p}$,

$${{\Delta \omega }\over{\omega _{0}}}\approx 
\pm {1\over{2Q}}{{I_{1}}\over{I_{SS}}}\qquad 
Q=R_{p}/\omega _{0}L \tag{14}$$

and, to ${\cal O}(g_{m1}^{2})$,

$$\omega _{q}\approx \omega _{0}\sqrt{1\pm {{I_{1}}\over{I_{SS}}}}
\approx \omega _{0}\left[1\pm {{I_{1}}\over{2I_{SS}}}\right]
\tag{15}$$

The sign depends on which of the two quadrature phases
is taken as reference.  Normally the mode with the largest
small signal loop gain, the $+$ sign in (8), i. e. $\omega
>\omega _{0}$, is the stable quadrature mode.  For weak
coupling, $I_{1}\ll I_{SS}$, $g_{m1}\ll \omega _{0}C_{T}$,
the pulling is a few per cent and is normally neglected
in a hand estimate,

$$f_{osc}\approx f_{0}={1\over{2\pi }}{\rm Re\,}
{1\over{\sqrt{LC_{T}}}}\tag{16}$$

the ordinary (differential) $LC$ resonance at $X_{i}-Y_{i}$.
E.{\eightrm G}. with the usual on chip $L=1-5\,{\rm nH}$,
$C_{T}=0.5-2\,{\rm pF}$, $Q\sim 5-10$, $R_{p}\sim 0.2-
1\,{\rm k\Omega }$, $g_{m}\sim 1-5\,{\rm mS}$,

$$f_{0}\sim 2-7\,{\rm GHz}\qquad 
\Delta f_{q}\sim {g_{m1}\over{4\pi C_{T}}}\sim 0.1-0.5\,{\rm GHz}
\tag{17}$$

for $I_{1}/I_{SS}\sim 1/3-1/2$.  In round numbers
$\Delta f_{q}/f_{0}\sim 5-15\%$.

With the metal ``X'' drawn in the figure literally as a
short $X_{1}=Y_{2}$, $Y_{1}=X_{2}$ the two physical coils
on each side are in parallel to ground, in series
differentially, so that the cold differential inductance is
$L_{d}=2(L\parallel L)=L$ and, in single ended notation,

$$f_{00}={1\over{2\pi \sqrt{(L/2)C_{T}}}}=
{{\sqrt{2}}\over{2\pi \sqrt{LC_{T}}}}\tag{18}$$

$\sqrt{2}$ times (10), and (8)--(15) apply with
$L\rightarrow L/2$.  Neglecting the $g_{m1}$ pulling this is
normally quoted simply as $f_{osc}\approx (2\pi\sqrt{LC})^{-1}$
($\sqrt{2}(2\pi\sqrt{LC})^{-1}$ with the literal $X$ short)
with $C$ the total tank capacity.  Any of the forms
(8), (13), (15) is accepted as the ``pulled'' quadrature
frequency.  In particular for the conventional $L_{d}=2L$
notation $f_{q}\approx f_{0}\sqrt{1+I_{1}/I_{SS}}$.  For
$I_{1}\ll I_{SS}$ this is indistinguishable from $f_{0}$.

> {\it Remark:}  In differential $2L$, $C/2$ notation
> $f_{0}=1/2\pi\sqrt{2L\cdot C/2}=1/2\pi\sqrt{LC}$.  The
> in phase normal mode is at $f_{0}$, the (stable)
> quadrature normal mode at $f_{0}+\Delta f$ given above.
> The circuit will normally lock on the quadrature mode and
> deliver $V_{X1}=V_{0}\cos\omega_{q}t$,
> $V_{Y1}=-V_{0}\cos\omega_{q}t$,
> $V_{X2}=V_{0}\sin\omega_{q}t$,
> $V_{Y2}=-V_{0}\sin\omega_{q}t$, i. e. four phases $0,\pi
> /2,\pi ,3\pi /2$ at $\omega_{q}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It gives the tank resonance and the correct coupling shift, Δω/ω₀ ≈ (I₁/Iₛₛ)/(2Q). However, it later gives a pulled-frequency expression without the required 1/Q factor, contradicting that result and overstating the shift.

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
With an ideal $G_{p}=0$ tank it is the
Rofougaran-Razavi injection locked loop.
Put for one node

$${\cal Y}_{p}(p)=G_{p}+pC_{p}+{1\over {pL}}\qquad 
p=s=j\omega \tag{*}$$

$C_{p}$ is the total capacity to the
incremental ground on the $X$, $Y$ node : the intentional
capacity plus $C_{gs}+C_{gb}+C_{gd}$ of the two $n$ MOS
in parallel on the node plus the capacity of the coil.
For a conventional differential capacity $C_{d}$ between
$X$ and $Y$ $C_{p}=C_{d}/2$.
$G_{p}=R_{p}^{-1}$ is the loss of the coil
$Q_{0}=R_{p}/\omega _{0}L=R_{p}\omega _{0}C_{p}$,
$\omega _{0}^{2}=1/LC_{p}$ is the unperturbed parallel
resonance.
In the small signal incremental circuit let

$$\eqalign{
g_{m}&=g_{m,ss} \cr 
g_{m,c}&=g_{m1}\cr}
\qquad {g_{m,c}\over {g_{m}}}\approx {{I_{1}}\over {I_{ss}}}
      \tag{**}$$

be the small signal $g_{m}$ of the $I_{ss}$,
differential pair and of the $I_{1}$, injection, pair.
Put

$$\eqalign{
V_{I}&=X_{1}-Y_{1}\cr 
V_{Q}&=X_{2}-Y_{2}\cr}$$

and, with the conventional sign,

$$V_{G,I}=G_{1l}-G_{1r}\qquad V_{G,Q}=G_{2l}-G_{2r}$$

so that for one side, e. {\it g.} the $I$ side, in the
incremental circuit, Fig.1, with ${{1}\over {pL}}+pC_{p}=
{\cal Y}_{p}-G_{p}$,

$$\eqalign{
0&={\cal Y}_{p}X_{1}+g_{m}\left(Y_{1}-S_{0}\right)
        +g_{m,c}\left(G_{1l}-S_{c}\right)\cr
0&={\cal Y}_{p}Y_{1}+g_{m}\left(X_{1}-S_{0}\right)
        +g_{m,c}\left(G_{1r}-S_{c}\right)\cr}\tag{1}$$

With an ideal tail ${\cal Y}_{t}^{-1}=0$

$$S_{0}={{X_{1}+Y_{1}}\over 2}\qquad 
  S_{c}={{G_{1l}+G_{1r}}\over 2} \tag{2}$$

so that, subtracting,

$${\cal Y}_{p}V_{I}-g_{m}V_{I}+g_{m,c}V_{G,I}=0\tag{3a}$$
and the same for the $Q$ side

$${\cal Y}_{p}V_{Q}-g_{m}V_{Q}+g_{m,c}V_{G,Q}=0\tag{3b}$$

with

$$V_{G,I}=aV_{Q}\qquad V_{G,Q}=bV_{I}\qquad a,b=\pm 1\tag{4}$$

according to the way the two wires $X_{1},Y_{1}\to
G_{2l},G_{2r}$ and $X_{2},Y_{2}\to G_{1l},G_{1r}$ are
strapped. $a=+1$ is ''straight'', $a=-1$ ''reversed''.
In the figure as normally drawn the two straps are of
opposite sign and the loop is non reciprocal.  In the
literal drawing of Fig.1 they are of the same sign.

*  {\it Symmetric strapping} $ab=+1$.

Eqs.(3) give

$$\left({\cal Y}_{p}-g_{m}\right)V_{I}+ag_{m,c}V_{Q}=0\tag{5a}$$
$$\left({\cal Y}_{p}-g_{m}\right)V_{Q}+bg_{m,c}V_{I}=0\tag{5b}$$

$$\left({\cal Y}_{p}-g_{m}\right)^{2}-ab\,g_{m,c}^{2}=0
\tag{6}$$

i. e. $ab=+1$,

$${\cal Y}_{p}-g_{m}=\pm g_{m,c}\tag{7}$$

With ${\cal Y}_{p}=G_{p}+jB_{p}$,
$B_{p}=\omega C_{p}-1/\omega L$,

$$\eqalign{
G_{p}-g_{m}&=\pm g_{m,c}\cr
B_{p}&=0\cr}\tag{8}$$

The two eigen modes $V_{Q}=\mp V_{I}$ are the conventional
in phase and anti phase modes.  Apart from the
$\pm g_{m,c}$ change of the start up condition the
circuit oscillates, to ${\cal O}(1/Q_{0})$,
at the unperturbed tank frequency,

$$B_{p}=0\;\;,\qquad 
\omega _{osc}=\omega _{0}={{1}\over {\sqrt{LC_{p}}}}
\tag{9}$$

$$f_{0}={{1}\over {2\pi \sqrt{LC_{p}}}}=
{{1}\over {2\pi \sqrt{LC_{d}/2}}}\tag{9a}$$

With the normal $0.5-2{\rm nH}$ integrated coil and
$C_{p}\sim 0.3-1.0{\rm pF}$,
$f_{0}\sim 3-10{\rm GHz}$,

$$f_{0}\approx {{5{\rm GHz}}\over 
\sqrt{L/{\rm nH}\;C_{p}/{\rm pF}}}\tag{9b}$$

e. {\it g.} $L=1{\rm nH}$, $C_{p}=0.5{\rm pF}$,
$f_{0}\approx 7{\rm GHz}$.
$C_{p}$ is to be taken large signal, $C_{p}\to
C_{p}+ \langle C_{gs}\rangle $ etc.  The $g_{m}\to
\langle g_{m}\rangle =2I_{ss}/V_{osc}$ in the
large signal steady state locks to $G_{p}\mp g_{m,c}$.
If $\langle g_{m}\rangle >G_{p}+|g_{m,c}|$ both modes
can start, the ``in phase'' mode $V_{Q}= -{\rm sgn}(a)
V_{I}$ with $\langle g_{m}\rangle +|g_{m,c}|=G_{p}$ is
normally the stable one.  For $|g_{m,c}|\ll g_{m}$
the distinction disappears.

*  {\it Anti symmetric - quadrature - strapping} $ab=-1$.

This is the normally quoted quadrature connection,
one strap straight, one strap reversed.  Then from (6)

$$\left({\cal Y}_{p}-g_{m}\right)^{2}+g_{m,c}^{2}=0\tag{10}$$

$${\cal Y}_{p}-g_{m}= \pm jg_{m,c}\tag{11}$$

$$\eqalign{
G_{p}-g_{m}&=0\cr
B_{p}&=\pm g_{m,c}\cr}\tag{12}$$

so that the two eigen vectors are in quadrature,

$$V_{Q}= \pm jV_{I}\tag{13}$$

i. e. with the usual sign

$$\eqalign{
X_{1}-Y_{1}&=V_{0}\cos \omega _{osc}t\cr
X_{2}-Y_{2}&=V_{0}\sin \omega _{osc}t\cr}\tag{14}$$

up to the interchange $I\rightleftharpoons Q$,
and

$$\omega _{osc}C_{p}-{1\over {\omega _{osc}L}}=
\pm g_{m,c}\tag{15}$$

$$C_{p}\omega _{osc}^{2}\mp g_{m,c}\omega _{osc}
-{1\over L}=0\tag{16}$$

$$\omega _{osc}^{\pm}=
{{\pm g_{m,c}+\sqrt{g_{m,c}^{2}+4C_{p}/L}}\over {2C_{p}}}
=\sqrt{\omega _{0}^{2}+\left({{g_{m,c}}\over {2C_{p}}}
\right)^{2}}\pm {{g_{m,c}}\over {2C_{p}}}\tag{17}$$

In large signal $g_{m,c}\to \langle g_{m,c}\rangle $,
$g_{m}\to \langle g_{m}\rangle $, $\langle g_{m}\rangle
=G_{p}$ for the steady state.  For weak coupling,

$$|g_{m,c}|\ll \omega _{0}C_{p}=Q_{0}G_{p}\tag{18}$$

$$\omega _{osc}^{\pm}\approx
\omega _{0}\pm {{g_{m,c}}\over {2C_{p}}}
=\omega _{0}\left[1\pm {{g_{m,c}}\over {2\omega _{0}C_{p}}}
\right]=\omega _{0}\left[1\pm {{1}\over {2Q_{0}}}
{{g_{m,c}}\over {G_{p}}}\right]\tag{19}$$

With (**), $g_{m,c}/G_{p}\approx
(g_{m}/G_{p})(I_{1}/I_{ss})\approx I_{1}/I_{ss}$ in the
steady state, $\langle g_{m}\rangle =G_{p}$,

$$\omega _{osc}\approx \omega _{0}
\left[1\pm {{1}\over {2Q_{0}}}{{I_{1}}\over {I_{ss}}}
\right]\approx \omega _{0}\pm {{\langle g_{m,c}\rangle}
\over {2C_{p}}}\tag{20}$$

$$\Delta f\approx \pm f_{0}{{I_{1}}\over {2Q_{0}I_{ss}}}
\approx \pm {{\langle g_{m,c}\rangle}\over {4\pi C_{p}}}
\tag{20a}$$

So to ${\cal O}(Q_{0}^{-1}I_{1}/I_{ss})$ the quadrature
oscillator still oscillates at the single tank frequency
(9).  The coupling only locks the two tanks in quadrature
and pulls the frequency by $\sim g_{m,c}/2C_{p}$.
For e. {\it g.} $g_{m,c}\sim 2-5{\rm mA/V}$,
$C_{p}\sim 0.5{\rm pF}$, $|\Delta f|\sim 0.3-0.8{\rm GHz}$,
normally $|\Delta f|/f_{0}\sim 5-10\%$ for $Q_{0}\sim 5-10$
and $I_{1}/I_{ss}\sim 0.3-1$.  In the strong coupling
limit (17) must be used.  The two signs in (17) correspond
to the two senses of rotation $V_{Q}=+jV_{I}$,
$V_{Q}=-jV_{I}$; only one is stable for a given sign of
$a=-b$, the other is the image obtained by interchanging
the two tanks.  Putting $g_{m,c}\to \langle g_{m,c}\rangle
\approx (2/\pi )g_{m,c}$ for the usual current limited
saturated switching gives the usual $\sim 20\%$ correction.

In compact form, with $m=g_{m,c}/g_{m}$,

$$\left|{\cal Y}_{p}(j\omega _{osc})\right|
 =\sqrt{g_{m}^{2}+g_{m,c}^{2}}\tag{21}$$

and $\arg {\cal Y}_{p}= \mp \tan ^{-1}m$.
For $ab=+1$ this reduces to $|\,{\cal Y}_{p}|=|g_{m}\pm
g_{m,c}|$, $\arg {\cal Y}_{p}=0$, {\it i.e.} (9).

Any of (9), (17), (19) is normally quoted as ``the
oscillation frequency'', the ${\cal O}(g_{m,c}/C_{p})$
pulling being often neglected, $\omega _{osc}\approx
\omega _{0}=1/\sqrt{LC_{p}}$.  The common source nodes
$S_{0},S_{c}$ move at $2\omega _{osc}$ and can be used as
a frequency doubler.  The amplitude condition is
$\langle g_{m}\rangle >G_{p}$, $\langle g_{m}\rangle \pm
\langle g_{m,c}\rangle >G_{p}$ in the symmetric case.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly gives the tank resonance and derives the quadrature coupling-induced shift, including the weak-coupling form Δω ≈ ±(gmc/Gp)ω0/(2Q) and its steady-state current-ratio equivalent. The extra exact solution and topology discussion do not undermine the estimate.

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
In the loose coupling limit the four tanks are
identical and uncoupled.  Put for one side, Fig.1,

$${\cal Y}_{t}=G_{t}+sC_{t}+{1\over {sL}}\qquad 
C_{t}=C+2C_{gd}+C_{gs}+C_{db}\tag{1}$$

$$G_{t}={1\over {R_{p}}}={R_{s}\over {\omega _{0}^{2}L^{2}}}
\qquad \omega _{0}^{2}={1\over {LC_{t}}}\tag{2}$$

and, in the conventional small signal notation,

$$g_{0}=g_{m}{\cal I}_{SS}\qquad 
  g_{c}=g_{m}{\cal I}_{1}\tag{3}$$

$$g_{0}\approx \sqrt{2k_{n}{W\over L}{\cal I}_{SS}}\;\;,
\qquad g_{c}\approx \sqrt{2k_{n}{W\over L}{\cal I}_{1}}
\approx g_{0}\sqrt{{\cal I}_{1}\over {\cal I}_{SS}}}\tag{4}$$

for the square law, $g_{c}/g_{0}={\cal I}_{1}/{\cal I}_{SS}$
for the bipolar.  With the sign convention of Fig.1 let

$$V_{1}=V_{X1}-V_{Y1}\qquad V_{2}=V_{X2}-V_{Y2}\tag{5}$$

$${\cal Y}_{t}V_{X1}+g_{0}V_{Y1}+g_{c}V_{G3}=0\tag{6}$$
$${\cal Y}_{t}V_{Y1}+g_{0}V_{X1}+g_{c}V_{G4}=0\tag{7}$$

etc.  E. {\rm g.} for the conventional Rofougaran
connection

$$\eqalign{
V_{G3}&=V_{X2}\;\;V_{G4}=V_{Y2}\cr
V_{G5}&=V_{Y1}\;\;V_{G6}=V_{X1}\cr}\tag{8}$$

so that, differentially,

$$\eqalign{
\left({\cal Y}_{t}-g_{0}\right)V_{1}+g_{c}V_{2}&=0\cr
-g_{c}V_{1}+\left({\cal Y}_{t}-g_{0}\right)V_{2}&=0\cr}\tag{9}$$

The conventional parallel connection is obtained with the
$+$ sign in both lines.  (8) is the anti parallel or
quadrature connection.  In compact form

$${\rm det}\left[{\cal Y}_{t}-g_{0}\pm jg_{c}\right]=0\tag{10}$$

$${\cal Y}(s)=g_{0}\pm jg_{c}\tag{11}$$

i.{\rm e.} in the linear small signal sense the circuit
has two complex conjugate pairs of poles.  With (1)

$$G_{t}+sC_{t}+{1\over {sL}}=g_{0}\pm jg_{c}\tag{12}$$

At threshold $G_{t}=g_{0}$ in the large signal sense,
$G_{t}=g_{0{\rm eff}}(A)<g_{0}$, and (12) gives for
$s=j\omega $ the steady state, Barkhausen, condition

$$j\left(\omega C_{t}-{1\over {\omega L}}\right)=\pm jg_{c}\tag{13}$$

$${\rm Re}:G_{t}=g_{0{\rm eff}}\tag{14}$$
$${\rm Im}:\;\omega C_{t}-{1\over {\omega L}}=\pm g_{c}\tag{15}$$

i. {\rm e.} apart from the ordinary $g_{0}R_{p}>1$ start
up condition the tank is pulled off its natural resonance
$\omega _{0}=1/\sqrt{LC_{t}}$ by the quadrature injection.
(15) is

$$\omega ^{2}\mp {g_{c}\over C_{t}}\omega -\omega _{0}^{2}=0\tag{16}$$

$$\omega _{1,2}={1\over 2}\left[\pm {g_{c}\over C_{t}}+
\sqrt{\left({g_{c}\over C_{t}}\right)^{2}+4\omega _{0}^{2}}\;
\right]>0\tag{17}$$

For $g_{c}\ll \omega _{0}C_{t}$, $g_{c}\sqrt{L/C_{t}}\ll 1$,
i. {\rm e.} for loose coupling ${\cal I}_{1}\ll {\cal I}_{SS}$,

$$\omega _{1,2}\approx \omega _{0}\pm {g_{c}\over {2C_{t}}}
-{1\over 8}{g_{c}^{2}\over {C_{t}^{2}\omega _{0}}}+\cdots \tag{18}$$

$$\Delta \omega \approx {g_{c}\over {2C_{t}}}
={1\over 2}\omega _{0}g_{c}\sqrt{L\over C_{t}}
={1\over 2}{g_{c}\over g_{0}}{1\over Q}\omega _{0}\tag{19}$$

$Q=R_{p}\sqrt{C_{t}/L}=\omega _{0}C_{t}R_{p}$ is the tank
$Q$,
$$f_{0}={1\over {2\pi \sqrt{LC_{t}}}}\tag{20}$$
is the ordinary differential $LC$ frequency, a few
${\rm GHz}$ for a normal monolithic spiral, $L\sim 2-10\,{\rm nH}$,
$C_{t}\sim 0.2-2\,{\rm pF}$,

$$f_{0}\approx {5\over {\sqrt{L_{{\rm nH}}C_{{\rm pF}}}}}\,{\rm GHz}\tag{21}$$

and the two eigen modes are split by

$$\Delta f\approx {g_{c}\over {4\pi C_{t}}}\tag{22}$$

on either side of $f_{0}$.  In the $\pm $ in (17)--(18)
the upper sign is the in phase, $V_{1}=V_{2}$, the lower
sign the quadrature, $V_{1}=\pm jV_{2}$, mode.  With the
sign convention (8) the stable large signal mode is the
low side

$$f_{Q}\approx f_{0}-{g_{c}\over {4\pi C_{t}}}
\approx f_{0}\left[1-{1\over {2Q}}{g_{c}\over g_{0}}\right]
\tag{23}$$

the other sign with the opposite twist.  The $+$ sign in
(9), conventional parallel coupling, gives
${\cal Y}_{t}-g_{0}=\pm g_{c}$, {\rm i.e.} no frequency
pulling to first order, the two modes are separated in
threshold, $G_{t}=g_{0}\pm g_{c}$.

For all practical purposes, $g_{c}\ll g_{0}$,

> {\it the circuit oscillates in quadrature,
> $V_{X1}=-V_{Y1}$, $V_{X2}=-V_{Y2}$, $V_{X1}=\pm jV_{X2}$,
> at the tank resonance (20) to ${\cal O}(g_{c}/\omega _{0}
> C_{t})$.}

E. {\rm g.} $L=5\,{\rm nH}$, $C_{t}=0.5\,{\rm pF}$,
$f_{0}\approx 3.2\,{\rm GHz}$, $g_{c}=2\,{\rm mA/V}$,
$\Delta f\approx g_{c}/4\pi C_{t}\approx 300\,{\rm MHz}$,
$g_{c}/\omega _{0}C_{t}\approx 0.2$.  With
${\cal I}_{1}/{\cal I}_{SS}\approx 1/4$, square law,
$g_{c}/g_{0}\approx 1/2$, $Q\sim 10$, $\Delta f/f_{0}\sim
2-5\%$.  In the very loose coupling limit normally used
for low phase noise quadrature generation,
${\cal I}_{1}\le 0.1{\cal I}_{SS}$,

$$f_{osc}\approx f_{0}= {1\over {2\pi }}{1\over {\sqrt{LC_{t}}}}
\tag{24}$$

quoted as $1/2\pi \sqrt{2LC}$ if $C$ is the single ended
capacitance to ground and $2L$ the differential inductance.
Any explicit tank capacitor $C$ simply adds to $C_{t}$.
If no explicit capacitor is used $C_{t}$ is the
parasitic capacitance at the $X,Y$ nodes,

$$C_{t}\approx C_{L}+{4\over 3}WLC_{ox}+2WC_{ov}+C_{db}+C_{sb}
\tag{25}$$

so that e. {\rm g.} with $C_{db}$ neglected

$$\omega _{0}\approx {1\over {\sqrt{LWLC_{ox}}}}\tag{26}$$

to within a factor $\sim 2$.  Including the usual
$1/2$ for the differential tank the often quoted form is
$f_{osc}\approx 1/2\pi \sqrt{LC_{gs}}$.  The more exact
large signal quadrature frequency is (17), {\rm i.e.}
to ${\cal O}(g_{c}^{2})$

$$f_{Q}\approx {1\over {2\pi }}\sqrt{{1\over {LC_{t}}}
+\left({g_{c}\over {2C_{t}}}\right)^{2}}\mp {g_{c}\over {4\pi C_{t}}}
\tag{27}$$

the $-$ sign being the normally observed stable
quadrature mode for the twist shown.  Changing the twist
interchanges the two signs.  With (4) this can be written
as

$${f_{Q}\over f_{0}}\approx 1\mp {1\over 2}g_{c}\sqrt{L\over C_{t}}
\approx 1\mp {1\over 2Q}\sqrt{{\cal I}_{1}\over {\cal I}_{SS}}
\tag{28}$$

square law, $1\mp ({\cal I}_{1}/2Q{\cal I}_{SS})$ bipolar,
so that for $Q\sim 5-15$ the pulling is normally $<10\%$.
Neglecting the pulling altogether $f_{osc}\approx
1/2\pi\sqrt{LC_{t}}$ is the usual textbook estimate.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It gives the tank resonance and a coupling-induced shift in the required form, Δω ≈ (gc/g0)ω0/(2Q), with the two modes on either side. Its additional gc/(2Ct) expression is part of the derivation and does not undermine the correct estimate.
